statement: In people who smoked cigarettes and were motivated to quit (almost all adults), in 131 randomised and quasi-randomised trials (133 comparisons, 64,640 people; Cochrane review, search to July 2017), being offered nicotine replacement in any form (gum, patch, lozenge or tablet, inhaler, nasal or oral spray, a combination, or a choice of products), compared with a placebo product or no nicotine replacement and the same behavioural support in both groups, increased the number not smoking 6 months or more after the start of the quit attempt: about 6 more people in 100 (162 against 105 in 1,000; risk ratio 1.55, 95% CI 1.49 to 1.61; people lost to follow-up counted as smoking). In the review's table the gain is about 2 more in 100 where the trials gave limited behavioural support (62 against 40 in 1,000) and about 8 more in 100 where they gave intensive support (232 against 150 in 1,000); these baselines are the review's assumed rates, while the risk ratio is the observed pooled result. The risk ratio was similar for gum (1.49, 1.40 to 1.60; 56 comparisons), patch (1.64, 1.53 to 1.75; 51), lozenge or tablet (1.52, 1.32 to 1.74; 8), inhaler (1.90, 1.36 to 2.67; 4) and nasal spray (2.02, 1.49 to 2.73; 4), and higher for oral spray (2.48, 1.24 to 4.94) from one trial of 479 people; these are each product against its own placebo or no-product group, so they do not show which product is better (the head-to-head comparisons are in the claim on ways of using nicotine replacement compared directly). The result held when high-risk trials were left out (1.61, 1.52 to 1.69), in the 12 trials at low risk of bias in every respect (1.53, 1.37 to 1.71) and in placebo-controlled trials (1.61, 1.53 to 1.70), but not clearly in 4 trials in antenatal clinics (1.22, 0.92 to 1.62). Follow-up ran from 6 to 24 months. Two small trials in adolescents did not detect an effect, and the authors say there is little evidence for people who smoke fewer than about 10 to 15 cigarettes a day. They also say that unpublished trials with less favourable results may be missing (the funnel plot is somewhat asymmetric) and that the size of the effect may be smaller than estimated, though in their view not enough to change the results significantly. By the editors' count about three in five of the 136 included studies named a drug company as funder or supplier of study product, and the review did not analyse results by funder. Certainty: high. Status: replicated.
plain: People who wanted to stop smoking were more likely to have stopped 6 months or more later if they were given nicotine gum, patches, lozenges, sprays or inhalers than if they were given a dummy product or nothing: about 16 in 100 against about 10 or 11 in 100, so about 6 more in 100. The gain was about 2 more in 100 where people got little support and about 8 more in 100 where they got a lot. Each kind of product did better than its own comparison group. These were people trying to stop, so the trials do not show what nicotine replacement does for anyone else. Small trials with poor results may be missing, and drug companies paid for many of the trials, so the true gain could be somewhat smaller.
population: People who smoked cigarettes and were motivated to quit, almost all adults (two small trials in adolescents), in clinics, primary care, hospitals, antenatal clinics, community and over-the-counter-like settings; 131 randomised or quasi-randomised trials, 133 comparisons, 64,640 people; Cochrane review, search to July 2017
exposure: Being offered nicotine replacement in any form (gum, patch, lozenge or sublingual tablet, inhaler, nasal spray, oral spray, a combination or a choice of products)
comparator: A placebo product or no nicotine replacement, with the same behavioural support in both groups (the amount of support differed between trials)
outcome: Not smoking 6 months or more after the start of the quit attempt (strictest definition each trial reported, confirmed with a breath or body test in most trials, people lost to follow-up counted as smoking)
magnitude: Abstinence at 6+ months: RR 1.55 (95% CI 1.49–1.61), fixed-effect, I² 39%, 133 comparisons (131 trials), 64,640 participants; the review's table assumes 105 per 1,000 without NRT and gives 162 per 1,000 (156–168) with it (difference 57 per 1,000, about 6 in 100, editors' subtraction). Limited behavioural support 40 vs 62 per 1,000 (60–64; about 2 more in 100); intensive support 150 vs 232 per 1,000 (224–242; about 8 more in 100). By product (RR; comparisons; participants): gum 1.49 (1.40–1.60; 56; 22,581; I² 40%), patch 1.64 (1.53–1.75; 51; 25,754; I² 24%), lozenge or tablet 1.52 (1.32–1.74; 8; 4,439; I² 71%), inhaler 1.90 (1.36–2.67; 4; 976), nasal spray 2.02 (1.49–2.73; 4; 887), oral spray 2.48 (1.24–4.94; 1 trial; 479), choice of product 1.37 (1.25–1.52; 7; 8,288). Sensitivity: without high-risk trials 1.61 (1.52–1.69); the 12 low-risk trials 1.53 (1.37–1.71); biochemically validated trials 1.62 (1.55–1.70); placebo-controlled trials 1.61 (1.53–1.70). Antenatal clinics 1.22 (0.92–1.62; 4 trials; 1,675). Follow-up 6 to 24 months.

publication_bias.note: Funnel plot somewhat asymmetric; about three in five trials with drug-company links (editors' count); not rated down, following the authors' reasoning; a stricter reading would be one level.

grade.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane review with a fixed-effect meta-analysis (AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card); the review rates the main outcome high. Risk of bias, not rated down: most trials were at unclear or high risk of bias (12 of 136 low in every respect, 36 high in at least one, adequate allocation concealment in 39), but the result in the 12 low-risk trials (1.53), in placebo-controlled trials (1.61) and in trials with biochemical confirmation (1.62) is as large as the overall 1.55, so the weaker trials do not appear to be producing the effect. Inconsistency, not rated down: I² 39%; 12 trials had lower quit rates with nicotine replacement than with control, each with an interval that included no difference; the lozenge or tablet subgroup (I² 71%) is driven by one trial. Indirectness, not rated down because the claim is limited to people motivated to quit in trials, ranks no product and says nothing about people who use nicotine without trying to quit. Imprecision, not rated down: 64,640 people and an interval of 1.49 to 1.61. Publication bias, not rated down but recorded: the funnel plot is somewhat asymmetric, the authors say unpublished trials with less favourable results may be missing and that the size of the effect may be smaller than estimated, a study they cite found slightly larger effects in drug-company-funded trials, and by the editors' count about three in five included studies name a drug company as funder or supplier of study product (the review did not analyse by funder). The authors judge that, with so many trials, adding smaller trials with lower ratios would not change the results significantly, and the better-controlled subsets show effects at least as large; the editors follow that reasoning but record that a stricter reading, taking the asymmetry and the company links as probable inflation, would give moderate. The same standard is applied to the vape claims, where the equivalent argument (many trials) is not available. Status replicated: the result comes from many trials by many groups, 12 of which pointed the other way (none with an interval excluding no difference); earlier versions of the same review are not counted as replication.

verification.flag_note: The brief's single claim on nicotine replacement (cl_nic_nrt) is staged as three: this one (against placebo or no replacement, by form), cl_nic_nrt_forms (ways of using it compared head to head, from the 2023 review) and cl_nic_nrt_harms (side effects and serious events), because their certainty differs and one claim carries one rating. Certainty follows Cochrane's high rating; the editors' reservation (funnel asymmetry, company links in about three in five trials, the authors' own wording that the effect may be smaller) is in the grade reasoning, and a stricter reading would be moderate. The baseline rates in the review's table are assumed rates, so the absolute figures are illustrative; the risk ratio is the observed result. Not read: individual trial risk-of-bias tables, Appendix 3 beyond the text, forest and funnel figures (images), reference lists. Overlap of trials between this review and the 2023 review (Theodoulou) was not checked; the two claims answer different questions. Reference records exist (hartmann-boyce_2018); no new reference is needed.

statement: In adults who smoked cigarettes and stopped for more than 18 hours, in prospective studies that compared people's ratings after stopping with their own ratings before (15 core studies of 11 to 178 people, as summarized second-hand in a single-author narrative review that searched 1990 to 2004 and added earlier studies for symptoms left unclear before; Hughes, 2007), stopping is associated with more anger or irritability, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, impatience, restlessness and waking during the night, often with more vivid dreams; in most of these studies these symptoms peaked within the first week and were back at or near the pre-quit level within 2 to 4 weeks (1 week for restlessness in one study). Across all the studies reviewed, including earlier ones, low mood rose in most that measured it but not in all, drowsiness gave contradictory results, and fatigue, headaches, sweating, a racing heart, tremor and skin rash were not found to rise; constipation, cough and mouth ulcers rose in one study each, and dizziness in two, with other studies not finding them. The review gives no sizes or frequencies: it counts studies, and its author chose the results on his own judgment. The 2-to-4-week course is an average: in two studies 38% and 61% of people followed other courses, with symptoms rising again around the third week or not falling, and one later study suggests that recalling withdrawal makes it seem longer than it was. Craving, hunger and weight were outside the review. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When people stop smoking, studies that asked them how they felt before and after found more irritability, anxiety, restlessness, trouble concentrating and waking at night. These were usually worst in the first week and mostly gone within 2 to 4 weeks, but in some people they lasted longer or came back. Tiredness, headaches and sweating did not go up. This comes from one expert's summary of older studies, which counted studies rather than measuring how strong the feelings were.
population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and stopped for more than 18 hours, in prospective studies: placebo or no-treatment arms of cessation trials, people quitting on their own, and people abstaining for a study
exposure: Stopping smoking cigarettes, followed from the first day to up to a year
comparator: The same people's ratings before stopping; a separate control group in 2 of the 15 core studies
outcome: Self-reported withdrawal symptoms (anger or irritability, anxiety, low mood, difficulty concentrating, drowsiness, fatigue, impatience, sleep problems, physical symptoms, restlessness) and how long they last
magnitude: No sizes, rates or intervals: counts of studies as summarized, for example anger lasting 2 weeks in 7 studies, 3 weeks in 1 and 4 weeks or more in 2; fatigue unchanged in 3 of 4 studies; sleep fragmentation increased in studies lasting 5 to 14 days; in two studies 38% and 61% of people did not follow the average course.

risk_of_bias.note: Almost all core studies compare ratings before and after quitting without a control group; outcomes are self-reported; the review did not appraise the studies and they cannot be appraised second-hand.

inconsistency.note: Consistent direction for the core symptoms; low mood and drowsiness are inconsistent and the claim says so.

indirectness.note: Seen only through a single-author narrative review that chose results on judgment (METHODS §6.3: second-hand).

imprecision.note: No estimate is claimed; the statement gives counts and says that sizes and frequencies are unknown.

publication_bias.note: Published studies only; not assessable here; not downgraded further.

grade.reasoning: Prospective within-person studies start low (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1 (before-after comparisons without controls in almost all core studies, self-report, no appraisal) and indirectness −1 (seen only through a narrative review whose author chose the results) give very low. Status replicated: the core symptoms rose in studies by several independent groups (for example Gilbert et al., Jorenby et al., Ward et al. and West et al., besides the author's own), although 5 of the 15 core studies are his group's and low mood is mixed. The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand.

statement: In a nationally representative US survey of 202,248 adults aged 25 or older (113,752 women and 88,496 men, interviewed in 1997 to 2004 and followed through death records for about 7 years on average, to the end of 2006), people who currently smoked cigarettes compared with people who had smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in their lives died at about three times the rate at ages 25 to 79 (adjusted hazard ratio 3.0 in women, 99% CI 2.7 to 3.3; 2.8 in men, 2.4 to 3.1). The ratio was largest for lung cancer (17.8 in women, 14.6 in men) and respiratory disease (8.5 and 9.0), about 3 for ischemic heart disease (3.5 and 3.2) and for stroke in women (3.2), and 1.7 for stroke in men, with an interval from 1.0 to 2.8. The authors estimate that about 6 in 10 of the deaths among people who currently smoked at these ages (62% in women, 60% in men) would have been avoided if their death rates from disease had matched those of people who never smoked. Scaled to US death rates for 2004, they estimate that 38 in 100 women and 26 in 100 men who currently smoked would survive from age 25 to 80, against 70 in 100 women and 61 in 100 men who never smoked, a difference of about 11 and 12 years of life. Compared with people who continued to smoke, people who had stopped gained about 10, 9, 6 and 4 years of life when they stopped at 25 to 34, 35 to 44, 45 to 54 and 55 to 64 years of age (read from survival curves). Those who stopped at 35 to 44 (median 39) still had 1.2 times the death rate of people who never smoked, against 3.0 for people who continued: the authors read this as an excess cut by about 90% and call the remaining excess substantial (about 1 in 6 of such people who died before 80 would not have died at the rate of people who never smoked). These are averages for groups, not what any one person would gain, and they concern cigarette smoking only. Smoking was recorded once, at the interview, so people who stopped afterwards stay in the smoking group; the amount smoked, other tobacco products, vapes and pouches were not examined; adjustment covered age, education, alcohol and body-mass index but not diet, physical activity or income; and the paper does not show the authors' checks of what adjustment, national scaling and leaving out the first two years of follow-up changed. The US Surgeon General's 2014 report, as summarized in its listed conclusions, judges the evidence sufficient to infer that cigarette smoking increases the risk of death from any cause in men and women and that it is the dominant cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and states that cigarette smoking is causally linked to disease in nearly all organs; those listed conclusions give no change in the risk of death or of the main diseases after stopping, apart from a better prognosis for people with cancer and, graded suggestive but not sufficient, a lower risk of advanced age-related macular degeneration. The cohort study was funded by the US National Institutes of Health (Fogarty International Center), the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Gates Foundation's Disease Control Priorities Project; no tobacco-industry funding is printed. Certainty: moderate. Status: single study.
population: US adults aged 25 or older in the National Health Interview Survey, interviewed 1997 to 2004 (113,752 women and 88,496 men analysed; 15,715 deaths to the end of 2006; mean follow-up about 7 years)
exposure: Currently smoking cigarettes at the interview (23,839 women and 23,348 men), counting people who stopped within 5 years before death as still smoking; stopping at 25 to 34, 35 to 44, 45 to 54 or 55 to 64 years of age (medians 29, 39, 49 and 59)
comparator: Having smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in a lifetime (67,524 women and 39,289 men); for stopping, people who continued to smoke
outcome: Death from any cause and from lung cancer, ischemic heart disease, stroke, respiratory disease and other causes at ages 25 to 79; modelled probability of surviving from age 25 to 80; years of life gained by stopping
magnitude: Adjusted hazard ratios (99% CI), current smoking against never smoking, ages 25 to 79, women / men: all causes 3.0 (2.7 to 3.3) / 2.8 (2.4 to 3.1); lung cancer 17.8 (11.4 to 27.8) / 14.6 (9.1 to 23.4); ischemic heart disease 3.5 (2.7 to 4.6) / 3.2 (2.5 to 4.1); stroke 3.2 (2.2 to 4.7) / 1.7 (1.0 to 2.8); respiratory disease 8.5 (6.1 to 11.8) / 9.0 (5.6 to 14.4); all cancers 3.2 (2.6 to 3.9) / 3.8 (3.1 to 4.8). Deaths from any cause in the never-smoked and current groups: 2,190 and 1,579 in women, 1,283 and 2,030 in men; all-cause ratios 3.1 and 2.8 after excluding people who stopped within 5 years before death and people with earlier heart disease, stroke or cancer. Share of deaths among people who currently smoked that would have been avoided at never-smoked disease death rates: 62% (59 to 65) in women and 60% (55 to 63) in men (accidents and injuries, about 7% of the excess, not counted). Probability of surviving from 25 to 80, scaled to 2004 US death rates, never smoked against currently smoking: women 70% (99% CI 64 to 76) against 38% (30 to 45); men 61% (55 to 67) against 26% (18 to 33); gaps of 32 and 35 percentage points (editors' subtraction) and about 11 and 12 years. Stopping against continuing to smoke: about 10, 9, 6 and 4 years of life gained at 25 to 34, 35 to 44, 45 to 54 and 55 to 64 (no intervals given in the text); hazard ratio 1.2 for those who stopped at 35 to 44 against people who never smoked, 3.0 for those who continued (excess of 0.2 against 2.0, about 90% less, editors' arithmetic); excess cut by about two thirds for stopping at 45 to 54.

evidence.locator: Methods › Study Design, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Results › Mortality According to Smoking Status, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: National Health Interview Survey adults interviewed 1997 to 2004 and linked to the National Death Index to 31 December 2006 (match success above 95%): 216,917 aged 25 or older, of whom 14,669 were dropped for a missing variable (9,058 women, 5,611 men), leaving 113,752 women and 88,496 men; mean follow-up 7 years (1.3 million person-years); 15,715 deaths (8,236 in women, 7,479 in men), 10,743 of them at ages 25 to 79. The sampling frame leaves out about 7 million of 226 million US adults (long-term care, prison, active-duty military); Black and Hispanic people are oversampled and weighted back to national proportions.
evidence.source_read: publisher full text (HTML), NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMsa1211128 (Supplementary Appendix and disclosure forms, both PDFs, not opened)

evidence.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Never smoked: fewer than 100 cigarettes in a lifetime. People who had stopped smoking: at least 100 cigarettes in a lifetime and none in the previous 5 years. People who had stopped within 5 years before death were counted as currently smoking, the authors' step against reverse causation. Age-stratified Cox models adjusted for education (3 levels), alcohol (4 levels) and body-mass index (3 levels), weighted to the survey; adding race made no material difference (not presented). Survival from 25 to 80 combines age-specific ratios, smoking prevalence and 2004 US death rates; scaling the survey's death rates up to national rates did not materially change the absolute differences (data not shown).

risk_of_bias.note: The study card rates the cohort 'some concerns' on ROBINS-E: smoking self-reported once at the interview, four adjustment variables, and sensitivity analyses reported as data not shown. None is expected to account for a threefold all-cause ratio, and measuring smoking once, with some people stopping later, pushes the ratios toward 1. Not downgraded.

inconsistency.note: One cohort was read; the authors describe four other studies as giving similar ratios (not read).

indirectness.note: The claim is restricted to the surveyed US adults, to cigarettes and to the outcomes measured. The 2014 report's conclusions are second-hand and are used as context, not for any figure.

imprecision.note: Intervals are narrow for all causes and the main causes; the stroke ratio in men (1.0 to 2.8) and the years-gained figures (no intervals given in the text) are less certain and are worded so.

large_effect.note: All-cause ratio about 3 with a lower limit of 2.4; lung cancer 15 to 18; the all-cause ratios stay at 3.1 and 2.8 after excluding recent quitters and people with earlier heart disease, stroke or cancer. The biases that remain (one baseline measurement, limited adjustment) are not expected to explain a ratio of this size, and the first runs toward 1.

dose_response.note: No ratio by amount smoked is printed in the paper, so no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational (a national survey linked to death records), so it starts low. Upgraded one level for a large effect: the all-cause ratio is about 3 (lower limit 2.4) and the lung cancer ratios are 15 to 18, they stay at 3.1 and 2.8 in the printed sensitivity analysis, and the biases that remain (smoking measured once, which pushes toward 1; four adjustment variables; cause-of-death misclassification, which does not touch the all-cause ratios) are not expected to produce a ratio of this size. Not downgraded for risk of bias (ROBINS-E: some concerns, none likely to account for a threefold ratio); read strictly, without the upgrade, the rating would be low. The rating applies to the all-cause, lung cancer, respiratory and heart disease ratios and to the survival figures; the stroke ratio in men (1.7, interval 1.0 to 2.8), the years of life gained by stopping (read from survival curves, with no intervals given in the text; the all-cause ratios for people who had stopped are in a supplementary table that was not opened) and the 90% figure (measured for one age group) are less certain, taken alone they would be rated low, and the statement words them so. The Surgeon General's 2014 conclusions are second-hand (a narrative review with no stated search) and are used for context only. Status single study because only the survey cohort was read: Jha et al. describe four other prospective studies as giving similar ratios, and reading them could move the status to replicated. The survey is run by a US federal agency and the analysis was funded by public bodies and a charitable foundation; no industry funding is printed (the disclosure forms were not opened).

statement: As described in the US Surgeon General's 2014 report (a narrative review with no stated search method; its figures are second-hand here), the burden of death and disease from tobacco in the United States is overwhelmingly caused by cigarettes and other combusted tobacco products; the report states this as a conclusion about products and does not divide the harm between nicotine and the other substances in smoke. For nicotine on its own, compared with burning tobacco and with no tobacco use, its chapter on nicotine grades six conclusions. Sufficient to infer a causal relationship: nicotine is acutely toxic at high enough doses (drawn from animal studies, medicine trials and poisoning reports, with no systematic dose-response assessment); nicotine activates biological pathways through which smoking raises the risk of disease (experimental research); nicotine exposure in the fetus has lasting adverse effects on brain development (the chapter's support is brief and experimental, with a pointer to a later chapter that was not read; it describes no human study that separates nicotine from the rest of the smoke); and nicotine adversely affects maternal and fetal health in pregnancy, contributing to preterm delivery and stillbirth (inferred from studies of smokeless tobacco in Sweden and India, trials of nicotine replacement in pregnancy and experiments; for example Swedish snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.43, smaller than for smoking (the report's printed figure for smoking is a misprint and is not quoted), and, in a trial of 250 pregnant women, higher birth weight in the nicotine-patch group than in the placebo group, 186 g, 95% CI 35 to 336, with no difference in quit rates, possibly because of less smoking; the chapter reads the studies together as supporting a modest role for nicotine in fetal growth restriction). Outside its graded conclusions, the chapter's summary says animal studies, including in primates, consistently show that nicotine may be the primary mediator of many of the adverse effects of maternal smoking on fetal lung development. Suggestive but not sufficient: nicotine exposure in adolescence may have lasting adverse effects on brain development (smoking in adolescence is linked to lasting cognitive and behavioural problems, but confounding makes cause hard to establish). Inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship: nicotine and cancer (genotoxicity data are mixed; animal studies mostly do not show nicotine alone to cause tumours; the one human follow-up of people who used nicotine replacement long term, a short one, had 75 lung cancers among 3,220 people followed for 7 more years, with no link to replacement use; at least some forms of smokeless tobacco raise the risk of cancers of the mouth, oesophagus and pancreas, by less than smoking and without raising many smoking-related cancers, which the chapter reads as suggesting nicotine may not be a strong tumour promoter in people, while cautioning that oral and inhaled exposure differ). The chapter has no numbered conclusion on the heart (its text says it is likely that nicotine's effects on heart rate, heart contraction, resistance in the coronary vessels and insulin sensitivity contribute to some extent to the cardiovascular risk of people who smoke) or on dependence (it carries earlier reports forward: nicotine is the major chemical in tobacco responsible for dependence, the risk depends on how fast and how much nicotine is delivered, not all forms of nicotine delivery carry the same risk of dependence, nicotine replacement medicines designed to minimise it carry a low risk, and cigarettes have been designed to raise the likelihood of dependence through contents and emissions beyond nicotine). It also reports modest thinking-enhancing effects of acute nicotine in adults who smoke during withdrawal (and, in its evidence summary, in adults who do not smoke), with little known about long-term effects; that authors with industry funding reported positive findings on nicotine and thinking almost exclusively, as cited; that the long-term effects of nicotine, compared with smoking and with no tobacco use, still need study; and that all tobacco products contain toxicants and so carry some health risk. Not measured: the share of smoking's harm that is due to nicotine, and long-term outcomes in people who use nicotine without smoke. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
population: People and laboratory animals exposed to nicotine on its own (as medicine, in smokeless tobacco or in experiments), and people who smoke, as reviewed in the US Surgeon General's 2014 report
exposure: Nicotine on its own, without the other substances in tobacco smoke
comparator: Burning tobacco (cigarette smoke), and no tobacco or nicotine use
outcome: Acute poisoning; disease-related biological pathways; fetal brain and lung development and pregnancy outcomes; adolescent brain development; cancer; heart disease; dependence; each as graded or described by the report
magnitude: No effect size is given for most conclusions. Where cited: Swedish population study 1999 to 2010, snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.43), smaller than for smoking (the smoking figure is printed as 2.27 with an interval of 2.62 to 2.91, a misprint because the estimate lies outside its own interval, so it is not quoted); preterm delivery 27% higher with smoking (Shah and Bracken 2000, as cited), with a rise of similar size for snus in Sweden; trial of nicotine patches in 250 pregnant women: birth weight 186 g higher (35 to 336), no difference in quit rates; Lung Health Study: 5,887 enrolled, 3,220 followed for 7 more years, 75 lung cancers, no link with nicotine replacement use. Grades: sufficient for 4 conclusions, suggestive but not sufficient for 1, inadequate for 1. The report apportions none of the harm between nicotine and smoke.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Toxicokinetics and Acute Toxicity of Nicotine › Acute Toxicity of Nicotine, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (the 3rd follows Table 5.1); Summary, 1st paragraph; Evidence Summary, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Acute toxicity data on nicotine are limited and come from three sources: animal studies, trials of nicotine as a medicine and poisoning reports. The animal studies do not adequately characterize acute toxicity; the medicine trials use amounts chosen, in part, because they are thought to be subtoxic; poisonings are documented, but it appears that the literature has not been assessed systematically for the relation between amount and effect; the commonly quoted human fatal oral amount is poorly documented (the chapter's literature search found no source for it). The Summary says nicotine has known acute toxicity and that poisoning is possible from ingesting nicotine-containing products. No amounts are used in this claim.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure › Reproductive Health Outcomes, 3rd paragraph; Fetal Growth Restriction, 1st paragraph; Preterm Delivery, 1st paragraph; Stillbirth, Perinatal Mortality, and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome, 1st paragraph; Summary, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Inference about nicotine alone in pregnancy comes from studies comparing prenatal smokeless tobacco with prenatal smoking (smokeless products do not expose people to combustion products but all contain nicotine; Swedish snus has lower levels of certain toxicants than conventional smokeless products) and from randomized trials of nicotine therapy in pregnant women. Fetal growth: smokeless tobacco shows only modest contributions to lower birth weight; Swedish population study 1999 to 2010, snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.43), smaller than for smoking (the smoking figure is printed as 2.27 with an interval of 2.62 to 2.91, so it is not quoted); a trial of 250 pregnant women found no difference in quit rates or saliva cotinine between nicotine-patch and placebo arms but a birth weight 186 g higher (35 to 336) in the patch arm, possibly due to less smoking; the chapter reads these as supporting a modest role for nicotine in fetal growth restriction. Preterm delivery: smoking linked to a 27% higher risk (Shah and Bracken 2000, as cited); rises of similar size with snus and with smoking in Sweden. Stillbirth: higher risk with smokeless tobacco in India and Sweden; in the Swedish study the smoking-related stillbirth risk fell markedly when antenatal bleeding and small-for-gestational-age deliveries were excluded while the snus risk stayed the same, which the chapter reads as both involving nicotine, with other factors possibly also contributing in smoking. Summary: the evidence supports the hypothesis that nicotine plays a key role in mediating the adverse effects of smoking on reproductive health, including preterm delivery and stillbirth.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure › Cancer › Genotoxicity, 1st paragraph; Experimental Animal Studies for Carcinogenicity, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Human Studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Summary, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Genotoxicity data are mixed (most studies negative; five positive: two for chromosomal aberration and sister chromatid exchange, and one each for micronuclei, an E. coli mutation assay and the Comet assay in nasal cells; DNA adducts also reported). Animal studies mostly do not show nicotine alone to be tumour-causing (one exception: sarcomas in one mouse strain); nicotine promotes tumours in some models but not those driven by tobacco-specific nitrosamines; the animal findings do not support nicotine as a complete carcinogen. People: very little data; the Lung Health Study is the only source on long-term nicotine replacement (5,887 enrolled, 3,220 followed 7 more years, 75 lung cancers, no link with replacement use; short follow-up); smokeless tobacco raises the risk of cancers of the mouth, oesophagus and pancreas (at least for some forms), less than smoking, and does not raise many smoking-related cancers, which suggests nicotine may not have a strong tumour-promoting effect, tempered by the different route (oral rather than inhaled). Summary: insufficient data to conclude that nicotine causes or contributes to cancer in humans; possible oral, oesophageal and pancreatic risks; substantial experimental evidence that nicotine is active in carcinogenic mechanisms; in vitro data suggestive but not supported overall by the most recent animal studies.

evidence.extracted: Acute nicotine has modest cognition-enhancing effects in adults who smoke during withdrawal (the evidence summary adds adults who do not smoke); a meta-analysis of double-blind placebo-controlled studies (nicotine given mainly as replacement products) found enhancement in 6 of 9 performance domains in people who do not smoke and in people who smoke and had been abstinent for up to 2 hours; less is known about long-term exposure. The chapter reports that a 1997 review found authors acknowledging industry funding reported positive findings on nicotine and cognitive performance almost exclusively while authors without industry funding reported positive and negative findings, that in studies of smoking and Alzheimer's disease the pooled odds ratios without industry funding were neutral or showed higher risk with smoking while industry-affiliated studies showed lower risk, and that industry ties are often not disclosed in articles citing such work. The report calls for information on the risks of long-term nicotine exposure compared with smoking and with no tobacco use at all, says long-term nicotine use may have adverse consequences for those exposed and harms the developing fetus, names cancer, cardiovascular and neurocognitive outcomes as of concern, and states that all tobacco products contain toxicants and so all tobacco product use poses some health risks.

Evidence on nicotine on its own in people is indirect: experiments in animals and cells, trials of medicines, and smokeless tobacco such as snus, which also contains other substances; the one long-term human follow-up of nicotine replacement was short.

statement: As summarized in the US Surgeon General's reports of 2006 and 2014 (narrative reviews that grade their conclusions; the figures are second-hand here, and the 2014 report builds on the 2006 one, so the two are not independent replication), people who do not smoke but breathe other people's tobacco smoke, compared with people who are not exposed, are linked to illness in the authors' graded judgments. In children (2006): sufficient to infer a causal relationship for sudden infant death syndrome, lower respiratory illness in infancy and early childhood (greatest from the mother's smoking), middle ear disease, cough, phlegm, wheeze and breathlessness and ever having asthma at school age, onset of wheeze illnesses in early childhood, lower lung function in childhood, and a small reduction in birth weight; suggestive but not sufficient for preterm delivery, onset of childhood asthma and several childhood cancers; inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship for fertility, spontaneous abortion, congenital malformations, and children's thinking and behaviour. In adults: sufficient for lung cancer in people who never smoked (pooled studies indicate a 20 to 30 percent higher risk from living with a person who smokes) and for coronary heart disease (pooled relative risks indicate a 25 to 30 percent higher risk), and for odour annoyance and nasal irritation; stroke was graded suggestive in 2006 and sufficient in 2014 (an increase of about 20 to 30%); several respiratory symptoms, adult-onset asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and breast cancer were graded suggestive, and others inadequate. The 2014 report adds that smokefree laws were followed by fewer coronary events in people under 65 (sufficient). The parts read give no relative or absolute risks for the children's outcomes or for adult outcomes other than lung cancer, coronary heart disease and stroke. The 2006 report states that there is no risk-free level of exposure to secondhand smoke; its chapter 1 gives no separate derivation or threshold analysis for the statement. By the editors' reading, the nearest reasoning in the part read is toxicological and mechanistic (more than 50 carcinogens in secondhand smoke; raised urinary levels of a tobacco-specific carcinogen's metabolites in people who do not smoke; a clot-promoting effect, harm to the lining of blood vessels and atherosclerosis in animals) together with the raised risks above and the report's statement that adults have immediate adverse effects on the cardiovascular system, while the report adds that the cancer risk is lower than from active smoking because the carcinogen dose is substantially lower and that, from what is known of dose and mechanisms, it anticipates only slightly or modestly raised risks for some associations, such as lung cancer. The report says exposure misclassification and near-universal background exposure may bias estimates toward no effect, that lifestyle differences may bias them the other way, and that uncertainty around pooled estimates may exceed what the statistics show; it also reports industry-linked criticism of the evidence. The chapters that review the evidence disease by disease (chapters 2 to 10 of the 2006 report), where any dose-response or low-exposure data would sit, were not read. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
population: Children and adults who do not smoke and are exposed to other people's tobacco smoke (secondhand smoke), as reviewed in the US Surgeon General's reports of 2006 (evidence to about 2005) and 2014
exposure: Breathing other people's tobacco smoke (secondhand smoke), at home, at work and elsewhere
comparator: People not exposed, or less exposed, to secondhand smoke, as defined in the studies the reports review (not read here)
outcome: Death and disease in children and in adults who do not smoke: sudden infant death, respiratory illness, ear disease, asthma, lung function, birth weight, lung cancer, coronary heart disease and stroke; and whether any level of exposure is without risk
magnitude: 2006 report, as summarized in its chapter 1: pooled studies indicate a 20 to 30 percent increase in the risk of lung cancer from secondhand smoke exposure associated with living with a person who smokes, and a 25 to 30 percent increase in the risk of coronary heart disease; 2014 report: an increase of about 20 to 30% in the risk of stroke. No relative risks, intervals or absolute risks are given in the part read for the children's outcomes or for the other adult outcomes; the size of the fall in coronary events after smokefree laws is not given in the conclusions. Grades by outcome as in the statement (sufficient, suggestive but not sufficient, inadequate). The 'no risk-free level' statement has no figure or threshold in the part read.

evidence.locator: Chapter 1 › Methodologic Issues › Misclassification of Secondhand Smoke Exposure, 3rd to 6th paragraphs; Misclassification of Secondhand Smoke Exposure › Use of Meta-Analysis, 3rd to 6th paragraphs; Confounding, 1st to 4th paragraphs (figure captions not counted)
evidence.extracted: Random misclassification of exposure tends to reduce the apparent effect; classifying some people who currently or formerly smoked as people who never smoked would tend to push the lung cancer association upward when smoking clusters between spouses, but the analyses cited cannot fully explain the observed increase this way; because exposure has been widespread and almost unavoidable there are no truly unexposed persons, so estimates may be biased downward. Meta-analysis is used with the recognition that the uncertainty around pooled estimates may exceed what conventional statistics show, because of biases in or selection of the studies; one analysis of 37 studies suggested that smaller studies gave higher risks, another found little evidence of publication bias, and efforts to find possibly missing studies are said to have yielded little or nothing that would alter published conclusions (the printed sentence is garbled); the pooled results were not decisive for the causal conclusions. Confounding: adults with more exposure tend to have less healthful lifestyles in US and UK surveys (how far this generalizes is uncertain), socioeconomic status may lie on the causal pathway, and confounding matters more as associations get weaker.

grade.reasoning: Findings of observational studies, biomarker and animal studies seen only through two narrative reviews. They start low (METHODS 6.3) and a claim seen only through reviews is downgraded for risk of bias (not appraisable) and indirectness (second-hand; the no-risk-free-level statement is supported only indirectly): very low, the floor. Very low here reflects how the claim is seen, not weak judgments by the reports, which grade many outcomes sufficient to infer a causal relationship. The relation is worded as an association; the causal wording belongs to the reports' own grades, which the statement attributes to them. Status single study: the 2014 report's secondhand smoke conclusions build on the 2006 report, so the two do not count as independent replication. The editors' reading of what the statement on a risk-free level rests on is labelled as theirs. It stays draft because it rests only on narrative reviews (METHODS 6.3 and 12). The 2006 report covers evidence to about 2005; the 2014 report updates stroke and adds smokefree law findings.

statement: In a systematic review without pooling by four authors at the US Food and Drug Administration's Center for Tobacco Products (22 articles from 16 prospective cohorts published before June 2014; seen here only through the review, which has no protocol and does not appraise the bias of the studies), people who currently smoked only cigars, with no history of cigarette or pipe smoking ('primary' cigar smoking), compared with people who never smoked or never used tobacco, were associated with higher death rates from cancers of the mouth, oesophagus, larynx and lung, and slightly higher death rates from all causes and from coronary heart disease. The figures come mainly from two American Cancer Society cohorts, CPS-I (followed 1959 to 1972; 15,191 people who smoked only cigars) and CPS-II (followed 1982 to 1994, men only; 7,888): oral cancer 7.92 (95% CI 5.12 to 11.69) and 4.0 (1.5 to 10.3); oesophageal cancer 3.60 (2.17 to 5.62) and 1.8 (0.9 to 3.7); laryngeal cancer 10.02 (4.01 to 20.64) and 10.3 (2.6 to 41.0); lung cancer 2.1 (1.63 to 2.65) and 5.1 (4.0 to 6.6); all causes 1.08 (1.05 to 1.12) in CPS-I; coronary heart disease 1.05 (1.00 to 1.11) and, in men aged 30 to 74, 1.30 (1.05 to 1.62); bladder cancer and stroke were not clearly raised. Ratios generally rose with the number of cigars a day and with reported inhalation (not for oesophageal cancer in CPS-II). In CPS-I: all causes 1.02, 1.08 and 1.17 for 1 to 2, 3 to 4 and 5 or more cigars a day, and 1.04, 1.19 and 1.60 for no, slight and moderate-to-deep inhalation; lung cancer 0.9 (0.54 to 1.66), 2.36 and 3.4 by the same amounts. In CPS-II: lung cancer 1.3 (0.7 to 2.4) at 1 to 2 and 7.8 (5.9 to 10.3) at 3 or more cigars a day, and 3.3 (2.3 to 4.7) without inhalation against 11.3 (7.9 to 16.1) with it. Among people reporting no inhalation, the ratios for cancers of the mouth, oesophagus and larynx were still raised in CPS-I (6.98, 3.4 and 10.6) but their intervals include 1 in CPS-II (3.2, 1.6 and 4.2). People with an earlier history of cigarette or pipe smoking ('secondary' cigar smoking) had higher ratios for lung cancer (6.29 against 2.1) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (4.39 against 1.42) in CPS-I. Studies that combined cigars and pipes pointed the same way (all causes 1.09 to 1.37 in people with no history of cigarette smoking, each interval starting at 0.98 or higher). The authors describe two other studies of cancer cases, the EPIC cohort and the INHANCE pooled analysis of head and neck cancer, as consistent with these results (not read). The review excludes people who currently smoke cigarettes and tabulates no estimates for them, so it does not show whether cigar smoking is more or less harmful than cigarette smoking, although its authors write that some cigar risks can be as high as or exceed those of cigarette smoking, especially at the highest amounts and levels of inhalation. For scale only, and not as a comparison made by either study: in a separate US survey cohort of 1997 to 2004 (Jha et al.), men who currently smoked cigarettes had 2.8 times the all-cause death rate and 14.6 times the lung cancer death rate of men who had smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in their lives (a different era, adjustment and comparison group from the cigar cohorts). The cohorts began between the 1940s and the 1980s and were largely white men in North America and Europe who smoked large cigars; most estimates are adjusted for age alone; no ratios were pooled; women, non-white people, younger adults and today's cigar products (varied shapes, sizes, tips and filters) are not covered, and studies were often too small to detect effects at the lowest amounts; and the review reports no absolute risks. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
population: People in 16 prospective cohorts enrolled from the 1940s to the 1980s, largely white men in North America and Europe who smoked large cigars; mainly two American Cancer Society cohorts (CPS-I, 15,191 people who smoked only cigars; CPS-II, men only, 7,888)
exposure: Currently smoking cigars only, with no history of cigarette or pipe smoking ('primary'); also with such a history ('secondary'); by cigars a day, self-reported inhalation and years of smoking
comparator: People who never smoked or never used tobacco; people who currently smoke cigarettes are excluded by design and no cigarette estimates are tabulated
outcome: Death from any cause and from cancers of the mouth, oesophagus, larynx, lung, pancreas and bladder, coronary heart disease, stroke, aortic aneurysm and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
magnitude: Primary cigar smoking against never smoking or never using tobacco, mortality ratios (95% CI), CPS-I / CPS-II: all causes 1.08 (1.05 to 1.12; 3,754 deaths) / not tabulated; oral cancer 7.92 (5.12 to 11.69) / 4.0 (1.5 to 10.3); oesophageal 3.60 (2.17 to 5.62) / 1.8 (0.9 to 3.7); laryngeal 10.02 (4.01 to 20.64) / 10.3 (2.6 to 41.0); lung 2.1 (1.63 to 2.65) / 5.1 (4.0 to 6.6); pancreatic 1.62 (1.22 to 2.11) / 1.3 (0.9 to 1.9); bladder 1.38 (0.89 to 2.04) / 1.0 (0.4 to 2.3); coronary heart disease 1.05 (1.00 to 1.11) / 1.30 (1.05 to 1.62) in men 30 to 74 and 0.93 (0.72 to 1.21) at 75 and over; stroke 0.96 (0.87 to 1.06) in CPS-I; aortic aneurysm 1.76 (1.29 to 2.35) in CPS-I; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 1.42 (0.96 to 2.03) in CPS-I. By cigars a day (1 to 2 / 3 to 4 / 5 or more), CPS-I: all causes 1.02 / 1.08 / 1.17; oral cancer 2.12 / 8.51 / 15.94; lung 0.9 / 2.36 / 3.4; CPS-II (1 to 2 / 3 or more): lung 1.3 / 7.8, oesophageal 1.8 / 1.9 (no gradient). By inhalation (none / slight / moderate-to-deep), CPS-I: all causes 1.04 / 1.19 / 1.60; lung 1.97 / 1.89 / 4.93; CPS-II (none / any): lung 3.3 / 11.3. Reporting no inhalation, CPS-I / CPS-II: oral 6.98 (4.13 to 11.03) / 3.2 (0.9 to 11.0); oesophageal 3.4 (1.90 to 5.61) / 1.6 (0.7 to 4.1); laryngeal 10.6 (3.87 to 23.07) / 4.2 (0.5 to 37.1). Secondary cigar smoking, CPS-I: lung 6.29 (5.01 to 7.79); chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 4.39 (3.02 to 6.16). Duration, CPS-II lung: 2.1 (1.0 to 4.2) under 25 years, 5.9 (4.5 to 7.7) at 25 or more. No absolute risks and no estimate for people who smoke cigarettes in the review. Separate cohort, for scale only: men who currently smoked cigarettes against men who smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes, all causes 2.8 (99% CI 2.4 to 3.1), lung cancer 14.6 (9.1 to 23.4) (Jha et al.).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors prioritize primary cigar smoking in the larger cohorts. Outcomes significantly associated with primary cigar smoking in one or both CPS cohorts: all causes, oral, oesophageal, pancreatic, laryngeal and lung cancers, coronary heart disease and aortic aneurysm; dose trends for the four cancers; raised risks of oral, oesophageal and laryngeal cancer with no inhalation, particularly in CPS-I, which they say is consistent with cigar smoke being inhaled regardless of self-report (one cited study); raised but mostly non-significant ratios at 1 to 2 cigars a day for those three cancers and aortic aneurysm. In CPS-I the risks were considerably higher for secondary than for primary cigar smoking for lung cancer (6.29 against 2.1) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (4.39 against 1.42), which they say could be due to different inhalation and could also be explained by lung damage from earlier cigarette smoking.

evidence.locator: Background, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: As cited by the review and not re-read: the International Agency for Research on Cancer concluded in 2004 that cigar and/or pipe smoking causes cancers of the lung and upper aerodigestive tract and found evidence that it is causally associated with cancers of the pancreas, stomach and bladder. In the EPIC cohort (incident cancers, median follow-up 9 years), 1,451 people had smoked only cigars (74% currently, 26% formerly); among those currently smoking only cigars the hazard ratio was 3.9 for lung cancer and 3.5 for upper aerodigestive tract cancer, the hazard ratio for any tobacco-related cancer was 1.6 and a significantly raised risk of any tobacco-related cancer was still seen when no inhalation was reported (the review gives no figure for it), and the combined risk of lung, upper aerodigestive tract and bladder cancers rose with cigars a day and was raised across small, medium and large cigars. In an INHANCE pooled analysis of 19 studies (13,935 cases and 18,691 controls), people who never smoked cigarettes but ever smoked cigars had an odds ratio of 2.54 (95% CI 1.93 to 3.34) for head and neck cancer, rising with frequency and duration, while the ratio was not raised among people who had ever smoked cigarettes.

evidence.extracted: Limits the authors state: studies largely of white men in North America and Europe who smoked cigars in the 1960s or earlier; the large cigar predominates, unlike today's market; limited data for stomach, colorectal and liver cancer; studies often underpowered at the lowest exposures. They call for contemporary cohorts with women, non-white people and younger adults, with detail on cigar type, number a day, inhalation, years of smoking and biomarkers. Not stated by the authors but visible in the tables: most estimates are adjusted for age alone, and the tables contain mismatches in cohort labels, cause-of-death codes and citations (listed on the study card).

evidence.extracted: The authors conclude that cigar smoking carries many of the same health risks as cigarette smoking, that risks vary with cigars a day and inhalation, and that some risks can be as high as or exceed those of cigarette smoking (the main-text conclusions add that this holds especially at the highest amounts and levels of inhalation; the abstract does not). The review tabulates no estimates for people who smoke cigarettes and excludes them by design, so this is not a result shown by its tables.

risk_of_bias.note: The review is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 on the study card (no protocol, no appraisal of the bias of the studies, no use of bias in interpretation, no pooling); the studies mostly adjust for age alone, rely on self-reported cigarette history and inhalation, and the tables contain cohort, code and citation mismatches.

inconsistency.note: The four cancers point the same way in every cohort that reports them; size differs between CPS-I and CPS-II (lung 2.1 against 5.1; oesophageal 3.60 against 1.8, not significant), which the review does not explain; both figures are given. Small cohorts disagree for all causes (Whitehall 0.48, 9 deaths) and heart disease; those outcomes are labelled less certain.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: the primary studies were not read. The cohorts are older, largely men and mostly large cigars, and the claim is restricted to them. A comparison with cigarette smoking is not made by the review.

imprecision.note: Intervals are wide for single outcomes, low amounts and no inhalation (several include 1) and are reported; the headline cancers are clearly raised in both large cohorts, so not rated down.

large_effect.note: Ratios of 4 to 10 for mouth and larynx cancer and 5.1 for lung cancer in CPS-II, adjusted for age, alcohol and smokeless tobacco, stay large. Misreported earlier cigarette smoking would inflate the ratios and is a remaining bias that runs away from the null, so this upgrade is applied with care (see the reasoning).

dose_response.note: Ratios rise with cigars a day, inhalation and (CPS-II) years of smoking for the four cancers, in both cohorts.

grade.reasoning: Observational cohorts seen only through a systematic review without pooling, so the claim starts low. Downgraded once for risk of bias (the review is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2, the studies are mostly adjusted for age alone, cigarette history and inhalation are self-reported, and the tables have mismatches) and once for indirectness (second-hand; old cohorts of largely men smoking large cigars). Upgraded for a large effect (several ratios of 4 to 10 for mouth and larynx cancer and 5 for lung cancer, still large in the model adjusted for alcohol and smokeless tobacco) and for a dose-response gradient (cigars a day, inhalation and years of smoking for the four cancers), the upgrades being applied to evidence already rated down for risk of bias; a strict reading, without the upgrades, would give very low, and the gap between the two is the possibility that people who reported never smoking cigarettes had in fact smoked them, which would inflate the ratios and which the dose gradients argue against but do not exclude. The rating applies to the cancers; the all-cause ratio (1.08), coronary heart disease (1.05 and 1.30), the no-inhalation ratios, the low-amount ratios and the juxtaposed cigarette figures are less certain and, taken alone, would be rated very low. Status replicated for the cancers: besides the two American Cancer Society cohorts, which share a research programme and are not independent of each other, the Dorn study, the Swedish census cohort and the Copenhagen City Heart Study give ratios in the same direction for lung cancer, and the Dorn study for mouth and larynx cancer (their estimates are for current cigar smoking whatever the earlier cigarette history, so earlier cigarette smoking can inflate them). The review's authors work for the regulator of tobacco products and declare no competing interests; no funding statement is printed. The claim does not say that cigars are more or less harmful than cigarettes, which the review does not test.

statement: In Swedish men who had never smoked, snus use compared with using no tobacco is associated with a higher rate of death from any cause in the largest pooled cohort analysis read here (eight cohorts, 169,103 men, 10,928 deaths, about 17 years of follow-up on average, editors' calculation): adjusted for age and body mass index only, the hazard ratio for men who used snus and no other tobacco was 1.28 (95% CI 1.20–1.35), for cardiovascular deaths 1.27 (1.15–1.41), for cancer deaths 1.12 (1.00–1.26) and for deaths from other causes 1.37 (1.24–1.52) (Byhamre et al., 2021; funded by a university department, Swedish regional authorities and a medical society; no conflicts declared). The paper prints deaths by group but no rates per person-year, and the groups differed (men who used snus were younger, mean age 29 against 38, and more often in the highest alcohol tertile, 37.9% against 20.2%), so the ratios cannot be turned into a number out of 100. The ratio rose with years of use (1.08 under 5 years, 1.29 at 15 years or more) but not clearly with weekly amount; it was 1.42 (1.21–1.66) without the construction-worker cohort, which supplied 87% of the deaths in the snus group (editors' arithmetic); and the cardiovascular ratio was 1.13 (0.93–1.38) with follow-up capped at 10 years, which the authors say calls for caution. For cancers, an independent systematic review of 15 studies that left out work linked to the tobacco industry (Valen et al., 2023; no funding statement on the page; no conflicts declared) gave, in its summary table and per 100,000 men (the snus figure being the no-tobacco figure with the hazard ratio applied), oesophageal squamous cell cancer 16 with no tobacco and 55 with snus (HR 3.5, 1.6–7.6; one cohort, 10 exposed cases), pancreatic cancer at 27 years 72 and 151 (RR 2.1, 1.2–3.3; 18 exposed cases), and cancer deaths 2,141 and 2,395, which is 2.1 and 2.4 in 100 men (editors' conversion; the row comes from Byhamre et al.), with raised ratios also for non-cardia stomach cancer (HR 1.4, 1.1–1.9) and rectal cancer (1.38, 1.07–1.77). Its authors rated these moderate certainty for the oesophagus and for the pancreas at 27 years and low for the others; the pancreatic ratio was 1.07 (0.77–1.50) in a pooled analysis over 36 years (very low), the rectal ratio 1.10 (0.91–1.34) with longer follow-up, and oral cancer (0.93, 0.59–1.44), lung cancer (0.8, 0.4–1.3) and colon cancer (1.08, 0.91–1.29) showed no clear difference. A narrative review supported by Swedish Match, a snus maker, and written by a long-term consultant to the tobacco industry (Lee, 2013) concluded that adverse health effects of snus have not been clearly identified and that any cancer risk is at most minimal and much less than that of smoking; it pooled heart attack in never-smoking Swedish men to RR 1.07 (0.98–1.16), or 1.00 (0.91–1.10) without one 1971–74 estimate, while its own results also show fatal heart attack 1.31 (1.09–1.58) against non-fatal 0.89 (0.79–1.00), heart failure up to 2.08 (1.03–4.22), and poorer survival after a cancer diagnosis in men who used snus only (1.13, 1.05–1.20), though less so than in men who smoked only (1.21, 1.17–1.25). IARC (2012) judged smokeless tobacco as a class carcinogenic to humans (Group 1: oral cavity, oesophagus, pancreas) without separating products, and notes that Swedish snus is made with extra controls on nitrosamines and that four northern-European studies of oral cancer found no overall association. A 2026 systematic review without meta-analysis, rated critically low confidence by the editors (Kopa-Stojak & Pawliczak, 2026), describes pooled heart attack, stroke, atrial fibrillation and pancreatic cancer estimates near 1 (1.04, 1.04, 1.07, 0.96) beside fatal heart attack 1.28 (1.06–1.55) and heart failure 2.08 (1.03–4.22). Against smoking the sources give little: Byhamre et al. left out men who had ever regularly smoked; Valen et al. report cancer estimates higher for smoking than for snus at most sites in the same studies, with overlapping intervals except for lung (Figure 4, not read as numbers), and say it is not known how far switching from smoking to snus reduces the benefit of stopping all tobacco; no source read compares the overall death rate of men who use snus with that of people who smoke, and the figure of no more than 1% of the effects of smoking in Lee's Discussion comes from his 2011 review, which was not read. These sources overlap heavily (the Swedish construction-worker cohort sits inside most estimates), tobacco use was recorded once at the start, women are almost absent, few men were followed beyond 70, and none of these studies can show that snus caused the differences. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: In large studies of Swedish men who had never smoked, using snus was linked to a death rate 28% higher than in men who used no tobacco, once age and weight were allowed for (hazard ratio 1.28; 1.27 for deaths from heart and blood-vessel disease). Over the years studied, 2.1 in 100 men who used no tobacco died of cancer; with the snus ratio applied, that becomes about 2.4 in 100. Cancers of the gullet (oesophagus) and pancreas were rare but more frequent in men who used snus: for the gullet, about 55 in 100,000 against 16 in 100,000 men who used no tobacco. Mouth and lung cancer showed no clear difference, and some results shrank with longer follow-up. A review supported by a snus maker concluded that harm has not been clearly identified; independent studies found the raised figures above. These studies cannot show that snus caused the differences, nearly all the men were Swedish, men who used snus drank more alcohol, and no study read measured how snus compares with smoking in deaths overall; for cancers, the figures for smoking were higher at most sites.
population: Men in Sweden who had never smoked, in cohorts recruited from the 1970s to 2010 (one dominant construction-worker cohort), with Norwegian cohort data in IARC's review, and in reviews of such studies; no data on women beyond one lymphoma estimate
exposure: Using snus (moist smokeless tobacco as made in Sweden), recorded once at the start of each study; mostly snus with no other tobacco
comparator: Men who never used any tobacco (the main comparison in every study read); men who formerly used snus; men who smoked (indirect, from the few comparisons within the same studies)
outcome: Death from any cause, from cardiovascular disease and from cancer; cancers of the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas and rectum; heart attack and heart failure; survival after a cancer diagnosis; and what IARC concludes for smokeless tobacco as a class
magnitude: Byhamre et al. 2021 (eight Swedish cohorts; never-smoking men; 124,256 never used tobacco, 39,156 current snus only, 5,691 former snus only; adjusted for attained age and body mass index): current snus only against never used, all-cause HR 1.28 (1.20–1.35; 1,410 deaths against 9,272), cardiovascular 1.27 (1.15–1.41; 443 against 3,444), cancer 1.12 (1.00–1.26; 332 against 2,660), other causes 1.37 (1.24–1.52; 511 against 2,098) (the groups differ in age, so death counts are not comparable between them; no absolute rates are printed); former snus only: all-cause 1.15 (1.02–1.31), cancer 1.26 (1.01–1.57), cardiovascular 1.13 (0.91–1.41), other causes 1.14 (0.89–1.45). By years of use, all-cause under 5 years 1.08 (0.88–1.32), 5–9 1.17 (1.00–1.36), 10–14 1.31 (1.12–1.52), 15 or more 1.29 (1.20–1.38), p for trend 0.001; by weekly amount 1.28, 1.17, 1.37, p for trend 0.09. Sensitivity: without the Construction Worker Cohort 1.42 (1.21–1.66), cardiovascular 1.39 (1.05–1.84), cancer 1.52 (1.15–1.99); follow-up capped at 10 years 1.34 (1.21–1.48), cardiovascular 1.13 (0.93–1.38); extra adjustment for education, alcohol and physical activity in six cohorts (158 snus-group deaths) 1.46 (1.22–1.75). Valen et al. 2023 (snus only against no tobacco; absolute risks per 100,000 men over each study's follow-up as in the review's table, no tobacco then snus, the snus figure being the no-tobacco figure with the hazard ratio applied): oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 16 then 55, HR 3.5 (1.6–7.6), moderate; pancreas at 27 years 72 then 151, RR 2.1 (1.2–3.3 in the table, 1.2–3.6 in the text), moderate, and HR 1.07 (0.77–1.50) at 36 years, very low; non-cardia stomach 237 then 332, HR 1.4 (1.1–1.9), low; rectum 339 then 468, HR 1.38 (1.07–1.77), low, and 1.10 (0.91–1.34) with longer follow-up; cancer deaths 2,141 then 2,395 (2.1 then 2.4 in 100 men, editors' conversion), HR 1.12 (1.00–1.26), low; oral cancer 0.93 (0.59–1.44), very low; lung RR 0.8 (0.4–1.3); colon HR 1.08 (0.91–1.29); all melanoma incidence rate ratio 0.65 (0.52–0.82). After a cancer diagnosis in construction workers: total mortality HR 1.13 (1.05–1.20), cancer death 1.15 (1.05–1.26). Lee 2013 (never-smoking Swedish men): heart attack or ischaemic heart disease, 13 estimates pooled, fixed-effect RR 1.07 (0.98–1.16), 1.00 (0.91–1.10) without the 1971–74 estimate; fatal heart attack 1.31 (1.09–1.58), non-fatal 0.89 (0.79–1.00); heart failure 1.28 (1.00–1.64; 75 exposed cases) and 2.08 (1.03–4.22; 14 cases); survival after a cancer diagnosis, all-cause RR 1.13 (1.05–1.20) snus only, 1.21 (1.17–1.25) smoking only, 1.17 (1.12–1.22) both; cancer-specific 1.15 (1.05–1.26) against 1.15 (1.10–1.21). IARC 2012: smokeless tobacco Group 1; northern-Europe oral cancer pooled 1.0 (0.7–1.3); Swedish oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma RR 3.5 (1.6–7.6); pancreas Norway 1.67 (1.12–2.50; 45 cases; 0.85, 0.24–3.07, in people who never smoked) and Swedish construction workers 2.1 (1.2–3.6; 18 cases), pooled 1.8 (1.3–2.5). Kopa-Stojak 2026 (as described, from primary analyses): heart attack 1.04 (0.93–1.17); fatal heart attack 1.28 (1.06–1.55); stroke 1.04 (0.92–1.17), death after stroke 1.32 (1.08–1.61); atrial fibrillation 1.07 (0.97–1.19); heart failure 2.08 (1.03–4.22) and 1.28 (1.00–1.64); cardiovascular death 1.70 (1.01–2.87) in people who used snus and never used tobacco; pancreatic cancer 0.96 (0.83–1.11) pooled against 2.0 (1.2–3.3) in one cohort; rectal cancer 1.40 (1.09–1.79).

evidence.extracted: Eight Swedish cohorts (recruited 1978 to 2010), men only, anyone who had ever regularly smoked cigarettes excluded: 169,103 men, 2,857,312 person-years (about 17 years each, editors' calculation), 10,928 deaths. 124,256 men (73.5%) had never used tobacco and 39,156 (23%) currently used snus and no other tobacco; 5,691 had formerly used snus and no other tobacco (in the cohorts that recorded former use). evidence.extracted: Leaving out the Construction Worker Cohort raised the all-cause, cardiovascular and cancer ratios for current snus use against never use of tobacco: all-cause 1.42 (1.21–1.66), cardiovascular 1.39 (1.05–1.84), cancer 1.52 (1.15–1.99); the other-cause ratio was 1.34 (0.97–1.86), against 1.37 in the full analysis, and its interval now includes 1. That cohort supplied 87% of the deaths in the current snus group (1,233 of 1,410) and 66% of those in the never-used group (6,116 of 9,272) (editors' arithmetic from Tables 3 and 4). Follow-up capped at 10 years: all-cause 1.34 (1.21–1.48), cancer 1.24 (1.02–1.52), other causes 1.57 (1.35–1.83), but cardiovascular 1.13 (0.93–1.38), no longer distinguishable from no difference; the authors say the cardiovascular result should be read with caution because of this inconsistency. Extra adjustment for education, alcohol and physical activity in six cohorts (158 snus-group deaths): all-cause 1.46 (1.22–1.75), cardiovascular 1.56 (1.14–2.14), cancer 1.51 (1.12–2.03), other causes 1.20 (0.83–1.72).

evidence.locator: Table 2; Discussion, 4th to 7th, 8th and 10th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The current snus group was younger (mean age 29 against 38 years), drank more (37.9% in the highest alcohol tertile against 20.2%) and more often had 10 to 12 years of education (52.6% against 38.7%) than men who never used tobacco (the alcohol and education percentages are within the cohorts that recorded them, which leaves out the Construction Workers Cohort); body mass index was similar (24.1 against 24.6). The authors name residual confounding and a single baseline measurement of exposure as weaknesses, and describe their findings as supporting an association, with public-health relevance if it is causal. Their suggested explanations (nicotine effects on blood vessels and heart rhythm, tumour promotion, poorer cancer survival, alcohol-linked injury and violence, risk-taking) were not tested in these data.
