risk_of_bias.note: Byhamre et al. (card sc_byhamre_2021: ROBINS-E overall high): the main model adjusts for age and body mass index only, tobacco use was recorded once, and the snus group was younger and drank more, so residual confounding could change the ratios materially. Valen et al. rated all 15 of their studies moderate risk of bias, mostly for the validity of exposure information; Lee (2013) and IARC (2012) are narrative reviews and Lee's is industry-supported (editors' checklist, cards sc_lee_2013 and sc_iarc_2012). Counted once for the confounding problem.

inconsistency.note: The sources read the same cohorts differently: Lee concludes adverse effects have not been clearly identified, while the independent review and IARC find raised cancer estimates. Within the data, estimates fall with longer follow-up (pancreas 2.1 at 27 years, 1.07 at 36 years; rectum 1.38, 1.10; cardiovascular 1.27, 1.13 at a 10-year cap), and heart attack incidence (1.04–1.07) differs from fatal heart attack (1.28–1.31). Part is explained by the dominant cohort and part is not.

indirectness.note: Men only, almost all Swedish, in one dominant occupational cohort recruited from the 1970s with tobacco use measured once; snus made before 1983 differs from later products and from snus elsewhere (IARC); the comparison with smoking is indirect (no cohort read compares death rates of men who use only snus with men who smoke; Byhamre et al. left out men who had smoked regularly).

imprecision.note: All-cause and cancer-death ratios are precise (10,928 deaths), but the site-specific cancer estimates rest on 10 to 73 exposed cases with wide intervals (oesophagus 3.5, 1.6–7.6; oral 0.93, 0.59–1.44) and the absolute risks are the review's, per 100,000 men, with the snus figure derived from the no-tobacco figure.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources. The independent review excluded industry-linked studies by design, which is stated; the industry-supported review is read beside it.

large_effect.note: The oesophageal ratio (3.5) rests on 10 exposed cases in one cohort and the all-cause ratio (1.28) is not large; no upgrade.

dose_response.note: The all-cause ratio rises with years of use (p for trend 0.001) but not clearly with weekly amount (p for trend 0.09; cardiovascular highest in the lightest group); years of use also follows age and cohort; no upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: Men who used snus drank more alcohol, so residual confounding would more plausibly raise than lower the ratios; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is downgraded one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor, so very low. Rated as worded: an association in never-smoking men, snus only against no tobacco; whether it is causal is a separate and unresolved question. The ratings in the Valen et al. review (moderate for the oesophagus and for the pancreas at 27 years, low for stomach, rectum and cancer deaths, very low for most others) are its authors' judgments from a different starting point and are reported, not adopted. Overlapping reports are counted once: the Swedish construction-worker cohort sits inside Byhamre et al., Valen et al., Lee, IARC and Kopa-Stojak, Valen et al.'s mortality row is the Byhamre analysis, and the survival-after-cancer result in Lee and in Valen et al. is the same study, so the agreement between them is not independent replication and the status is contested, not replicated.

debate.question: Does using snus make men who never smoked more likely to die, or to get certain cancers, than men who use no tobacco, and how large is any difference compared with smoking?
debate.evidence_yes: The largest pooled cohort analysis (Byhamre et al., 2021; 169,103 never-smoking Swedish men, 10,928 deaths; funded by a university department, Swedish regional authorities and a medical society; no conflicts declared) found that men who used snus only died at a rate 28% higher than men who never used tobacco (HR 1.28, 1.20–1.35), with the ratio rising with years of use (1.08, 0.88–1.32, under 5 years; 1.29, 1.20–1.38, at 15 years or more; p for trend 0.001) and staying raised in the sensitivity analyses (1.42 without the largest cohort; 1.46 with extra adjustment for education, alcohol and physical activity in six cohorts; 1.34 with follow-up capped at 10 years); former snus use was also linked to a higher rate (1.15, 1.02–1.31). An independent systematic review that left out tobacco-industry-linked studies (Valen et al., 2023; no conflicts declared, no funding statement on the page) rated the evidence moderate certainty that snus raises the risk of oesophageal and pancreatic cancer (HR 3.5, 1.6–7.6; RR 2.1, 1.2–3.3) and low for stomach and rectal cancer and for cancer deaths, and reported poorer survival after a cancer diagnosis (1.13, 1.05–1.20). IARC (2012) found sufficient evidence that smokeless tobacco as a class causes cancers of the oral cavity, oesophagus and pancreas, and weighed the same Swedish oesophageal (3.5) and pancreatic (2.1) findings with a Norwegian pancreatic cohort at 1.67 (1.12–2.50). Even the industry-supported review's own results show fatal heart attack 1.31 (1.09–1.58) with non-fatal 0.89, heart failure up to 2.08 (1.03–4.22) and poorer survival after a cancer diagnosis; the 2026 systematic review lists fatal heart attack 1.28 (1.06–1.55) and cardiovascular death 1.70 (1.01–2.87) in people who used snus and never used any tobacco.
debate.evidence_no: The industry-supported narrative review (Lee, 2013; supported by Swedish Match, a snus maker, with earlier reviews supported by Philip Morris Products and the European Smokeless Tobacco Council; the author is a long-term consultant to the tobacco industry and the paper says the sponsor was not involved) concludes that adverse health effects have not been clearly identified and that any cancer risk is at most minimal and far below that of smoking; it pools heart attack in never-smoking men to 1.07 (0.98–1.16), or 1.00 (0.91–1.10) leaving out one 1971–74 estimate, and lists cancers of the oropharynx, oesophagus, stomach and lung as unassociated. Parts of the independent evidence also point to a small or null effect: four northern-European oral-cancer studies found no overall association (IARC; pooled 1.0, 0.7–1.3); only one of four northern-European oesophageal studies was significant; Valen et al. found no clear difference for oral (0.93, 0.59–1.44), lung (0.8, 0.4–1.3) or colon cancer, a pooled pancreatic ratio of 1.07 (0.77–1.50) at 36 years and a rectal ratio of 1.10 (0.91–1.34) with longer follow-up; Byhamre et al. found the cardiovascular ratio no longer different from 1 with follow-up capped at 10 years (1.13, 0.93–1.38), and describe an association whose public-health relevance holds only if it is causal. The 2026 systematic review lists pooled heart attack (1.04), stroke (1.04), atrial fibrillation (1.07) and pancreatic cancer (0.96, 0.83–1.11) near no difference, though the editors rate its confidence critically low and its abstract reads several of these null results as increases.
debate.neither_can_show: Whether snus causes any of the differences: tobacco use was recorded once at the start, men who used snus drank more (37.9% in the highest alcohol tertile against 20.2%) and were younger, the main model adjusted for age and body mass index only, 13.2% of never-smoking men who used snus against 6.7% of men who never used tobacco had a later record showing smoking in one study, and about 30% of men using snus only may later stop or move to smoking (a Swedish study cited by Valen et al.). Whether the findings hold for women (one lymphoma estimate, no cases), young people, men over 70, other countries or today's products; Swedish snus made before 1983 was fermented and differs from later products (IARC). How the overall death rate of men who use snus compares with that of people who smoke: no source read measures it, and the figure of no more than 1% of the effects of smoking comes from a 2011 review that was not read. How far the sources are independent: the Swedish construction-worker cohort supplies most of the deaths in Byhamre et al. (87% in the snus group), most participants in Valen et al.'s pooled analyses (two thirds, and 72% of pancreatic cases) and several of the estimates in the other three, and Valen et al.'s mortality row is the Byhamre analysis, so agreement between them is not independent replication. The industry-supported review and the independent ones draw largely on the same cohorts, so many of their differences come from how the same data are read, not from different data.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). From the sources read: in Swedish men who never smoked, the largest pooled analysis finds a death rate 28% higher in men who used snus only than in men who never used tobacco, and an independent systematic review finds more oesophageal and pancreatic cancer in single cohorts (moderate certainty by its authors) and probably more stomach and rectal cancer and cancer deaths (low); other estimates, such as oral and lung cancer, show no clear difference. The sources agree on more than their headlines suggest: Lee and Valen et al. both judge the cancer risk of snus to be below that of smoking, both report the same poorer survival after a cancer diagnosis in construction workers who used snus (1.13), and the industry-supported review's own results include a raised fatal heart attack figure. They differ on the cancers: Lee concludes that adverse effects have not been clearly identified, while IARC (a verdict on smokeless tobacco as a class) and Valen et al. judge a cancer hazard probable, and the pancreatic estimate fell from 2.1 at 27 years to 1.07 in a 36-year pooled analysis whose follow-up runs to 2013, after the search dates of both Lee and IARC. The strongest argument for a raised risk is the consistency of the all-cause ratio across sensitivity analyses (1.28 to 1.46) and its rise with years of use; the strongest against is that the cancer-site results rest on few cases from one cohort and shrink with longer follow-up, that confounding is possible, and that the sources overlap. The editors give no number for how snus compares with smoking in deaths overall, because none of the sources read measures it. Both halves belong together: for cancers, the estimates in these studies are lower for snus than for smoking, and they are not zero.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Cohorts that measure tobacco use repeatedly over decades, adjust fully (alcohol, education, diet, early-life factors), include women and younger and older men, and report absolute rates for men who use snus only, men who smoke, men who used both and men who used neither, so that the comparison with smoking can be read directly; analyses outside the construction-worker cohort with enough cases for the oesophagus and pancreas (10 and 18 exposed cases in the main estimates), and follow-up beyond 36 years; designs that handle confounding, such as comparisons of siblings or of men who stopped; and a pre-specified systematic review that includes industry-supported and independent studies and appraises both with the same tool. None of the sources read reports these.

statement: Nicotine pouches (tobacco-free oral pouches) have been measured in laboratories and surveys far more than in people. Laboratory analyses found nicotine in all the products sold as containing it, in very different amounts, and tobacco-specific nitrosamines absent or in small amounts, well below the amounts reported for snus. An independent German government laboratory (Mallock et al., 2024; intramural funding, no competing interests declared) analysed one pouch of each of 46 products from 20 producers bought online in 2021 (a convenience sample): the 44 that contained nicotine held 1.79 to 47.5 mg per pouch (median 9.48), and the nitrosamine NNN was found in 24 of them (9 below the quantification limit), at most 12.9 ng per pouch; the authors set this beside up to 1,190 ng NNN per pouch of snus and 33 to 323 ng per cigarette in smoke, figures from other studies on other bases. A study designed, interpreted and written by Swedish Match, maker of ZYN pouches and General snus, whose four authors are its employees (Back et al., 2023), found no nitrosamine above its quantification limit (0.01 µg/g, roughly 4 to 8 ng per pouch by the editors' arithmetic) in two ZYN variants, one batch each, against NNN 0.44 and NNK 0.19 µg/g in General snus in the same study, and quantified 4 or 5 of 43 compounds (nicotine included) in ZYN against 19 in snus. A 2026 scoping review (Travis et al., 2026) lists three further analyses: 1.41 to 8.11 mg per pouch in 70 US products, 6.4 against 12.3 mg in tobacco-based pouches in 50, and 2.20 to 56 mg in 31 sold in Germany, with measured nicotine generally at or below the label. In surveys, use is low but rising. In the US, current use among young people in 2024 was 1.8 in 100 (National Youth Tobacco Survey, middle and high school; 0.8 in 100 in 2021) and 2.6 in 100 (Monitoring the Future, grades 10 and 12; 1.3 in 100 in 2023; most also vaped), but 0.2 in 100 among 12- to 17-year-olds in the PATH study in 2022–23; among adults in 2022–23 it was 0.4 to 0.8 in 100; elsewhere current use ranged from 0.4 in 100 (adults in England, 2023) to 19 in 100 (youth and adults in Australia, 2023), from surveys of different kinds. Use was more likely in males, younger people and people who currently or formerly smoked, vaped or used smokeless tobacco; US sales rose from 327 to 1,046 million units between July 2021 and May 2024. In people, pouches have been followed for 6 months at most. A 2026 systematic review without meta-analysis (Kopa-Stojak & Pawliczak, 2026; critically low confidence by the editors) found 15 pouch studies, none following disease or death. In a non-industry-funded German crossover study of adults who smoked daily (as described by the scoping review), a 30 mg pouch gave more nicotine than a cigarette and 20 mg and 6 mg pouches less, and the 20 mg and 30 mg pouches raised systolic blood pressure and arterial stiffness comparably to a cigarette; industry-funded series found 4 mg and 8 mg pouches below a cigarette and, in people who used snus, pouches giving more nicotine than snus, and nicotine peaked later with pouches (20 to 42 minutes) than with a cigarette (5 to 7). In a small US survey sample, nicotine breakdown products in people who used only pouches were comparable to those in people who smoked, with lower cadmium and uranium; in a 4-week trial, nitrosamine levels were not lowered in people who cut their cigarettes with pouches. Oral findings were compared in small studies: oral lesions in 79 in 100 young Swedish adults who used pouches against 89 in 100 who used snus (a cross-sectional comparison of 126 and 63 people), and less gum inflammation after 24 weeks in an Altria-funded trial of adults who switched from smoking to pouches than in those who kept smoking. The scoping review's authors say the health effects remain largely understudied, that evidence of short-term benefit from switching is limited and mainly industry-funded, and that pouches may be a less hazardous alternative to traditional tobacco but are not risk-free. No source read follows heart disease, cancer, lung disease or death in people who use pouches, or compares them with people who use no nicotine on any health outcome; the product analyses read come from Germany, the United States and a few other countries, and the independent one bought its products in 2021. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (the contents and survey findings).
plain: Nicotine pouches have been measured in laboratories and surveys far more than in people. A German government laboratory tested 46 pouch products and found nicotine in widely different amounts and small amounts of one family of cancer-linked chemicals (nitrosamines) in 26 of the 44 that held nicotine, far below the amounts reported for snus; a test paid for by the maker of ZYN found none above the lowest amount it could measure in its own pouches. In US surveys in 2024, between 1.8 and 2.6 in 100 school-age young people said they currently used pouches (in one survey most also vaped), and fewer than 1 in 100 adults did in 2022–23. In people, pouches have been followed for 6 months at most and no study read has followed illness or death, so nobody yet knows how they compare with snus, with smoking or with using no nicotine for health. Small studies show that pouches deliver nicotine more slowly than a cigarette, in amounts that vary with the pouch, from less to more than a cigarette. The authors of the latest review say pouches may be less hazardous than traditional tobacco but are not risk-free.
population: Tobacco-free nicotine pouches on sale in Germany (46 products bought online in 2021), the United States and other countries; people who use them in national surveys (US youth and adults 2021 to 2024, other countries), crossover studies of 30 to 42 adults and small trials of 30 to 100 adults; a 2026 scoping review of 135 studies to September 2025
exposure: Nicotine pouches: measured product contents; use as reported in surveys; short-term effects in single sessions up to 6 months of follow-up
comparator: Snus; cigarettes; nicotine gum and lozenges; people who use no nicotine (the last not compared on any health outcome in the sources read)
outcome: Measured nicotine, nitrosamine and other constituents; how many people use pouches and who they are; short-term nicotine uptake, blood pressure, arterial stiffness and biomarkers; health outcomes in people (none beyond 6 months, none for disease or death)
magnitude: Mallock et al. 2024 (46 products, 20 producers, bought online January–May 2021; 44 with nicotine, 2 nicotine-free): nicotine 1.79–47.5 mg per pouch, median 9.48 (interquartile range 5.50–16.6), two above 40 mg; median extract pH 8.8 (range 5.5–10.5); printed milligram content on 15 of 44, a score or word on 38, none on 4; tobacco-specific nitrosamines found in 26 of 44: NNN in 24 (9 below the quantification limit of about 0.4 ng), NNK in 3, NAT in 6, NAB in 5; highest per pouch NNN 12.9 ng, NNK 5.4, NAT 2.7, NAB 5.6 (one pouch per product, single analysis); for comparison the authors cite up to 1,190 ng NNN and 120 ng NNK per pouch of snus, 2 ng NNN per gram of nicotine gum and 33–323 ng NNN and 40–246 ng NNK per cigarette in smoke (other studies, other bases). Back et al. 2023 (Swedish Match; 7 products, one batch each): nitrosamines none of ten above quantification limits (0.01 µg/g for NNN, NNK, NAT, NAB) in two ZYN variants and two nicotine replacement products; General snus NNN 0.44, NNK 0.19 µg/g; moist snuff NNN 3.63 and 2.53, NNK 2.27 and 0.92; compounds quantified (nicotine included) of 43: lozenge 2, ZYN moist 4, ZYN dry 5, gum 9, snus 19, moist snuff 26 and 27; ZYN dry and moist formaldehyde 10.3 and 1.5, chromium 0.160 and 0.099, ammonia 62 and 66 µg/g, nickel 0.067 in the dry variant only; total nicotine mg/g ZYN dry 7.63, ZYN moist 12.00, snus 8.13, lozenge 3.20, gum 1.30. Travis et al. 2026 as described (135 studies to September 2025; no risk-of-bias assessment): US 70 tobacco-free products 1.41–8.11 mg per pouch; 50 pouches 6.4 (SD 3.5) against 12.3 (SD 8.2) mg in tobacco-based pouches, free-base share 63.4% against 47.2%; 31 pouches in Germany 2.20–56 mg. US youth current use: National Youth Tobacco Survey (middle and high school) 0.8% (2021) to 1.8% (2024), lifetime 1.9% to 3.5%; Monitoring the Future (grades 10 and 12) 1.3% (2023) to 2.6% (2024), lifetime 3% to 5.4%; PATH ages 12–17 (2022–23) lifetime 0.9%, current 0.2%; of adolescents currently using in 2024, 29% frequent and 22% daily. US adults 2022–23: PATH lifetime 3.3%, current 0.8%; TUS-CPS 2.7% and 0.4%. Other countries, lifetime (current): British youth 2024 3.3% (1.2%); Quebec adolescents 3.7% (2.6%); Australia 2023 26% (19%); Finland 2022 14.4% (3.7%); Poland adults 2024 9.2% (4.3%); Canadian college students 2024 27% (12%); England adults 2023 current 0.4%. Nicotine uptake: independent German crossover 30 mg > cigarette > 20 mg > 6 mg (peak and total over 4 hours; time to peak 5 minutes for the cigarette, 20 minutes for the 6 mg pouch); industry series 4 mg and 8 mg below a cigarette, 12 mg and 8 mg mini comparable or higher, time to peak 35–40 minutes against 5–7; in adults using snus, 6, 9 and 11.2 mg pouches gave higher peak and 60-minute nicotine than 11.2 mg snus. 20 mg and 30 mg pouches raised systolic pressure and arterial stiffness comparably to a cigarette. Sales 327 million units (July 2021) to 1,046 million (May 2024). Kopa-Stojak 2026: 15 pouch studies, longest follow-up 6 months, none on disease or death; crossover trials of 30–42 adults; a 6-month online cohort (n = 1,863 at start) quitting odds 1.29 (1.04–1.59) for fruit-flavoured and 1.04 (0.82–1.28) for mint-flavoured pouches; Saudi surveys without comparison groups (for example bloating 66.7%, difficulty breathing 40.5%).

evidence.extracted: Nicotine uptake: in a non-industry-funded five-arm randomized study of pouches sold in Germany, in adults who smoked daily, a 30 mg pouch gave the highest peak and total nicotine over 4 hours, then a cigarette, then 20 mg and 6 mg pouches (time to peak 5 minutes for the cigarette, 20 minutes for the 6 mg pouch); in adults who used smokeless tobacco daily, 8 mg pouches delivered comparable or more nicotine than smokeless tobacco after 30 minutes of use; in industry-funded series, 4 mg and 8 mg pouches gave lower peak and total nicotine than a cigarette and 12 mg and 8 mg mini-size pouches comparable or higher, with time to peak 35 to 40 minutes against 5 to 7 for a cigarette; in adults who used Swedish snus (a study the review lists under industry-funded here, but under non-industry-funded in its ratings section), peak and 60-minute nicotine from 6, 9 and 11.2 mg pouches were higher than from 11.2 mg snus (twice as high for the 11.2 mg pouch), and pouches delivered nicotine slightly faster than snus and nicotine gum. Four of eight new pharmacokinetic trials were industry-funded (British American Tobacco, Japan Tobacco International). The abstract says uptake from pouches of 6 mg or more typically exceeds that from cigarettes, which the 6 mg result in this section does not show; the Discussion gives 6 mg or more for the earlier review's studies and 8 mg or more for this update.

risk_of_bias.note: The product analyses are samples of convenience or chosen by a maker (46 products bought online in Germany in 2021; 7 products, 2 pouch variants, picked and supplied by the funder), one pouch per product in a single analysis, with nitrosamine results of at most 12.9 ng per pouch and many below the quantification limit (cards sc_mallock_2024 and sc_back_2023, overall high on the worst-domain rule). The scoping review made no risk-of-bias assessment (AMSTAR 2 critically low), and the systematic review is critically low confidence. Industry funding is reported as printed and the findings are set beside independent ones, not dropped.

inconsistency.note: The figures differ for known reasons (different products, markets, populations and quantification limits) and agree in direction: nitrosamines low or absent in both the independent and the maker's analyses, nicotine content varying widely, use low and rising. The uptake studies differ with strength, as expected.

indirectness.note: Product content is not health; the human measures are short sessions or weeks and mostly seen through two reviews; the products were bought in 2021 to 2025 in a few countries; the independent analysis compares with snus and cigarettes using other studies' figures on other bases; no source read compares pouches with using no nicotine on any health outcome.

imprecision.note: Wide ranges (nicotine 1.41 to 56 mg per pouch across studies) show variation between products, not imprecision of an estimate; surveys are large; trial effects are not part of this claim.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources. 12 of the 73 new studies in the scoping review are industry-funded and are set beside the others; the maker's analysis and the independent one agree in direction.

large_effect.note: Descriptive claim; not upgraded for large effect (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Nicotine uptake rose with pouch strength in the crossover studies, but that is a pharmacokinetic finding, not a health effect; no upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: Not applicable to a description of contents and prevalence.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive evidence starts low like other observational evidence and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. The claim is worded as a description of measurements (contents, prevalence, short-term measures) and of what has not been measured (disease or death, anything beyond 6 months), not as an effect of pouches on health, so it is rated as worded and not upgraded for a large effect. Status replicated applies to the contents and survey findings, shown by independent laboratories and surveys that agree in direction (the independent German laboratory, the maker's laboratory and the analyses described by the scoping review; US national surveys); it does not apply to health effects, for which there is no evidence beyond short studies. Overlapping reports are counted once: the systematic review and the scoping review share some primary studies (for example two crossover trials and the oral-health trial), the systematic review cites both laboratory papers read here and the scoping review cites neither.

statement: In people who smoked and were motivated to quit, in randomised and quasi-randomised trials comparing ways of using nicotine replacement (Cochrane review, search to April 2022; 16 trials with 12,169 people for combination use, 8 trials with 3,319 people for fast-acting forms against the patch), combination nicotine replacement (a patch plus a fast-acting form such as gum, lozenge, inhaler or nasal spray), compared with a single form, increased the number not smoking 6 months or more after the start of the quit attempt: about 4 more people in 100 (174 against 137 in 1,000, 95% CI 160 to 187; risk ratio 1.27, 1.17 to 1.37; I² 12%; people lost to follow-up counted as smoking). The ratio was similar against the patch alone (1.24, 1.13 to 1.37; 13 trials) and against a fast-acting form alone (1.30, 1.09 to 1.54; 6 trials); a third subgroup, one trial in which most people were lost to follow-up, gave a much larger ratio (5.16, 1.18 to 22.59). It was unchanged without the trials at high risk of bias, and a funnel plot of the 16 trials showed no sign of publication bias, which the authors read with caution because the number is small. A fast-acting form alone (lozenge, nasal spray, gum or inhaler), compared with the patch, showed no clear difference: 148 against 164 in 1,000, about 2 fewer in 100 with fast-acting forms (interval 4 fewer to 1 more; risk ratio 0.90, 0.77 to 1.05; I² 0%; 8 trials, one of them in adolescents; unchanged without the high-risk trials or the adolescent trial), with no clear difference for any single form (lozenge 0.94, 3 trials; nasal spray 0.90, 2 trials; gum 0.58, 2 trials and 118 people; inhaler 0.59, 1 trial and 222 people), so the interval does not rule out the patch doing somewhat better. People in these trials smoked about 20 or more cigarettes a day on average, so the results say little about lighter smoking; the review's comparisons of doses, lengths of use and timing, which gave mixed results, are not covered here. By the editors' count 9 of the 16 combination trials and 6 of the 8 fast-acting-against-patch trials named a manufacturer as funder, sponsor, supplier of product or employer of authors; the review judged company funding less relevant to comparisons between ways of using nicotine replacement and did not assess it. Certainty: high. Status: replicated.
plain: When trials compared ways of using nicotine replacement, people who used a patch plus a fast-acting form, such as gum or lozenges, did better than people who used one form alone: about 17 in 100 were not smoking 6 months or more later, against about 14 in 100, so about 4 more in 100. A fast-acting form on its own and the patch showed no clear difference, though the trials cannot rule out the patch doing a little better (about 2 fewer in 100 with fast-acting forms; the range runs from 4 fewer to 1 more). Many of the trials were backed by the makers of the products, and the review did not check whether that changed the results.
population: People who smoked and were motivated to quit, mostly smoking about 20 or more cigarettes a day, in randomised and quasi-randomised trials of ways of using nicotine replacement (68 trials, 43,327 people in the review; 16 trials, 12,169 people for combination use; 8 trials, 3,319 people for fast-acting forms against the patch); Cochrane review, search to April 2022
exposure: Combination nicotine replacement (a patch plus a fast-acting form: gum, lozenge, inhaler or nasal spray); a fast-acting form alone
comparator: A single form of nicotine replacement (patch alone, or a fast-acting form alone); for the fast-acting forms, the nicotine patch
outcome: Not smoking 6 months or more after the start of the quit attempt (strictest definition, people lost to follow-up counted as smoking)
magnitude: Combination vs single form: RR 1.27 (95% CI 1.17–1.37), I² 12%, 16 studies, 12,169 participants; 137 vs 174 per 1,000 (160–187), about 4 more in 100 (editors' subtraction: 37 per 1,000). Against patch alone 1.24 (1.13–1.37; 13 studies; 9,552; I² 28%); against a fast-acting form alone 1.30 (1.09–1.54; 6; 2,364; I² 0%); against a choice of single form 5.16 (1.18–22.59; 1 study; 253; high risk of bias). Fast-acting form vs patch: RR 0.90 (0.77–1.05), I² 0%, 8 studies, 3,319 participants; 164 vs 148 per 1,000 (126–172), about 2 fewer in 100 (interval 4 fewer to 1 more, editors' subtraction). By form: lozenge 0.94 (0.79–1.12; 3; 1,707), nasal spray 0.90 (0.64–1.27; 2; 1,272), gum 0.58 (0.26–1.31; 2; 118), inhaler 0.59 (0.22–1.60; 1; 222).

grade.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane review (AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card) whose two pools used here the review rates high. Risk of bias, not rated down: 9 of 68 trials were low risk in every domain and 28 high in at least one, but the review reports that restricting each pool to low-risk trials gave a consistent estimate and that removing high-risk trials changed the interpretation only for the timing comparison, which is outside this claim. Inconsistency, not rated down (I² 12% for combination use, 0% for fast-acting forms against the patch). Indirectness, not rated down: the claim is limited to people motivated to quit who smoked about 20 or more cigarettes a day in trials. Imprecision, not rated down: the combination interval (1.17 to 1.37) is far from no difference; the fast-acting-against-patch result is reported as no clear difference with its whole interval (0.77 to 1.05), which does not exclude a quit rate about a fifth lower with fast-acting forms, and the claim says so; the review's high rating rests on 3,319 people. Publication bias, not rated down: the funnel plot for combination use (16 trials) shows no asymmetry, though the authors caution that 16 is few, and the fast-acting-against-patch pool has too few trials for a funnel plot. The editors record that a manufacturer is linked to 9 of 16 combination trials and 6 of 8 fast-acting-against-patch trials (editors' count), that the review did not assess this, and that a stricter reading, taking company-linked trials as a possible source of inflation, would give moderate. Status replicated: the combination result is pooled from 16 trials by many groups with little heterogeneity. The 2018 review of nicotine replacement against control and this review may share trials (not checked); this claim rests on this review alone.

statement: In people who smoked and joined trials of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking, chest pain or palpitations were reported more often with nicotine replacement than with placebo or no replacement: 2.5% against 1.4% (about 1 more in 100; odds ratio 1.88, 95% CI 1.37 to 2.57; the 15 trials that reported them, 11,074 people, including trials outside the review's main analysis; Cochrane review, search to July 2017). That review did not pool other side effects, because the trials reported them too differently, and lists them by form: with gum, hiccups, stomach upset, jaw pain and tooth or mouth problems; with the patch, skin irritation (up to 54% of people in one source it cites, usually mild); with the inhaler and sprays, irritation of the mouth, throat or nose, cough and runny nose; with sublingual tablets, hiccups, mouth burning, sore throat, cough, dry lips and mouth ulcers. Serious events were not pooled against placebo or no replacement: a patch trial in people with cardiovascular disease and six trials in pregnancy did not detect more serious events with nicotine replacement. In a later review comparing ways of using nicotine replacement (68 trials; search to April 2022), serious events were too few to compare (combination against a single form: 3 against 1 in 1,000, interval 1 to 18, seven events in total; risk ratio 4.44, 0.76 to 25.85; 5 trials, 2,888 people; low certainty), and more people stopped treatment because of side effects with fast-acting forms than with the patch (23 against 5 in 1,000; risk ratio 4.23, 1.54 to 11.63; 3 trials, 1,482 people; very low certainty), including 3.0% with a nasal spray against 0.9% with the patch in one trial of 922 people. All of this comes from treatment lasting weeks to months in people motivated to quit, so it cannot show how often rare serious events happen or what longer use does. Certainty: low (for the chest pain or palpitations result; the later review's figures carry its own lower ratings, and the lists of local effects are not graded). Status: mixed.
plain: In trials of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking, side effects were mostly local, depending on the form: skin irritation with patches, and effects in the mouth, throat or nose with gum, lozenges, sprays and inhalers. Chest pain or palpitations were reported by about 2.5 in 100 people given nicotine replacement and about 1.4 in 100 given a dummy product or nothing. Serious health events were too few and too unevenly reported to say whether nicotine replacement changes them. More people stopped treatment because of side effects with fast-acting forms than with the patch (about 23 in 1,000 against 5 in 1,000). All of this comes from weeks to months of use.

magnitude: Chest pain or palpitations: OR 1.88 (95% CI 1.37–2.57), 15 trials, 11,074 participants; 2.5% with NRT vs 1.4% with control (about 1 more in 100, editors' subtraction). Serious adverse events, combination vs single form: RR 4.44 (0.76–25.85), 5 trials, 2,888 participants; 1 vs 3 per 1,000 (1–18); seven events in total; low certainty. Withdrawals due to treatment: combination vs single form RR 1.12 (0.57–2.20; 5 trials; 3,070; I² 73%; 12 vs 14 per 1,000; very low); fast-acting form vs patch RR 4.23 (1.54–11.63; 3 trials; 1,482; 5 vs 23 per 1,000, 8–63; very low); nasal spray vs patch RR 3.47 (1.15–10.46; 1 trial; 922; 3.0% vs 0.9%). Serious events, fast-acting form vs patch: 3 of 4 trials (1,252 participants) had none; the fourth RR 1.75 (0.52–5.92; 642); very low certainty.

risk_of_bias.note: Side effects defined and collected differently across trials; only 15 of 136 trials reported chest pain or palpitations; many trials unblinded.

grade.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high; the rating is for the main finding, chest pain or palpitations, and the other figures in the statement are labelled with the lower ratings the 2023 review gave them. Risk of bias, one level: side effects were not defined, timed or collected in a common way (the 2018 review did not pool them because of extensive variation in reporting), the chest pain or palpitations result comes from the 15 trials that reported them out of 136, 43 trials had no matched placebo, and in the 2023 review two of the four or three trials behind the serious-event and withdrawal rows were at high risk of bias. Imprecision, one level: by the editors' arithmetic from the percentages, assuming equal group sizes, the chest pain or palpitations result has about 200 events, fewer than the 300 usually wanted, and serious events were so few (seven in the combination comparison) that the 2023 review took two levels. Inconsistency, not rated down for the main finding; the withdrawal figure for combination use has I² 73% and is labelled very low. Indirectness, not rated down: the claim is limited to what trials of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking recorded. An earlier meta-analysis of this outcome (12 studies, OR 2.06) overlaps these trials and is not counted as independent replication. Status mixed because most harm outcomes were too variably reported to pool, not because trials disagreed about chest pain or palpitations. The claim does not use figures from the cited network meta-analysis (not checked) or the 2023 review's comparisons of doses and timing, which are on that review's study card.

verification.flag_note: Harms are staged apart from cl_nic_nrt because the evidence is weaker (the 2018 review did not rate or pool them; the 2023 review rated serious events low and withdrawals very low). Left on the study cards only: higher-dose patch withdrawals and serious events, palpitations with early (pre-quit) use. The 2023 plain language summary says nicotine replacement is safe to use on the strength of the 2018 review; this claim does not repeat that wording, because the 2018 review did not pool serious events and found chest pain or palpitations at 2.5% against 1.4% (see the Theodoulou card). statement: In adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials of nicotine vapes (80 trials, 29,861 people in the Cochrane living review, searched to 1 January 2026; 11 trials with 4,114 people compared with nicotine replacement and 7 trials with 1,918 people compared with vapes without nicotine; the trial supplied the vape in most), being given a nicotine vape, compared with nicotine replacement, increased the number not smoking at 6 months or longer: about 4 more people in 100 (10 against 6 in 100, interval 7 to 13; risk ratio 1.61, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.12; I² 55%); and, compared with a vape without nicotine, by about 2 more in 100 (8 against 6 in 100, interval 6 to 10; risk ratio 1.34, 1.05 to 1.69; I² 0%) (analysed as allocated, with people lost to follow-up counted as smoking). The 6 in 100 is the review's assumed quit rate with limited behavioural support, not the trials' observed rate; the risk ratios are the pooled results. Leaving out the one industry-funded trial in each comparison gave 1.72 (1.23 to 2.39) against nicotine replacement and 1.28 (1.01 to 1.64) against vapes without nicotine, and leaving out high-risk trials gave 1.74 (1.30 to 2.34) and 1.40 (1.09 to 1.81). The review rates the comparison with nicotine replacement high certainty; the editors rate it moderate, because I² is above the 50% mark the review itself calls substantial, its funnel plot is asymmetric (which the authors say could reflect unpublished small trials) and the pool has only 11 trials. How long people kept vaping could not be pooled against nicotine replacement (5 trials, I² 95%): at 6 months or longer more people in the vape group than in the nicotine replacement group were still using their allocated product in 3 trials, and there was no difference in 2. In the five trials that reported product patterns, more people in the vape groups were vaping without smoking (risk ratio 4.40, 1.27 to 15.28; I² 78%; 2,776 people), fewer were using neither cigarettes nor a vape (0.49, 0.26 to 0.91), and possibly fewer were smoking without vaping (0.76, 0.58 to 1.01, an interval that includes no difference; 4 trials; I² 83%); the review's text gives no absolute counts for these, and they are less certain than the quit rates. All participants were adults, follow-up for quitting was 6 months or longer, the trials used regulated nicotine vapes, and the review says longer-term effects are unknown. Of the 80 trials, 8 had tobacco or vaping industry support, and six review authors are authors of included trials (who state they took no part in the inclusion or risk-of-bias decisions for those trials). Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials, adults who were given a vape with nicotine were more likely to be not smoking 6 months or more later than adults given nicotine patches, gum or similar: about 10 in 100 against about 6 in 100. They also did a little better than adults given a vape without nicotine: about 8 in 100 against about 6 in 100. At the end, in 3 of 5 trials, more people given vapes were still using them than people given nicotine replacement were still using theirs. These were adults in trials where the vape was handed out, and people were followed for 6 months or more; what happens after that is not known.
population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials of nicotine vapes (80 trials, 29,861 people in the review; 11 trials, 4,114 people against nicotine replacement; 7 trials, 1,918 people against vapes without nicotine); the vape was supplied by the trial in most; Cochrane living review, search to 1 January 2026
exposure: Being given a nicotine vape (cartridge, refillable, pod or disposable devices)
comparator: Nicotine replacement therapy (patch, gum, lozenge or combinations); a vape without nicotine
outcome: Not smoking at 6 months or longer (strictest definition, biochemically confirmed where possible, people lost to follow-up counted as smoking); still using the allocated product, vaping or smoking at that point
magnitude: Cessation at 6+ months. Vs NRT: RR 1.61 (95% CI 1.23–2.12), I² 55%, 11 trials, 4,114 participants; 6 per 100 (assumed) vs 10 per 100 (7–13), about 4 more in 100 (1–7), editors' subtraction; Cochrane high, editors moderate. Vs non-nicotine vape: RR 1.34 (1.05–1.69), I² 0%, 7 trials, 1,918 participants; 6 per 100 (assumed) vs 8 per 100 (6–10), about 2 more in 100 (0–4); moderate. Sensitivity: vs NRT without the industry-funded trial 1.72 (1.23–2.39), without the 2 high-risk trials 1.74 (1.30–2.34); vs non-nicotine without the industry-funded trial 1.28 (1.01–1.64), without the high-risk trial 1.40 (1.09–1.81). Use afterwards vs NRT (not graded): allocated product still in use at 6+ months not pooled (5 trials, I² 95%); vaping without smoking RR 4.40 (1.27–15.28; I² 78%; 2,776); neither vaping nor smoking RR 0.49 (0.26–0.91; I² 31%; 2,776); smoking without vaping RR 0.76 (0.58–1.01; I² 83%; 4 trials; 2,543).

grade.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane living review (random-effects with Hartung-Knapp intervals; AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card). The claim carries the rating of its weakest link. For the comparison with vapes without nicotine the review itself gives moderate (one level for imprecision: fewer than 300 quits; not downgraded for risk of bias, as the one high-risk trial removed gives a larger estimate). For the comparison with nicotine replacement the review gives high, with no downgrade; the editors give moderate, for these reasons: I² is 55%, above the 50% line the review's own Methods call substantial (the review downgraded the adverse-event outcome of the same comparison for I² 72%); the pool's funnel plot is asymmetric, which the Discussion says may reflect publication bias or differences between trials; and with 11 trials the argument the 2018 nicotine replacement authors rely on (so many trials that smaller ones would not change the result) is not available. The editors did not add a second level, because the estimate is unchanged without the industry-funded trial or the high-risk trials and its interval stays well above no difference. The claim is therefore moderate on either route and the senior author may keep the review's high for the comparison with nicotine replacement. Risk of bias, not rated down: 6 of the 11 trials against nicotine replacement were low risk and 2 high; people could not be blinded to vape against patch or gum, but quitting was assessed with biochemical confirmation where possible. Indirectness, not rated down: the claim is limited to adults in trials with trial-supplied, regulated vapes. The use-afterwards figures (product patterns, continued use) are not graded by the review, are heterogeneous (I² 95%, 78%, 83%) and have absolute counts only in figures that were not read; the editors regard them as low certainty and the statement labels them as less certain. One industry-funded trial sits in each pool (Russell 2021, Caponnetto 2013); results hold without them. Status replicated: the comparison with nicotine replacement and the comparison with vapes without nicotine each rest on several trials from different groups and countries; some groups contributed more than one trial and six review authors are authors of included trials. The review is a living review: later updates will change the numbers.

verification.flag_note: Staged as three claims instead of the brief's one: this one (nicotine vape against nicotine replacement and against vapes without nicotine, with how long people kept vaping), cl_nic_vapes_stopping_support (against support only or no support, low certainty) and cl_nic_vapes_harms (side effects and serious events), so that each keeps its own rating; the senior author may merge them. Certainty differs from Cochrane for the comparison with nicotine replacement (review: high; editors: moderate, reasons in the grade reasoning); the claim reads moderate either way because the non-nicotine comparison is moderate. The absolute quit rates in the review's tables are built from an assumed baseline, not observed rates. Absolute numbers still vaping or smoking at 6 months are not in the text (forest plots are images and were not read), so the use-afterwards figures are relative only. This is the sixth update of a living review: re-check at the next one. Not read: supplementary materials, forest and funnel figures, trial reports. Review authors with ties: six are authors of included trials and state they took no part in rating them (declarations on the card). No new reference is needed (lindson_2026 exists).

statement: In adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials (11 trials, 7,214 people; Cochrane living review, searched to 1 January 2026), being given a nicotine vape, compared with behavioural support only or no support, was followed by more people not smoking at 6 months or longer: about 4 more in 100 (9 against 5 in 100, interval 7 to 11; risk ratio 1.75, 95% CI 1.39 to 2.20; I² 13%; analysed as allocated, with people lost to follow-up counted as smoking). The 5 in 100 is the review's assumed quit rate with limited support, not the trials' observed rate. The review rates this low certainty, because the trials could not be blinded and the vape groups had more support than the comparison groups, so part of the gap may come from the extra support rather than the vape; its funnel plot is also asymmetric. Leaving out the one industry-funded trial (JUUL Labs) gave 1.53 (1.30 to 1.79). Being advised to use a vape without being given one showed no clear difference from no such advice (risk ratio 1.02, 0.88 to 1.19; 2 trials, 2,652 people; not graded by the review). Follow-up for quitting was 6 months or longer, all participants were adults, and the review says longer-term effects are unknown. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: When adults who smoked were given a vape with nicotine, more of them were not smoking 6 months or more later than adults given counselling only or nothing: about 9 in 100 against 5 in 100. But the trials could not hide who got the vape, and the vape groups usually got more support too, so the real gap could be smaller. Advising people to vape, without giving them a vape, made no clear difference.
population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials of nicotine vapes in which the comparison group got behavioural support only or no support (11 trials, 7,214 people; Cochrane living review, search to 1 January 2026); two further trials of advice to use a vape (2,652 people)
exposure: Being given a nicotine vape (refillable in five trials, cartridge in three, pod in three), alone or with the trial's support
comparator: Behavioural support only, or no support (brief advice or nothing)
outcome: Not smoking at 6 months or longer (strictest definition, biochemically confirmed where possible, people lost to follow-up counted as smoking)
magnitude: Cessation at 6+ months vs behavioural support only or no support: RR 1.75 (95% CI 1.39–2.20), I² 13%, 11 trials, 7,214 participants; 5 per 100 (assumed) vs 9 per 100 (7–11), about 4 more in 100 (2–6), editors' subtraction; low certainty. Without the industry-funded trial (Xu 2023) 1.53 (1.30–1.79). Advice to use a vape without supplying one vs no advice: RR 1.02 (0.88–1.19), I² 0%, 2 trials, 2,652 participants; unchanged without the high-risk trial; not graded.

grade.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane living review (AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card). Risk of bias, two levels, as the review rates it: the trials could not be blinded and the vape groups received more support than the comparison groups, so some of the difference may come from the extra contact rather than the vape; of the 80 trials in the review 41 were at high risk of bias, and the one trial in this pool with low risk overall gives only a very imprecise result on its own. Inconsistency, not rated down (I² 13%). Indirectness, not rated down: the claim is limited to adults in trials where the vape was supplied. Imprecision, not rated down: 7,214 people and an interval from 1.39 to 2.20. Publication bias, not rated down: the pool's funnel plot is asymmetric (11 trials; the authors say not diagnostic), which the editors do not count as a further level because small unblinded trials that favour the vape are the same worry as the risk-of-bias rating; counting it would give very low. The result holds without the one industry-funded trial (JUUL Labs). The advice-only comparison is not graded by the review; it rests on two trials (one in people who already vaped, one high risk) and its interval (0.88 to 1.19) allows both a modest benefit and a modest harm, so it supports no more than no clear difference. Status replicated: 11 trials by different groups give the same direction with little heterogeneity; the review is a living review and later updates will change the numbers.

verification.flag_note: Staged apart from cl_nic_vapes_stopping so that the weaker comparison keeps its own rating (low, as Cochrane gives it). Relation is-associated-with (not a causal verb) because the certainty is low and the arms differed in support. The advice-only result is placed here because its comparator is no advice; the review does not grade it. The 5 in 100 baseline is an assumed rate. The funnel asymmetry is noted but not counted as an extra level (see the grade reasoning): a stricter reading would be very low. Not read: supplementary materials, forest and funnel figures, trial reports. Living review: re-check at the next update.

statement: In adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials of nicotine vapes (Cochrane living review, searched to 1 January 2026; follow-up from 1 week to about 2 years), the evidence is insufficient to say whether a nicotine vape, compared with nicotine replacement or with a vape without nicotine, changes the risk of serious or other adverse events: no clear difference was seen, but events were few. Serious adverse events: 7 against 6 in 100 with a vape against nicotine replacement (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI −0.01 to 0.02; 10 trials, 4,045 people; moderate certainty) and 2 against 2 in 100 against a vape without nicotine (0.00, −0.01 to 0.01; 11 trials, 1,786 people; low certainty, fewer than 100 events). Any adverse event: 39 against 41 in 100 against nicotine replacement (risk ratio 0.95, 0.72 to 1.24; 8 trials, 3,107 people; low certainty; I² 72%) and 46 against 46 in 100 against a vape without nicotine (1.01, 0.95 to 1.08; 6 trials, 909 people; moderate certainty). Against behavioural support only or no support the certainty is very low: serious events 3 against 3 in 100 (0.00, −0.00 to 0.01; 18 trials, 5,032 people; 10 of the 18 trials recorded none) and any adverse event 52 against 43 in 100 (risk ratio 1.22, 1.00 to 1.49, an interval that touches no difference; 11 trials, 2,801 people). No trial in the comparisons with nicotine replacement had tobacco or vaping industry funding; one or two trials in each of the other two comparisons did, and leaving them out did not change the review's reading of any of these results (for any adverse event against support only or no support the risk ratio then read 1.26, 0.96 to 1.66). Trials that could not be pooled reported more throat or mouth irritation, cough or dry mouth with vapes in some trials and fewer breathing symptoms in others, and more nausea with nicotine replacement in one. The trials used regulated nicotine vapes in adults for up to about 2 years; the review says longer-term effects are unknown, that its conclusion relates to people using regulated vapes to stop smoking and not to people who have never smoked, and that products containing cannabis or illicit products may have different harm profiles. Certainty: low (for the comparisons with nicotine replacement and with a vape without nicotine; very low against support only or no support). Status: replicated.
plain: In these trials, serious health problems were about as common in people given a nicotine vape as in people given nicotine patches, gum or similar (about 7 in 100 against 6 in 100) or a vape without nicotine (about 2 in 100 in both). Side effects of any kind were also about as common with those two comparisons. Against counselling only or nothing the evidence is weaker, and the vape groups reported somewhat more side effects (about 52 in 100 against 43 in 100, though the range includes no difference). None of the trials against patches, gum or similar was paid for by the vaping or tobacco industry; one or two in each of the other comparisons were, and the review found that leaving them out did not change its reading. The trials were too small and too short (up to about 2 years) to show rare or later harms.
population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials of nicotine vapes; adverse events 8, 6 and 11 trials (3,107, 909 and 2,801 people) and serious adverse events 10, 11 and 18 trials (4,045, 1,786 and 5,032 people) against nicotine replacement, vapes without nicotine, and support only or no support; follow-up 1 week to about 2 years; Cochrane living review, search to 1 January 2026

comparator: Nicotine replacement therapy; a vape without nicotine; behavioural support only or no support
outcome: Any adverse event and serious adverse event during follow-up of one week or longer (self-report and medical records)
magnitude: Serious adverse events (risk difference; per 100 with comparator vs vape): vs NRT 0.01 (−0.01 to 0.02), 6 vs 7 (5–8), 10 trials, 4,045 participants, moderate; vs non-nicotine vape 0.00 (−0.01 to 0.01), 2 vs 2 (1–3), 11 trials, 1,786, low; vs behavioural support only or no support 0.00 (−0.00 to 0.01), 3 vs 3 (3–4), 18 trials, 5,032, very low. Any adverse event (RR): vs NRT 0.95 (0.72–1.24), 41 vs 39 per 100 (30–51), 8 trials, 3,107, I² 72%, low; vs non-nicotine vape 1.01 (0.95–1.08), 46 vs 46 per 100 (44–50), 6 trials, 909, moderate; vs support only or no support 1.22 (1.00–1.49), 43 vs 52 per 100 (43–64), 11 trials, 2,801, I² 58%, very low. Industry-funded trials left out (Table 2): none to remove against NRT; against a vape without nicotine any adverse event 1.01 (0.95–1.08) and serious events −0.00 (−0.01 to 0.01), unchanged; against support only or no support the review reports no change in reading for serious events, and any adverse event reads 1.26 (0.96–1.66), I² 60%.

imprecision.note: Serious events against vapes without nicotine: fewer than 100 events (two levels in the review); against nicotine replacement fewer than 300 events, and any adverse event against NRT: imprecision and I² 72%.

grade.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high; the rating is for the comparisons with nicotine replacement and with vapes without nicotine, and the comparison with support only or no support, which the review rates very low, is labelled in the statement rather than allowed to set the claim's rating (METHODS §6.3; the same approach as the all-cause estimate in the methamphetamine mortality claim). Imprecision, two levels: serious adverse events against vapes without nicotine rest on fewer than 100 events (the review's two levels); against nicotine replacement the review took one level for fewer than 300 events, and for any adverse event against nicotine replacement one level for imprecision and one for inconsistency (I² 72%); all reach low. Risk of bias, not rated down for these two comparisons (the review does not downgrade them; for support only or no support it takes levels for unblinded assessment and differential contact). Indirectness, not rated down: regulated vapes supplied in trials, adults, up to about 2 years. Relation insufficient-evidence because the intervals do not exclude a difference of about 2 serious events in 100 against nicotine replacement and the trials were too short and too small to show rare or later harms (METHODS §6.3: no detectable effect needs an interval that excludes meaningful effects). Status replicated for the main finding, serious events, whose pools have I² 0% in all three comparisons; adverse events overall are less consistent (I² 72% and 58%), which the statement shows. Living review: later updates will change the numbers.

verification.flag_note: Staged apart from the quitting claims because harms carry lower ratings. Certainty follows Cochrane's ratings for each comparison; the claim-level rating is set by the two comparisons with another product (low), with the comparison against support only or no support (very low) labelled in the statement, as in the methamphetamine mortality model. Relation insufficient-evidence is a cautious choice (see the grade reasoning); the senior author may prefer does-not-detectably-change for serious events against nicotine replacement (moderate certainty). Not covered here, by design: exposure to chemicals and long-term disease (other readers' claims); biomarkers and lung function in these trials (on the card). Not read: supplementary materials, the unpooled trials' own reports.

statement: In adults who smoked and joined four small randomised trials of oral nicotine pouches (284 people; 7 days to 8 weeks; three of the four trials enrolled people not planning to quit; Cochrane review, search to 13 January 2025, with ten further trials ongoing), the evidence is insufficient to say whether pouches help people stop smoking or cut down, whether compared with continuing to smoke, with a nicotine e-cigarette or with a lower-strength pouch. Compared with continuing to smoke as usual, 1 of 18 people given pouches had quit at week 8 against 0 of 9 (risk ratio 1.58, 95% CI 0.07 to 35.32; one trial, 27 people; very low certainty); among people still smoking, cigarettes per day differed by −1.07 (−12.72 to 10.58; 19 people). Compared with a nicotine e-cigarette (the same trial of 45 people, at high risk of bias), 1 of 18 had quit with pouches against 4 of 18 with e-cigarettes (0.25, 0.03 to 2.02; 36 people; low certainty), and people still smoking smoked 5.32 more cigarettes a day with pouches (−2.16 to 12.80; 26 people). Between two pouch strengths (one registry-listed trial), 2 of 15 had quit at the higher strength against 0 of 15 at the lower at week 4 (5.00, 0.26 to 96.13; 30 people). None of these differences can be told from chance. No trial compared pouches with nicotine replacement for quitting (one cross-over trial of 63 people reported side effects only), none followed people beyond 8 weeks, none included people who vape or use other products, and the review found no study of pouch uptake and smoking in the population. No serious adverse events were recorded in any arm of the three trials that reported them (1 to 8 weeks; very low to low certainty); other adverse events were reported in different ways and were mostly mild or uncommon. In the one trial funded by a tobacco company (53 people, about one week), urine and blood measures of smoke exposure were lower with pouches than with continued smoking (a tobacco-specific nitrosamine marker, NNAL, 265 ng/g creatinine lower, 95% CI 180 to 351, from 330; carboxyhaemoglobin 6.7 percentage points lower, 5.1 to 8.3, from 11.3%; very low certainty); it is the only trial in the review to measure those two against continued smoking, and an independent trial of 19 people that measured exhaled carbon monoxide found it lower with pouches, with an interval that included no difference. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Only four small trials have tested nicotine pouches in people who smoke: 284 people in all, followed for 1 to 8 weeks. They are too small to say whether pouches help people stop smoking or cut down. In the one trial that reported quitting against carrying on smoking, 1 of 18 people given pouches had stopped and none of 9 who carried on; and 1 of 18 given pouches had stopped against 4 of 18 given vapes. No serious health problems were recorded, but the trials were short. One trial paid for by a tobacco company found lower levels of smoke chemicals in the body after about a week of pouches than after smoking as usual; it was the only trial to measure these, so nothing independent can be set beside it. Ten more trials are under way.
population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and joined four small randomised trials of oral nicotine pouches (284 people; 7 days to 8 weeks; three trials enrolled people not planning to quit); Cochrane review, search to 13 January 2025; ten further trials ongoing

comparator: Continuing to smoke as usual; a nicotine e-cigarette; a lower-strength pouch (and, for side effects only, snus and nicotine gum)

Cigarettes per day among people still smoking: vs continued smoking MD −1.07 (−12.72 to 10.58), 19; vs e-cigarette MD 5.32 (−2.16 to 12.80), 26; higher vs lower strength, log scale MD −0.20 (−0.27 to −0.13), 30. Serious adverse events: none in any arm (3 trials; vs continued smoking 2 trials, 124 participants, very low; vs e-cigarette 1 trial, 26, low; higher vs lower strength 2 trials, 77). Biomarkers vs continued smoking (Rensch 2023, industry-funded, 53 participants): NNAL MD −265.30 ng/g creatinine (−350.64 to −179.96), COHb MD −6.7% (−8.33 to −5.07); very low.

risk_of_bias.note: None of the four trials low risk; three high; unblinded arms, unequal interventions; the comparison with continued smoking rests on one high-risk trial.

indirectness.note: Quitting at 4 to 8 weeks only; three trials enrolled people not planning to quit; all participants smoked.

imprecision.note: Five quits in all across the comparisons; intervals from 0.03 to 96.

publication_bias.note: Ten ongoing trials; industry reports not searched; recorded, not rated.

grade.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane systematic review that found no meta-analysis worth pooling (AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card). Risk of bias, two levels: none of the four trials was at low risk and three were high, with unblinded arms and unequal interventions in the two trials that matter for quitting; the comparison with continued smoking rests on one trial at high risk of bias (the review's two levels). Indirectness, one level: quitting was measured at 4 to 8 weeks, not the 6 months that the claim's question needs, three of the four trials enrolled people not planning to quit, and no trial included people who vape or use other products. Imprecision, two levels: five people had quit across all comparisons, and the risk ratios' intervals run from 0.03 to 96. Inconsistency does not arise (single trials). Publication bias, not rated down but recorded: ten further trials are ongoing and industry reports were not searched. The total of five levels is more than the three available, so the rating is very low; it is not changed by the biomarker result, which is a separate outcome from one tobacco-industry trial (very low), with no independent trial to set beside it. Relation insufficient-evidence (METHODS §6.1). Status single study: the comparison with continued smoking and the comparison with e-cigarettes come from the same trial of 45 people, the higher-against-lower-strength comparison from a registry record of one trial, and the review's plain language summary speaks of two studies behind those comparisons when both come from one trial.

verification.flag_note: The review's search ended in January 2025 with ten ongoing trials, so this claim will be out of date as they report; reader 69's claim cl_nic_pouches covers what pouches contain and who uses them. The claim says plainly that the evidence is thin, as asked. The biomarker finding comes from one tobacco-industry trial with no independent counterpart for those outcomes; it is set in the statement beside that fact, not dropped. Rated very low although the review rates the e-cigarette comparison low: the claim covers the whole question (stopping or cutting down), and its weakest link is the comparison with continued smoking. Not read: the four trial reports, supplementary materials 1 to 6, the flow diagram and risk-of-bias figure (images), the reference list. No new reference is needed (hartmann-boyce_2025 exists).
