statement: In adults who smoked or had smoked cigarettes, vaping as the only product, compared with smoking cigarettes only, is associated with much lower levels of tobacco-specific nitrosamines, carbon monoxide and most other smoke chemicals in urine, breath and blood, but not with a clear fall in nicotine itself, and the levels stay above those of people who use no tobacco or nicotine; in the national survey, and in a smaller cross-sectional comparison, people who both vaped and smoked did not show the lower levels. The main data are from the first wave (2013–2014) of the US PATH survey (Goniewicz et al., 2018; 247 adults who only vaped, 93% of whom had smoked before, against 2,411 who only smoked; funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Food and Drug Administration's Center for Tobacco Products, whose staff took part in the analysis and in preparing and approving the manuscript; one author reports advisory fees from Johnson & Johnson and grant support from Pfizer, and another an honorarium from Pfizer and unpaid contact with Juul Labs staff): the nitrosamine metabolite NNAL was 4.887 against 203.5 pg/mg creatinine (about 98% lower), the acrylonitrile marker 3.959 against 123.9 ng/mg (97% lower), the acrolein marker 108.0 against 271.5 (60% lower) and cadmium 0.193 against 0.277 (30% lower), while most other metals and the markers for toluene, benzene and carbon disulfide did not differ. Total nicotine equivalents were 2.000 against 27.90 nmol/mg (about 93% lower), but only 59% of the people who only vaped (161 people, as printed) reported using nicotine-containing e-cigarettes; in the UK review's five pooled analyses of people who vaped against people who smoked at least weekly, nicotine and its metabolites did not differ significantly, and the National Academies judged nicotine intake in experienced adults who vape comparable to that from cigarettes (the committee's judgment: substantial evidence). Switching and confinement studies point the same way for the other chemicals. A 2023 systematic review of nine studies (1,299 adults who smoked, one week to 8 months, eight at high risk of bias; funded by an Oxford University grant, Cancer Research UK and infrastructure funding from the National Institute for Health Research; authors' declarations include consultancy and research funding from Pfizer and consultancy to Johnson & Johnson Japan on nicotine replacement; two included studies, Cravo 2016 and Morris 2022, are marked industry funded) found exhaled carbon monoxide 9.57 ppm lower with vaping only than with smoking only (95% CI −17.30 to −1.83; 3 studies) and 12 of 13 other biomarkers lower with none higher, those rows resting on the two industry-funded studies. The UK review (2022; commissioned by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities; no declarations of interest on the pages read; its authors say many pooled findings came from tobacco industry-funded trials in confinement lasting up to 7 days) pooled studies of people who vaped against people who smoked and found lower NNAL (58%), NNN (90%), the acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA (71%), the acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA (94%) and the butadiene metabolite MHBMA (83%), and lower blood carboxyhaemoglobin in two analyses. The National Academies (2018; contract with the Food and Drug Administration; its Reviewers page lists one reviewer employed by British American Tobacco Research and Development Centre; its online table of study sponsors was not read) judged it conclusive that completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens. The publicly funded survey and the industry-funded trials point the same way. Against people who use no tobacco or nicotine, people who only vaped had higher levels in the survey (NNAL 4.887 against 0.921 pg/mg; also lead, cadmium, a pyrene marker and the acrylonitrile marker), and the UK review found significantly higher nitrosamines in three cross-sectional analyses, no significant difference for most volatile compounds (the acrylonitrile metabolite excepted, over three times higher in one study), higher nicotine in four analyses and mixed results for metals; its authors say cross-sectional data make it hard to separate exposure from vaping from earlier smoking, and that a trial and a cross-over study suggest nitrosamine metabolites might fall to the levels of people who use no nicotine. In the one small study with an abstinent group, exhaled carbon monoxide at 12 weeks was 1 ppm in both the vaping group (16 people) and the abstinent group (12). Against people who both vaped and smoked, the survey's dual group had higher levels than people who only smoked (total nicotine equivalents 43.70 against 27.90 nmol/mg; NNAL 262.6 against 203.5 pg/mg) at similar numbers of cigarettes a day (15.1 against 15.4), and the National Academies describe a smaller cross-sectional comparison (181 people) in which nitrosamine and volatile-compound metabolites in people who did both were similar to those in people who only smoked; in the switching studies exhaled carbon monoxide was 1.91 ppm lower with both than with smoking only (95% CI −3.38 to −0.45) and 4.40 ppm lower with vaping only than with both (−12.04 to 3.24, an interval that includes no difference). Against another form (product content, not body levels), the National Academies report tobacco-specific nitrosamines in e-liquids and aerosol at low levels, typically similar to those in pharmaceutical nicotine products. Markers of potential harm after switching are less settled: in the UK review, acute vaping and acute smoking each lowered the arteries' flow-mediated dilation in the short term, one trial found it improved after four weeks of switching, and C-reactive protein was lower than in people who smoke in pooled cross-sectional data but not in controlled studies; its authors draw only limited conclusions. What this does not show: these are levels of chemicals, not illness; the UK review could not summarise exposure beyond 12 months and says the degree of any residual risk remains unclear; most people who vaped had smoked for years, so earlier smoking may contribute to some markers; the survey's devices were early-generation and its group of people who only vaped was small; nickel, chromium and flavoring compounds were not measured there; and people who vape and have never smoked are almost absent from these data. Certainty: low. Status: replicated for the lower nitrosamine, carbon monoxide and volatile-compound levels (the survey, the switching studies and the reviews overlap in part and are not counted as separate replications); the nicotine and dual-use comparisons are mixed.
plain: In a large US survey from 2013 to 2014, adults who only vaped had far less of the harmful chemicals from smoke in their urine than adults who only smoked: about 98% less of a cancer-linked tobacco chemical (a nitrosamine) and about 60% to 97% less of several others. Short switching studies in the US and Europe found the same pattern for carbon monoxide and other chemicals; some were paid for by tobacco companies, and the survey, which companies did not fund, agrees. Nicotine itself was not clearly lower in the pooled studies. People who only vaped still had more of some of these chemicals than people who used no tobacco or nicotine, and in the survey people who both vaped and smoked had as much as people who only smoked, or more. These are measures of what gets into the body, not of illness, most of the people who vaped had smoked before, and the studies lasted from one session to about a year.
population: Adults who smoked cigarettes or had smoked them: US adults in the first wave (2013–2014) of the national PATH survey (247 who only vaped, 93% of them had smoked before; 2,411 who only smoked; 792 who did both; 1,655 who had never used tobacco), adults in nine short switching and confinement studies (1,299 people; Greece, Italy, Poland, the UK and the US; one week to 8 months), and the studies pooled by the UK review (2022; 24 to 60 studies per chemical, follow-up from one session to 12 months) and described by the National Academies (2018); people who vape and have never smoked are almost absent
exposure: Vaping (e-cigarettes) as the only product: in the survey, self-reported current use every day or some days and no other tobacco (59% of the group reported nicotine-containing e-cigarettes, as printed); in the switching and confinement studies, being given or switching to an e-cigarette
comparator: Smoking cigarettes only (main comparison); doing both (vaping and smoking); using no tobacco or nicotine (the survey's never-used group; abstainers in one small study)
outcome: Levels of nicotine, tobacco-specific nitrosamines (NNAL), carbon monoxide and other smoke chemicals (volatile compounds, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, metals) measured in urine, breath and blood; short-term markers of potential harm (inflammation, oxidative stress, flow-mediated dilation, heart rate, blood pressure) after switching. These are measures of what reaches the body, not of disease.
magnitude: Against people who only smoke (levels in urine unless stated; absolute values before relative). National survey (PATH, 2013–2014; 247 people who only vaped against 2,411 who only smoked; geometric means per mg creatinine): total nicotine equivalents 2.000 (95% CI 1.100–3.500) against 27.90 (23.80–32.70) nmol, about 93% lower; NNAL 4.887 (3.817–6.257) against 203.5 (181.7–227.9) pg, about 98% lower; acrylonitrile marker 3.959 (3.002–5.219) against 123.9 (109.9–139.7) ng, 97% lower; acrolein marker 108.0 (95.93–121.6) against 271.5 (255.1–289.0) ng, 60% lower; acrylamide marker 56.05 against 136.4 ng, 59% lower; naphthalene marker 62% and pyrene marker 47% lower; cadmium 0.193 against 0.277 ng, 30% lower; nearly all other metals and the toluene, benzene and carbon disulfide markers similar (percentages recomputed by the editors from the printed means, within one point of the text). 2023 systematic review (nine studies, 1,299 adults, one week to 8 months): exhaled carbon monoxide, vaping only against smoking only −9.57 ppm (−17.30 to −1.83; 3 studies); 12 of 13 other biomarkers lower with vaping only, none higher, one (NNN) not different. UK review (McNeill et al., 2022), pooled analyses of people who vaped against people who smoked: NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94% and NNN 90% lower (5 analyses); 3-HPMA 71%, CNEMA 94% and MHBMA 83% lower (15 analyses; formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive); blood carboxyhaemoglobin significantly lower (2 analyses); nicotine and its metabolites not significantly different (5 analyses, against people who smoked at least weekly). Against people who use no tobacco or nicotine: survey, never-used group (1,655 people) against people who only vaped: NNAL 0.921 (0.819–1.035) against 4.887 pg (81% lower), lead 0.351 against 0.432 ng, cadmium 0.149 against 0.193 ng, pyrene marker 0.128 against 0.161 ng, acrylonitrile marker 1.315 against 3.959 ng (about 66% lower); all major nicotine metabolites, all nitrosamines, 4 metals, 1 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon and 4 volatile-compound markers were higher in the group that only vaped. UK review: nitrosamines significantly higher in 3 cross-sectional analyses; nicotine significantly higher in 4; volatile compounds not different in 10 analyses except CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study); metals mixed, mostly higher; other toxicants (9 studies, not pooled) higher. One study with an abstinent group: exhaled carbon monoxide at 12 weeks 1 ppm (SD 1) in 16 people who vaped and in 12 who abstained. Against people who both vaped and smoked: survey, both group (792 people) against smoking only: total nicotine equivalents 43.70 (39.80–48.10) against 27.90 nmol; NNAL 262.6 (240.0–287.3) against 203.5 pg; the smoking-only group was lower by 15% for the pyrene marker, 10% for the acrolein marker and 15% for the acrylonitrile marker; lead and cadmium did not differ; cigarettes a day 15.1 against 15.4. Switching studies: exhaled carbon monoxide, vaping only against both −4.40 ppm (−12.04 to 3.24; 2 studies); both against smoking only −1.91 ppm (−3.38 to −0.45; 2 studies); of 25 biomarkers, 12 lower with vaping only, 5 lower with both (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon metabolites, one study of 22 people) and 8 not different or inconsistent. Markers of potential harm (UK review): flow-mediated dilation lowered in the short term by both acute vaping and acute smoking and improved by 4 weeks of switching in one randomized trial; C-reactive protein lower than in people who smoke and similar to people who use no nicotine in pooled cross-sectional data (3 studies), not confirmed in controlled or longitudinal studies; LDL cholesterol no difference; blood pressure lower than in people who smoke and similar to people who use no nicotine in pooled cross-sectional analyses of people who had vaped for at least 3 months or a year; heart rate lower than in people who smoke when the groups were mutually exclusive; pulse wave velocity may fall after a sustained switch (longest follow-up 4 months). Follow-up: a single session to 7 days (acute) or 8 days to 12 months in the UK review; one week to 8 months in the 2023 review; the survey is a single time point.

evidence.locator: Results › e-Cigarette–Only Users vs Cigarette-Only Smokers, 1st paragraph; Methods › Data Source, 5th paragraph; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 4th paragraph; Figure 1 legend footnotes
evidence.extracted: PATH Wave 1 (2013–2014): 247 adults who only vaped against 2,411 who only smoked cigarettes (220 against 2,322 for the volatile-compound markers), geometric means per mg creatinine, adjusted for creatinine, age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, marijuana use in the past 30 days and weekly hours of second-hand smoke (figure legends add cigarettes per day). Total nicotine equivalents 2.000 (95% CI 1.100–3.500) against 27.90 (23.80–32.70) nmol, about 93% lower (t = 8.53); NNAL 4.887 (3.817–6.257) against 203.5 (181.7–227.9) pg, about 98% lower (t = 27.96); acrolein marker 108.0 (95.93–121.6) against 271.5 (255.1–289.0) ng, 60% lower; acrylonitrile marker 3.959 (3.002–5.219) against 123.9 (109.9–139.7) ng, 97% lower; acrylamide marker 56.05 against 136.4 ng, 59% lower; naphthalene marker about 62% and pyrene marker 47% lower; cadmium 0.193 against 0.277 ng, 30% lower. Nearly all other metals and three volatile markers (toluene, benzene, carbon disulfide) were statistically similar. Overall lower in the vape-only group: all major nicotine metabolites, 2 minor alkaloids, all nitrosamines, 1 metal, all polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and 17 volatile compounds. Percentages recomputed by the editors from the printed means.

evidence.locator: Abstract › Design; Methods › Data Source, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2, rows 'Use nicotine-containing e-cigarettes' and 'Use flavored e-cigarettes'; Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 to 3 legends
evidence.extracted: Of the 247 adults who only vaped, 93% (229) had smoked cigarettes before (the former established smokers among them, who had smoked at least 100 cigarettes in their lifetime, had quit a mean of 3.5 years earlier and had smoked a mean of 19.0 cigarettes a day), only 18 had never smoked, 56% (147) vaped every day, and only 59% (161 people, percentage as printed) reported using nicotine-containing e-cigarettes (38% of the dual group); 44% used flavored ones. Cross-sectional analysis of Wave 1 only (Abstract). Authors' stated limits: device generation not recorded; cadmium in the group that only vaped may remain from earlier smoking (long half-life, 93% had smoked); most markers have short half-lives (mean 1.5 to 10 hours); the 2013–2014 period corresponds to the increasing availability of first-generation devices, and later-generation devices may give higher exposure, so the results may be conservative; e-cigarettes may also generate unique exposures (nickel and chromium given as examples) or exposures not designated as harmful constituents, such as those tied to flavorings; some volatile-compound laboratory results were outstanding when the analyses were run, so weighted estimates for those markers may not reflect the target population. Weighted response 54.0% for the household screener and 63.6% for the adult interview among those giving urine.

Authors' stated limits: data came from short confinement studies that do not generalise readily or from non-randomised groupings open to unmeasured confounding; for every outcome other than carbon monoxide there were too few data to pool; products varied; no individual participant data; only one study gave data on abstainers. Scope: nicotine exposure was not analysed (the authors say it is not necessarily a measure of harm).

evidence.extracted: Conclusions 5-1 to 5-3 (the committee's judgments): most e-cigarette products contain and emit numerous potentially toxic substances besides nicotine (5-1, conclusive); the number and amount vary widely with product and how the device is operated (5-2, conclusive); except for nicotine, under typical conditions of use, exposure to potentially toxic substances is significantly lower than from combustible tobacco cigarettes (5-3, substantial). Chapter 18 sets out four direct comparisons of smoke and aerosol: levels of selected toxicants in smoke 9 to 450 times those in aerosol (calculated from published data assuming 15 puffs per cigarette); toxicants emitted 82 to more than 99% lower per puff, depending on the regulatory list and puffing method (150 chemicals examined, 25 detected); about 1,500 times more harmful or potentially harmful constituents in smoke than in aerosol or room air; of 11 metals, higher in the aerosol for four, within the smoke range for five and lower for two.

evidence.locator: Summary › Harm Reduction, Conclusion 18-1; Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched › Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure, 2nd to 10th paragraphs and Synthesis; Chapter 4 › Switching Studies, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Conclusion 18-1 (the committee's judgment: conclusive evidence): completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens in cigarette smoke. The chapter's synthesis says all studies showed significantly reduced biomarkers of exposure in people who substituted e-cigarettes for cigarettes. Examples: a 5-day randomized study of 105 people (urinary biomarkers 29 to 95% lower and exhaled carbon monoxide 27 to 89% lower after partial or complete switching; people who used both products and replaced half their cigarettes had 7 to 38% reductions and 1 to 20% higher nicotine equivalents); 40 people followed for four weeks (exhaled carbon monoxide 80% lower with e-cigarettes only and 52% lower with both products; acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 79% and 60% lower); and a cross-sectional comparison of 181 people in five groups in which long-term exclusive e-cigarette use had lower NNAL than every other group while nitrosamine and volatile-compound metabolites in people who used both products were similar to those in people who only smoked. Studies ranged from 13 to 420 people with follow-up of 5 days to 12 weeks, apart from one randomized study of 48 people followed for 8 months; the 12-week trial of a manufacturer's product (developed by Fontem Ventures B.V., per Chapter 18) had 40.2% compliance in its unconfined phase.

evidence.extracted: Conclusion 4-1 (conclusive): nicotine exposure from e-cigarettes is highly variable and depends on product characteristics and how the device is operated. Conclusion 4-2 (substantial): nicotine intake among experienced adults who use e-cigarettes can be comparable to that from cigarettes. Behind them: 27 acute clinical studies (blood nicotine in people new to e-cigarettes much lower than from their usual cigarettes, and in experienced people it could reach the range of a typical cigarette) and seven switching studies (three reported no significant change in nicotine exposure; four suggested that some e-cigarettes were ineffective nicotine delivery devices compared with cigarettes). Nicotine yield rises with device power, e-liquid nicotine and puff duration (Chapter 4 synthesis).

evidence.extracted: Tobacco-specific nitrosamines were found in e-liquids and aerosol at low levels, typically similar to those in pharmaceutical nicotine products (the chapter says this is probably attributed to pharmaceutical-grade nicotine); one study of 12 brands found two nitrosamines in aerosol from all but three, and another of three liquids found none in 100-puff aerosol. Carbonyls such as formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein in aerosol were in most cases lower than in smoke (for example 86 to 544 times lower for three carbonyls in one comparison), but very high formaldehyde levels were also reported. Metals: aerosol contains metals (5-4, substantial), whose origin could be the coil, other device parts or the liquid; the number of metals could be greater than in cigarette smoke except cadmium, which is markedly lower (5-5, limited); few, mostly small studies of first- and second-generation devices; one biomarker study of 64 people supported an inhaled contribution to the internal dose of chromium and nickel.

evidence.locator: Chapter 7 › Main findings › Nicotine, 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Chapter 7, nicotine (60 studies, 5 from the UK): large variation by design, definitions, biomarker and sample type and exposure duration. Five meta-analyses (1 longitudinal, 4 cross-sectional) of nicotine and its metabolites in people who vaped and people who smoked at least weekly found no significant differences. Four meta-analyses against people who use no nicotine found significantly higher levels in people who vape. Narrative summaries: with more experience of vaping, people can reach nicotine levels similar to smoking; levels varied with device characteristics; no discernible difference between adults and adolescents.

evidence.locator: Chapter 7 › Main findings › Volatile organic compounds, 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Chapter 7, volatile organic compounds (24 studies, 5 from the UK). Against people who smoke, 15 meta-analyses (4 longitudinal, 11 cross-sectional): most showed significantly lower levels in people who vape, with reductions of 71% for the acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA, 94% for the acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA and 83% for the 1,3-butadiene metabolite MHBMA; for formaldehyde and toluene the evidence was inconclusive. Against people who use no nicotine, 10 cross-sectional meta-analyses found no significant difference except for CNEMA, which was over 3 times higher in one study. Young people: broadly the same direction.

evidence.extracted: Chapter 7, tobacco-specific nitrosamines (28 studies, 3 from the UK). Against people who smoke, 5 meta-analyses (2 longitudinal, 3 cross-sectional) all showed significantly lower levels in people who vape: NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94%, NNN 90%. Against people who use no nicotine, 3 cross-sectional meta-analyses all showed significantly higher levels; the authors write that cross-sectional data make it difficult to distinguish exposure from vaping from previous tobacco use, and that a randomized trial and a cross-over study indicate that nitrosamine metabolite levels might fall to those of people who use no nicotine. Young people: same direction, with a smaller difference between people who vape and people who smoke than in adults.

evidence.locator: Chapter 7 › Main findings › Other potential toxicants, 1st paragraph; Chapter 7 › Main findings › Carbon monoxide, 1st, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Chapter 7 › Main findings › Metals, 1st, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Chapter 7 › Main findings › Secondhand exposure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Chapter 7, other toxicants: nine studies (1 from the UK, no meta-analyses): the very limited findings generally suggested levels lower in people who vape than in people who smoke and higher than in people who use no nicotine. Carbon monoxide (33 studies, 3 from the UK): two meta-analyses against people who smoke both found significantly lower blood carboxyhaemoglobin; none against people who use no nicotine, but interventional studies suggested that exposure in people who switch completely might fall to levels like those of people who use no nicotine. Metals (10 cross-sectional studies, none from the UK, no meta-analyses): relative findings mixed; absolute findings mixed, most showing higher exposure in people who vape. Secondhand exposure (6 studies): short exposures gave no detectable change in nicotine, volatile compound or nitrosamine biomarkers; longer exposures during heavy sustained vaping gave significant increases.

evidence.extracted: Chapter 7 design: two review questions (effects of vaping and secondhand exposure on markers associated with the risk of health conditions; effects in people with existing conditions on disease outcomes); no study answered the second for exposure biomarkers. Comparisons were relative (against people who smoke) and absolute (against people who use no nicotine); studies varied in quality and definitions (for example grouping people who vape and smoke with exclusive vaping, or comparing occasional vaping with daily smoking). Follow-up was a single use to 7 days (acute) or 8 days to 12 months; the authors write that they were unable to summarise findings on longer-term (more than 12 months) vaping exposure, with some studies allowing too little wash-out for biomarkers with long half-lives. Meta-analyses were run wherever possible, but inconsistent designs, reporting, group definitions and exposure periods meant only a few studies could be pooled.

evidence.extracted: The authors' reading (Chapter 7, Implications): compared with smoking, vaping leads to a substantial reduction in biomarkers of toxicant exposure, but the degree of any residual risk remains unclear, mainly because of a lack of comparisons between long-term former smokers who do and do not vape, or with people who have never smoked or vaped. Most studies had some methodological concerns; a lack of difference from people who use no nicotine may reflect insensitive methods, background exposures or truly similar exposure. Historical tobacco use can greatly affect many biomarkers and most people who vape previously smoked for a long time; the authors ask for strict definitions of exclusive vaping and biological checks of status. They state that many pooled findings came from tobacco industry-funded randomized trials in confinement lasting up to 7 days and call for independent research outside confinement and with longer follow-up.

evidence.extracted: Chapter 8, markers of potential harm (41 unique studies in 43 publications): the authors list obscuring differences (different markers; group definitions with smoking or vaping status usually not checked by a biological test; mostly acute exposures, while these markers take weeks or months to normalise after people stop smoking; confounding and few controlled studies). Oxidative stress: LDL cholesterol no difference; HDL inconsistent; 8-isoprostane mixed; limited evidence for the rest. Inflammation: pooled data from 3 cross-sectional studies showed C-reactive protein lower than in people who smoke and similar to people who use no nicotine, and lower sICAM-1 than in people who smoke, but controlled and longitudinal studies did not confirm this; no definite conclusion. Endothelial function (none pooled): acute vaping (with or without nicotine) and acute smoking each reduced flow-mediated dilation in the short term; a single randomized trial found that 4 weeks of switching from smoking to vaping improved it; no controlled study compared people who vape with people who use no nicotine. Platelet activation (4 studies): no conclusions. The authors' summary: acute vaping might cause endothelial dysfunction as much as acute smoking but switching might improve endothelial function in the longer term. Their implications: research on these markers is at an early stage, most studies cannot inform the medium or long term, and studies of people who vape and have never smoked are needed.

evidence.extracted: Chapter 11, cardiovascular markers (41 studies, 27 of them cross-over or acute-exposure designs; mixed quality; no longer-term summary possible). Heart rate (31 studies, 9 pooled): acutely, vaping raised heart rate less than smoking; in longer-term comparisons heart rate was lower in people who vape than in people who smoke when the groups were mutually exclusive. Blood pressure (30 studies, 9 pooled in 10 meta-analyses): cross-sectional meta-analyses of people with at least 3 months or a year of vaping found lower blood pressure than in people who smoke and no difference from people who use no nicotine (the authors presume most had stopped smoking). Pulse wave velocity (9 studies, none pooled): may fall after a sustained switch, but the longest follow-up was 4 months; it rose after acute nicotine vaping but not non-nicotine vaping. One randomized trial found that switching improved flow-mediated dilation after one month.

risk_of_bias.note: The survey is rated some concerns on ROBINS-E (card sc_goniewicz_2018: one time point, a small group that only vaped and was almost entirely people who had smoked, self-reported product use, no device or nicotine content); the 2023 review is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (card sc_hartmann_boyce_2023) and eight of its nine studies are at high risk of bias; the National Academies report and the UK review are provisional on their cards (critically low and low-confidence placeholders, the UK Methods being unread); the UK authors write that most studies had methodological concerns and that many pooled findings came from short industry-funded trials in confinement. Counted once.

inconsistency.note: For the headline contrast (vaping only against smoking only; nitrosamines, carbon monoxide, volatile compounds) every source goes the same way. The size differs (NNAL about 98% lower in the survey, 58% in the pooled analyses; acrolein marker 60% against 71%), which fits the markers, follow-up and the pooling of mixed group definitions (editors' reading). The nicotine contrast and the comparison of people who vape and smoke do diverge (survey and pooled cross-sectional data against confinement studies); they are outside the rating and are stated as mixed.

indirectness.note: Direct for the claim as worded: adults who smoked or had smoked, markers of what reaches the body, studies of one session to about 12 months, devices of 2013 to about 2021. The wording does not extend to disease, to people who have never smoked, to products on sale now or to exposure over years. Parts of the numbers are seen only through reviews (UK pooled analyses, National Academies); the survey was read in full.

imprecision.note: The headline contrasts are large against their intervals (NNAL t = 27.96; pooled carbon monoxide −9.57 ppm, −17.30 to −1.83). The size is imprecise (three studies in the pooled carbon monoxide estimate; 247 people who only vaped in the survey) and is reported with its intervals.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by any source read. The industry-funded trials and the publicly funded survey agree in direction, which limits the concern for the headline contrast.

large_effect.note: Ratios of about 0.02 to 0.4 for the nitrosamine metabolite NNAL, the acrylonitrile and acrolein markers and carbon monoxide, adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education and other exposures; the remaining biases (earlier smoking in the vaping group, current smoking misreported as vaping only) work toward smaller differences, not larger.

dose_response.note: Within the survey, levels were higher in people who vaped every day than some days and, among people who did both, rose with how often they smoked (exploratory analyses; the supplement was not read); not counted, because the claim concerns the contrast between groups.

plausible_confounding.note: Not applied; the direction of residual confounding differs by contrast.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence (a cross-sectional survey; non-randomised and some randomized short studies behind the reviews) starts low. Downgraded once for risk of bias; not downgraded again for the same problem in another domain. Upgraded once for a large effect, applied to evidence already rated down for risk of bias: a strict reading, without the upgrade, gives very low, and the gap between the two is the chance that the lower levels are partly produced by who chooses to vape and how they are classified, which the direction of the main biases (toward smaller differences) and the consistency across a survey, short switching studies and four syntheses argue against but do not exclude. The rating applies to the headline contrast only (people who only vaped against people who only smoked, for nitrosamines, carbon monoxide and volatile compounds). The nicotine comparison, the comparison of people who vape and smoke, the metals, the product-content comparison with pharmaceutical nicotine products and the markers of potential harm after switching are less certain and, taken alone, would be rated very low. The reviews' graded judgments (conclusive, substantial, moderate) are their authors' judgments from a different starting point and are reported, not adopted. Funding is set out in the statement: the industry-funded trials are read beside the publicly funded survey and neither is dropped. Overlap: the 2023 review, the UK pooled analyses and the National Academies chapters share primary studies and are not independent replications; the survey is independent of them. Rated as worded: an association in levels of chemicals, which is not a claim about disease.

statement: In US adults followed for up to about four years in the national PATH cohort, and in three reviews commissioned by governments, the evidence is insufficient to say whether vaping, compared with using neither cigarettes nor e-cigarettes, changes the risk of heart disease, stroke or long-term lung disease, and the sources read give no cancer rates for people who vape; this is not evidence that vaping has no effect. The cohort found no detectable difference in newly reported heart disease or stroke between people who only vaped and people who used neither, with wide intervals and few events, and a higher rate of newly reported lung conditions in people who had used e-cigarettes, which smoking history may explain. Heart (Berlowitz et al., 2022, a research letter; PATH Waves 1 to 5, 2013–2019; funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, the Food and Drug Administration's Center for Tobacco Products and the American Lung Association; one author reports grants from Johnson & Johnson): of 24,027 adults with no heart disease at the start, 1,487 reported a new diagnosis of heart disease or stroke over up to four years: 764 of 14,832 who used neither product, 41 of 822 who only vaped, 569 of 6,515 who only smoked and 113 of 1,858 who did both (counts, not rates: the groups differ in age and follow-up; the age-adjusted rates as printed were, in that order, 8.0, 9.7, 14.8 and 17.1 per 1,000 person-years, which the editors could not reproduce from the counts). After adjustment for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, body mass index, blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, family history, marijuana use, pack-years and other tobacco, the hazard ratio against using neither was 1.00 (95% CI 0.69–1.45) for people who only vaped, 1.53 (1.30–1.79) for people who only smoked and 1.54 (1.21–1.96) for people who did both; for heart attack, heart failure or stroke alone (15 events among people who only vaped) 1.35 (0.75–2.42), 2.20 (1.73–2.81) and 2.08 (1.40–3.09). Against people who only smoked the ratio was 0.66 (0.46–0.94) for people who only vaped (0.61, 0.34–1.09, for the narrower outcome) and 1.01 (0.81–1.26) for people who did both (0.94, 0.65–1.36). The outcomes were self-reported and not adjudicated; the comparison group included people who had stopped smoking; and people who only vaped had more pack-years than that group (mean 11.0 against 4.2, with spreads several times the means), so past smoking may account for part of a difference or hide one. Lungs (Xie et al., 2020; PATH Waves 1 to 4, 2013–2018; same funders; one author reports grants from Ethicon, a Johnson & Johnson subsidiary, and other authors report federal grants and, for one, personal fees from several pharmaceutical companies): of 21,618 adults with no respiratory condition at the start, 1,460 (6.8%) reported a new diagnosis of asthma, COPD, emphysema or chronic bronchitis. After adjustment for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, region, smoking history (never; former by years since quitting; current by pack-years), other tobacco, other drug use, body mass index and chronic conditions, the adjusted rate was 26.06 against 20.41 per 1,000 person-years (about 2.6 against 2.0 in 100 a year, editors' conversion) in people who had ever used e-cigarettes at the start against people who had not (rate ratio 1.28, 1.10–1.48), with the same ratio for former use (1.28), which includes people who had tried 1 or 2 puffs, and a similar one for current use (1.31, 1.08–1.59); by condition, COPD 1.62, emphysema 1.54, chronic bronchitis 1.33 and asthma 1.24 (1.01–1.53). Adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity alone the ratios were much larger (2.14 for any condition, 5.03 for COPD), which shows how much depends on handling past smoking; use was recorded at the first wave only; 401 people (16.0% of those currently vaping) had never smoked cigarettes, so most had smoked; and the ratio was 1.20 (0.99–1.45) among people with no chronic condition at the start. Residual confounding by how much people smoked and when they stopped is likely, and the authors say causality cannot be established. The reviews. The National Academies (2018; contract with the Food and Drug Administration; its Reviewers page lists one reviewer employed by British American Tobacco Research and Development Centre; its online table of study sponsors was not read) found no available evidence whether e-cigarette use is associated with coronary heart disease, stroke or peripheral artery disease, none whether e-cigarettes cause respiratory disease, none on intermediate cancer endpoints and none on long-term illness or death in people who both vape and smoke; it judged the evidence substantial for a short-term rise in heart rate and moderate for a rise in diastolic blood pressure after nicotine intake, moderate for more cough and wheeze, and for an association with more asthma attacks, in adolescents who vape (four cross-sectional, self-reported studies), limited for better lung function or fewer COPD flare-ups in adults with asthma or COPD who switched from smoking (small studies), and substantial for fewer short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems when people switched completely from smoking (mostly small studies). The UK review (2022; commissioned by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities; search to July 2021; no declarations of interest on the pages read) said that, as in 2018, there is still no available evidence on clinical cardiovascular outcomes and that the extent of cardiovascular risk remains uncertain, rated the evidence from lung tests insufficient either way and limited for fewer COPD flare-ups in adults who switch completely (two reports on one group of patients), and presented no cancer incidence data; the review questions it lists concern markers linked to risk and people with existing conditions, so the pages read do not show a search for new disease in the general population (editors' reading; the Methods are in a PDF not read). The Australian review (Banks et al., 2023; Department of Health and the National Health and Medical Research Council; no relevant disclosures; searches to July 2020, with major reviews to December 2021) rated clinical cardiovascular outcomes and invasive cancer as no available evidence and asthma, bronchitis and COPD as insufficient evidence in people who smoke and no available evidence in people who do not, with certainty low or very low, and judged the direct effect on clinical disease largely unknown; it also judged it conclusive that vaping products cause an acute lung injury (EVALI), largely with THC-containing products, though in the largest study 14% of cases reported only nicotine products. The heart analysis appeared after all three reviews' searches ended; the lung analysis appeared after the Australian top-up search and neither is named in the Australian paper's reference list or on the UK pages read; a published critique (Mendelsohn et al., 2022, a commentary on the 2022 report to the Australian Department of Health on which the Australian review is based; no funding statement; two of its four authors were or are board members of the Australian Tobacco Harm Reduction Association, a registered health promotion charity that accepted unconditional seed funding from the vape retail industry until March 2019, and both state they have never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies; one is the author of a book titled Stop Smoking Start Vaping; the other two declare no interests; the full statement is in the anchor) argues that the review should have compared vaping with continuing to smoke, weighed net effects on the population and judged evidence on quitting by the same standard as evidence on starting to smoke, and that the 14% of lung-injury cases reporting only nicotine products do not show a link with nicotine, because many patients who denied vaping THC were later found to have done so; it cites no study of how often heart disease, lung disease or cancer occur in people who vape, only short-term measures after switching (mostly from studies that share authors) and a modelled cancer estimate, so it and the review disagree on the comparison and on which kinds of evidence count, not on disease rates, which neither measured. Not known: whether vaping causes any heart disease, lung disease or cancer in people who have never smoked, over more than four years or with current devices; whether the higher rate of lung conditions reflects vaping or past smoking; and cancer rates. Certainty: very low. Status: single study (two analyses of one cohort, which share data and some authors and are not independent replications).
plain: In two analyses of one large US study (more than 20,000 adults followed for up to four years), people who only vaped did not have a clearly different rate of new heart disease or stroke from people who used no cigarettes or e-cigarettes (hazard ratio 1.00, range 0.69 to 1.45, from only 41 cases), while people who smoked, or smoked and vaped, had about 1.5 times the rate. The same study found more new lung conditions such as COPD and asthma in people who had used e-cigarettes (about 2.6 against 2.0 in 100 people a year), but most of them had smoked, and allowing fully for past smoking is hard. Three reviews commissioned by governments, whose searches ended before the heart analysis was published, found no evidence or too little evidence on heart attack, stroke, long-term lung disease or cancer from vaping, so no one can yet say whether vaping causes them. A lung injury outbreak (EVALI) was linked to vaping products, mostly ones containing THC. The studies are short, rest on what people reported and cannot show cause.
population: US adults in the national PATH cohort followed from 2013–2014 for up to about four years: 24,027 with no heart disease or stroke at the start (heart analysis, Waves 1 to 5) and 21,618 with no asthma, COPD, emphysema or chronic bronchitis at the start (lung analysis, Waves 1 to 4); most of the people who vaped had smoked (in the lung analysis 16.0% of those currently vaping had never smoked cigarettes); and the reviews of the wider literature by the National Academies (2018), the UK government (2022; search to July 2021) and the Australian government (2023; studies to July 2020, major reviews to December 2021)
exposure: Vaping (e-cigarette use): current use of any frequency, updated at each wave (heart analysis), or ever, former or current use at the first wave only (lung analysis), with or without smoking
comparator: People who used neither cigarettes nor e-cigarettes (the heart analysis's reference group, which includes people who had stopped smoking); people who only smoked cigarettes; people who both vaped and smoked; in the lung analysis, people who had never used an e-cigarette (including people who smoked)
outcome: Newly reported, self-reported diagnoses of heart disease or stroke (heart analysis) and of asthma, COPD, emphysema or chronic bronchitis (lung analysis) over up to about four years; and what three reviews concluded about heart disease, lung disease and cancer
magnitude: Absolute counts and rates before ratios. Heart (Berlowitz et al., 2022; PATH Waves 1 to 5; 24,027 adults with no heart disease at the start; up to 4 years): new self-reported diagnosis of heart disease or stroke in 764 of 14,832 people who used neither product, 41 of 822 who only vaped, 569 of 6,515 who only smoked and 113 of 1,858 who did both (counts only; the groups differ in age and follow-up); age-adjusted rates as printed per 1,000 person-years 8.0, 9.7, 14.8 and 17.1 in that order (not reproducible from the counts). Hazard ratios against using neither, fully adjusted: only vaping 1.00 (0.69–1.45), only smoking 1.53 (1.30–1.79), both 1.54 (1.21–1.96); for heart attack, heart failure or stroke (519 cases, 15 among people who only vaped) 1.35 (0.75–2.42), 2.20 (1.73–2.81) and 2.08 (1.40–3.09). Against people who only smoked: only vaping 0.66 (0.46–0.94) and 0.61 (0.34–1.09); both 1.01 (0.81–1.26) and 0.94 (0.65–1.36). Adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity alone, only vaping against neither 1.16 (0.82–1.66) and 1.55 (0.87–2.76). Lungs (Xie et al., 2020; PATH Waves 1 to 4; 21,618 adults with no respiratory condition at the start; up to about 4 years): 1,460 (6.8%) with at least one new diagnosis (asthma 804, emphysema 336, COPD 573, chronic bronchitis 948 new diagnoses); adjusted rate per 1,000 person-years for any condition: never used 20.41 (18.65–22.17), ever 26.06 (22.63–29.49), former 26.12, current 26.68 (21.83–31.52) (about 2.0 against 2.6–2.7 in 100 a year, editors' conversion); for single conditions, never against ever: COPD 6.48 against 10.49, emphysema 3.74 against 5.76, chronic bronchitis 12.18 against 16.23, asthma 10.73 against 13.31. Rate ratios against never use (fully adjusted, ever / former / current): any condition 1.28 (1.10–1.48) / 1.28 (1.09–1.51) / 1.31 (1.08–1.59); chronic bronchitis 1.33 / 1.31 / 1.33; emphysema 1.54 / 1.42 / 1.69; COPD 1.62 / 1.66 / 1.57; asthma 1.24 (1.01–1.53) / 1.19 (0.95–1.50) / 1.32 (1.01–1.72). Adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity alone the ratios for ever use were 2.14 (any condition), 4.02 (emphysema) and 5.03 (COPD). Among people with good or better self-rated health (18,649): former 1.21 (1.00–1.47), current 1.43 (1.14–1.80); among people with no chronic condition at baseline (14,865): ever 1.20 (0.99–1.45), former 1.11 (0.90–1.37), current 1.40 (1.09–1.79). Reviews (the authors' own gradings): National Academies 2018 conclusions 9-1 (clinical cardiovascular outcomes, no available evidence), 11-1 (respiratory disease, no available evidence), 10-1 (intermediate cancer endpoints, no available evidence), 18-3 (long-term illness or death in people who vape and smoke, no available evidence), 11-4 (cough and wheeze in adolescents, moderate), 11-2 and 11-3 (adults with asthma or COPD who switch, limited); UK review 2022: clinical cardiovascular outcomes still no available evidence, cardiovascular risk uncertain, lung tests insufficient, no cancer incidence data; Australian review 2023: clinical cardiovascular outcomes and invasive cancer no available evidence, asthma, bronchitis and COPD insufficient in people who smoke and no available evidence in people who do not, certainty low or very low, EVALI conclusive (14% of cases in the largest study reported only nicotine products, 2% only non-nicotine products). Follow-up: up to 4 years in both cohort analyses; the reviews' evidence mostly concerns short-term effects.

evidence.locator: 1 Introduction, 1st to 4th paragraphs; reference 1
evidence.extracted: The commentary critiques the review of vaping by Banks and colleagues funded by the Australian Department of Health, citing the 2022 report to the Department (reference 1; the 2023 article read for this claim is based on it and appeared later). In the authors' view the review failed its aims because it did not compare the relative risk of the harms of vaping with those of cigarettes, did not consider the net public health impact, ignored evidence that vaping is effective for stopping smoking, and confused causation and correlation in reading the link between youth vaping and later smoking; and it applied different standards of evidence to the two questions, accepting a causal reading of observational associations for starting to smoke while rejecting similar observational evidence on quitting and treating trials that found vaping helps people quit with scepticism. The authors say they summarise evidence inconsistent with the review's main findings; they describe no search and no formal appraisal of their sources. These criticisms concern the question asked, the comparison and the standards of evidence, not new measurements of disease.

evidence.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: On the comparison, the authors hold that a meaningful assessment of the risk of vaping nicotine compares it with the far greater risk of continuing to smoke, because most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods (no source given). This is a disagreement of method with the review, which in its 2023 version states that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to measure effects of e-cigarettes, that people who neither smoke nor vape should be the main comparison group and that comparisons with smoking cannot reliably show the direct health effect (the Australian review's Limitations anchor above). The commentary does not discuss residual confounding by smoking, the reason the 2023 article gives for its choice.

evidence.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 6th to 9th paragraphs; references 34 to 45
evidence.extracted: On heart and lung outcomes the commentary cites no study of how often heart attack, stroke or chronic lung disease occur in people who vape, and it agrees that human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited; it states that most cardiovascular effects of vaping are consistent with those of nicotine (transiently raised pulse and blood pressure, cardiac contractility, arrhythmogenesis) and that nicotine may pose some risk in people with existing cardiovascular disease. Its evidence of benefit concerns people who switched from smoking: sustained falls in blood pressure (two studies), better vascular function after 4 weeks (one study), and improved respiratory symptoms, lung function, asthma, COPD, mucociliary clearance and fewer infections, with seven of the nine human studies or reviews it cites sharing authors (references 35, 36 and 38 to 42, by the author lists printed). The review rated changes after switching in people with asthma, bronchitis or COPD as insufficient evidence and clinical cardiovascular outcomes as no available evidence (anchors above), so the two weigh the same small body of switching studies differently and do not disagree about disease rates, which neither has.

evidence.extracted: On the 2019 US lung-injury outbreak (EVALI), the authors call a causal role for nicotine vaping highly implausible: they say the outbreak was strongly linked to vitamin E acetate added to illicit THC vaping oils and disappeared after its removal from the illicit supply (CDC, reference 46), and that the 14% of patients who denied using THC and had vaped nicotine do not prove a causal link with nicotine vaping products, because many patients who denied vaping THC were later found to have done so and no other causal agent has been identified in nicotine e-liquids (references 47 and 48; no numbers given). The review's own wording is a causal link largely for THC-containing products, with 14% of cases in its largest study reporting only nicotine products (anchor above), so the disagreement is about how far self-reported product use can be trusted.

risk_of_bias.note: Both cohort analyses are rated high on ROBINS-E (cards sc_berlowitz_2022 and sc_xie_2020): residual confounding by smoking history, since most people who vaped had smoked, the heart analysis's reference group includes people who had stopped smoking and the group that only vaped had more pack-years (mean 11.0 against 4.2, spreads several times the means); self-reported, non-adjudicated diagnoses; exposure recorded at the first wave only in the lung analysis. The three reviews are provisional or critically low on AMSTAR 2 (cards sc_nasem_2018, sc_banks_2023, sc_mcneill_2022). Counted once.

inconsistency.note: The two analyses answer different questions (heart and lung) and do not conflict; the three reviews agree that clinical outcomes have not been studied, and the cohort results do not contradict them.

indirectness.note: Direct for the claim as worded (newly reported diagnoses in adults over up to four years, and what reviews found). The wording does not reach cancer, people who have never smoked, longer use or current devices, and says so.

imprecision.note: Only 41 (any heart disease or stroke) and 15 (heart attack, heart failure or stroke) events occurred among people who only vaped, so the hazard ratios 1.00 (0.69–1.45) and 1.35 (0.75–2.42) fit a lower rate, no change or a clearly higher rate; the intervals for single lung conditions are wide (for example asthma, current use 1.32, 1.01–1.72).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable. Both cohort analyses use data from one federally funded study and declare no tobacco or vape industry funding; the reviews are reported as they state their own evidence.

large_effect.note: The lung ratios (about 1.2 to 1.7) are modest and fell sharply when smoking history was added; the heart ratio for people who only vaped is 1.00. No upgrade.

dose_response.note: Exploratory highest rates with every-day use, first use before age 25 and established use (values in a supplement not read); not counted.

plausible_confounding.note: Residual confounding by smoking more plausibly raises the lung ratios, while reverse causation (people with early symptoms switching to vaping) could hide an association; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational cohorts start low. Downgraded once for risk of bias (both analyses rated high on ROBINS-E) and once for imprecision (few events in people who only vaped), which reaches the floor, very low. Rated as worded: the claim is that the evidence is insufficient to say whether vaping changes the risk of heart or lung disease, not that vaping has no effect; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. The three reviews' judgments (no available evidence, insufficient evidence, low or very low certainty) are their authors' judgments and are reported, not adopted. Overlap: the heart and lung analyses are two analyses of one cohort that share data and some authors, so they are not independent replications; the reviews overlap in the studies they draw on. The acute lung injury outbreak (EVALI) is outside the rating: the Australian review judged it conclusive, largely with THC-containing products. A published critique of the Australian review (Mendelsohn et al., 2022) disputes its comparison group and standards of evidence but brings no data on disease rates, so it changes no rating. Funding is set out in the statement: no tobacco or vape industry funding is declared for the cohort analyses or the reviews read; the pharmaceutical and device-company ties of some authors are listed as printed, and the sponsors of the studies in the National Academies report are in an online table that was not read.

statement: In US adults who used only e-cigarettes every day (156 people), compared with adults who smoked only cigarettes every day (3,430), in the first wave (2013–2014) of the national PATH survey, the e-cigarette group said yes less often to each of four dependence questions: self-rated dependence 77.2% against 94.0%, strong cravings 72.8% against 86.9%, difficulty keeping from using where it was prohibited 5.6% against 28.6%, and feeling they really needed to use 71.5% against 88.5% (adjusted odds ratios for the cigarette group 2.85 to 6.92, every interval excluding 1); they also waited longer after waking before first use (adjusted geometric mean 29.2 against 20.0 minutes) (Liu et al., 2017). Dependence symptoms were therefore common among adults who only vaped every day, and less common than among adults who only smoked every day. Other surveys, read only as the National Academies describe them, point the same way (a 2012–2013 US telephone survey of 124 against 3,963 adults; a second analysis of the same PATH wave; a voluntary web survey of 3,609 people who vaped daily and recalled their earlier smoking), as do 2021 surveys of young people in England (52.5% of 16–19-year-olds who vaped rated themselves a little or very dependent, against 83% of those who smoked; McNeill et al., 2022). The National Academies judged the evidence that vaping results in dependence symptoms substantial, that the risk and severity are lower than for cigarettes moderate, and that product features (device type, nicotine concentration, flavouring, brand) are an important determinant moderate (the committee's judgments; the UK review restates them); the Australian review judged the evidence in people who smoke limited and in people who do not smoke substantial (Banks et al., 2023). Where product features were measured, in a voluntary web survey, higher dependence scores went with larger, more advanced devices and with a higher nicotine concentration of the liquid. These are one-time surveys with no follow-up. Nearly all of the e-cigarette group (92.9%) had smoked before and earlier smoking was not adjusted for; the people who keep vaping daily are a small selected share of those who try it; one item (difficulty refraining where use is prohibited) is a less valid indicator for e-cigarettes; there is no agreed scale for comparing the two; the surveys date from 2012–2014 and cannot speak to newer products such as nicotine-salt liquids and disposables, which the UK and Australian reviews describe as little studied; and nothing read follows dependence over time or compares dependence on vaping with dependence on smoking in people who have never smoked. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In a large US survey from 2013 to 2014, adults who only vaped every day reported signs of dependence less often than adults who only smoked every day: 77 in 100 rated themselves as dependent, against 94 in 100 of those who smoked, and 6 in 100 found it hard to go without where use was banned, against 29 in 100. Other surveys in the US and England pointed the same way. So daily vaping was linked to dependence, but to less of it than daily smoking. Nearly all the people who vaped had smoked before, the surveys are one-off snapshots from before newer products such as disposables became common, and no study read can say how dependent a person who never smoked becomes.
population: Adults in the United States who used only e-cigarettes, or only cigarettes, every day (PATH Wave 1, 2013–2014); young people aged 11 to 19 in England (2021 surveys); other adult surveys as described by the National Academies
exposure: Daily use of e-cigarettes only
comparator: Daily use of cigarettes only
outcome: Dependence symptoms (self-rated dependence, strong cravings, difficulty keeping from using where prohibited, feeling a need to use, time to first use after waking) and dependence index scores
magnitude: Daily e-cigarette-only (n = 156) vs daily cigarette-only (n = 3,430), PATH Wave 1, weighted: self-rated dependence 77.2% vs 94.0% (adjusted odds ratio for the cigarette group 6.92, 95% CL 4.46–10.73); strong cravings 72.8% vs 86.9% (2.85, 1.92–4.23); difficulty keeping from using where prohibited 5.6% vs 28.6% (6.39, 2.85–14.32); felt they really needed to use 71.5% vs 88.5% (3.89, 2.36–6.40); time to first use after waking, adjusted geometric mean 29.16 (24.39–34.87) vs 20.03 (18.66–21.49) minutes (editors' calculation: ratio 1.46). As described by the National Academies: US National Adult Tobacco Survey 2012–2013, daily e-cigarette-only n = 124 vs cigarette-only n = 3,963, every symptom less common in the e-cigarette group (for example use within 30 minutes of waking 46.1%, 35.1–57.4); PATH Wave 1 item-response index, e-cigarette-only (n = 437) 1.37 SD units below cigarette-only (n = 8,689); web survey of 3,609 people who vaped daily, index 8.1 vs 14.5 for recalled smoking. England 2021, 16–19-year-olds: rated themselves a little or very dependent 52.5% of those who vaped vs 83% of those who smoked (McNeill et al., 2022).

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: In the 2013–2014 PATH Wave 1 adult survey, 156 adults who used only e-cigarettes every day and 3,430 who smoked only cigarettes every day (weighted shares of the analysis sample 4.6% and 95.4%) answered four yes/no questions. The e-cigarette group said yes less often to each (weighted, each p < 0.0001): considered themselves addicted 77.2% vs 94.0%; ever had strong cravings 72.8% vs 86.9%; found it difficult in the past 12 months to keep from using where it was prohibited 5.6% vs 28.6%; ever felt they really needed to use 71.5% vs 88.5%. First use within 5 minutes of waking 15.1% vs 24.0%; after more than 60 minutes 10.9% vs 12.1%.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC5868349

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 3
evidence.extracted: Adjusted odds ratios for the cigarette group against the e-cigarette group (95% CL), adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education and poverty status: addicted 6.92 (4.46–10.73); strong cravings 2.85 (1.92–4.23); difficult to refrain where prohibited 6.39 (2.85–14.32); really needed to use 3.89 (2.36–6.40). Time to first use after waking, geometric mean in minutes, adjusted (home smoking rules added): 29.16 (24.39–34.87) in the e-cigarette group vs 20.03 (18.66–21.49) in the cigarette group; unadjusted 23.46 (19.47–28.27) vs 19.25 (18.25–20.30). Editors' calculation: ratio of adjusted geometric means 1.46.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC5868349

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Ascertainment of Study Population, 5th paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: Of the 156 in the e-cigarette group, 145 (92.9%) had formerly smoked cigarettes at the survey's established level, 10 (6.7%) had only experimented with smoking and 1 (0.4%) had never used any tobacco product. The authors state that over three quarters of the group considered themselves addicted, and that only 6.8% of adults who had ever tried an e-cigarette used one daily against 23.8% of adults who had tried a cigarette and smoked daily, so the exclusive daily comparison picks the most dependent people who vape. The groups also differed on poverty (below the poverty level 14.6% vs 35.0%) and on home rules (use allowed anywhere at any time at home 61.9% vs 26.5%).
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC5868349

evidence.locator: Study limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Conclusions
evidence.extracted: The authors name as limits that amount used per day could not be compared (the units for e-cigarettes and cigarettes differ, because e-cigarette products vary in device, liquid nicotine concentration and flavour), that duration of use could not be reliably calculated, and that most adults who had used e-cigarettes in the past 30 days also used other products, so dependence is hard to attribute to one product (they were excluded). They call for future studies of exposure biomarkers such as cotinine and of how dependence develops over time and differs by device and liquid characteristics, noting that the longitudinal design of PATH will help. Editors' reading: the dependence items are self-reported; the design is a single survey wave, so nothing follows people over time.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC5868349

evidence.locator: Chapter 8 › Epidemiology › Nationally Representative Studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies: the 2012–2013 National Adult Tobacco Survey (a representative US telephone survey, identical wording for each product) compared 124 adults who used only e-cigarettes every day with 3,963 who smoked only cigarettes every day. Each dependence symptom was significantly less common in the e-cigarette group (for example use within 30 minutes of waking 46.1%, 95% CI 35.1–57.4; withdrawal symptoms 22.8%, 14.8–33.4) and not significantly different from people who smoked cigars daily (131). The committee notes that comparisons were not adjusted for prior tobacco history or demographics and that the market then held early-model devices.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)

evidence.locator: Chapter 8 › Epidemiology › Nationally Representative Studies, 3rd to 7th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The committee's account of Liu et al. (2017) repeats its figures (156 vs 3,430; 77.2% vs 94.0%; 5.6% vs 28.6%) and reads it as strong evidence that dependence symptoms are fairly high among adults who only vape every day but not as high as among adults who only smoke every day. Its limits: prior tobacco history was not adjusted for (92.9% of the e-cigarette group had smoked), so group differences may reflect earlier exposure, and the item on difficulty refraining where use is prohibited is probably a less valid indicator for e-cigarettes because fewer places restrict them (61.9% of the e-cigarette group could use theirs anywhere at home, against 26.5% of the cigarette group).
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)

evidence.locator: Chapter 8 › Epidemiology › Nationally Representative Studies, 8th to 11th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies: a separate analysis of PATH Wave 1 (437 adults who used only e-cigarettes in the past year, daily or not, and 8,689 who only smoked cigarettes) used a 16-item dependence index tested for equal validity across products. Average severity was 1.37 standard deviation units lower for the e-cigarette-only group than for the cigarette-only group, comparable to cigar-only and higher among daily than non-daily e-cigarette-only participants (difference 0.40 SD). 3 of the 24 items were dropped as invalid indicators and 16 were retained as having minimal or no differential validity across products. The sample partly overlaps Liu et al. (same survey wave; this analysis included daily and non-daily users, Liu et al. daily users); the committee calls the two non-redundant data sources, but the editors count them as one dataset.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)

evidence.locator: Chapter 8 › Epidemiology › Anonymous Web Surveys of E-Cigarette Users, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies: a voluntary anonymous web survey (December 2012 to August 2014; 3,609 people who vaped every day and had not smoked in the past 30 days, recruited on vaping and medical websites; 42% reported advocating for e-cigarettes online) compared dependence on e-cigarettes with their recall of earlier smoking: mean index 8.1 (SD 3.5) vs 14.5 (3.7). E-cigarette scores were higher with longer use, larger devices with a button, higher price and a higher nicotine concentration of the liquid. A second analysis of the same data (1,048 first-generation vs 3,373 advanced devices) found higher scores with advanced devices (8.3 vs 7.1 with first-generation) and a shorter time to first use after waking (38.7 vs 67.3 minutes), although their liquid had a lower nicotine concentration (15.1 vs 19.1 mg/mL). The committee notes the sample is not representative and that recall of earlier smoking could bias the comparison.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)

evidence.locator: Chapter 8 › Conclusions, Conclusion 8-1
evidence.extracted: The National Academies judged that there is substantial evidence that e-cigarette use results in symptoms of dependence on e-cigarettes, resting on several supportive findings from good-quality observational studies with very few or no credible opposing findings (symptoms of appreciable prevalence or severity; more frequent or longer use goes with more symptoms), supported by abuse-liability studies. This is the committee's judgment.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)

evidence.locator: Chapter 8 › Conclusions, Conclusion 8-2
evidence.extracted: The National Academies judged that there is moderate evidence that the risk and severity of dependence are lower for e-cigarettes than for combustible cigarettes, resting on several supportive findings from fair-quality studies with very few or no credible opposing findings; chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out. This is the committee's judgment.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)

evidence.locator: Chapter 8 › Conclusions, Conclusion 8-3
evidence.extracted: The National Academies judged that there is moderate evidence that variability in product characteristics (nicotine concentration, flavouring, device type and brand) is an important determinant of the risk and severity of e-cigarette dependence: some findings link nicotine concentration, flavouring, device generation and brand to outcomes indicating dependence risk, with very few or no credible opposing findings. This is the committee's judgment.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)

evidence.locator: Summary page › Chapter 5: Nicotine › Main findings › Nicotine dependency, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Main findings page › 5. Nicotine, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The UK review states that there was substantial evidence from previous reports (National Academies, the Committee on Toxicity and its own 2018 report) that vaping can result in symptoms of nicotine dependency, and moderate evidence that the risk and severity are lower than for cigarette smoking and vary with product characteristics such as device type and nicotine concentration; its pharmacokinetic review is consistent with this. It adds that many scales are used and there is no consensus on the best scale for vaping dependence, which makes comparison with smoking difficult, and cites a systematic review suggesting higher nicotine concentrations might increase abuse potential and appeal. The grading statements rest on earlier reports and existing evidence, not a new independent finding; the point about scales is this review's own finding.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Summary page › Chapter 3: Vaping among young people › Main findings › Perceived addiction and urges to vape, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: In the 2021 ITC Youth survey of 16–19-year-olds in England, 52.5% of those who currently vaped felt a little or very addicted to vaping (42.8% did not) against 83% of those who currently smoked who felt a little or very addicted to smoking (14.5% did not). Urges almost daily or more: 44.5% of those who vaped (16.8% never) against 66.6% of those who smoked (urges daily or several times a day; 4.7% never). In the 2021 ASH-Y survey of 11–18-year-olds, 41.5% of those who vaped had no urges and 23.5% strong to extremely strong urges, against 24.3% and 31.4% of those who smoked. The summary page does not say the groups were exclusive or adjusted.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Summary page › Chapter 5: Nicotine › Implications › Improved surveillance and further research, 4th to 6th paragraphs; Need for global standards and protocols, 1st paragraph; Chapter 3 › Implications › Further monitoring and research, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The UK review states that dependence on vaping assessed in 2021 appears lower than on smoking for young people and that further research is needed on dependence by type of product, nicotine type and nicotine strength. It calls for longitudinal studies of how dependence changes with experience, for measurements across products in people who have never smoked and start nicotine through vaping, and for a global consensus on how to measure dependence so that vaping and smoking can be compared.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Results › Health outcomes, Box 3, row 'Dependence and abuse liability (52)'; Box 2, same row
evidence.extracted: The Australian umbrella and top-up review (52 studies on dependence and abuse liability: 13 randomised trials, 1 cohort, 17 non-randomised intervention studies, 21 cross-sectional surveys) rates substantial evidence that nicotine e-cigarette use leads to dependence on e-cigarettes in people who do not smoke; in people who smoke, limited evidence that it leads to dependence, limited evidence that abuse liability is lower than for cigarettes or higher than for nicotine replacement products, and insufficient evidence that abuse liability is influenced by flavour and nicotine content. This is graded more cautiously than the National Academies' moderate rating for the comparison with cigarettes.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC10952413

risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional self-report comparisons (card sc_liu_2017: ROBINS-E overall high). The e-cigarette group is selected (nearly all had formerly smoked; few of those who try e-cigarettes use them daily) and prior tobacco history, length of use and amount per day are not adjusted for; one item is a less valid indicator for e-cigarettes. The other surveys are read only through the National Academies' account, which itself flags a non-representative web sample with recall of earlier smoking.

inconsistency.note: Every source read points the same way; the size of the gap differs by item and survey.

indirectness.note: The data are from surveys of 2012–2014, before newer products such as nicotine-salt liquids and disposables were common (the National Academies call generalizability to products of that time questionable, and the UK and Australian reviews list newer products and dependence by product type as little studied); several sources are second-hand, and the UK review's dependence statements restate National Academies and earlier reports (counted once, as are the two PATH analyses).

imprecision.note: Intervals on the adjusted odds ratios exclude 1; the smallest e-cigarette groups are 124 and 156 people.

large_effect.note: Adjusted odds ratios are 2.85 to 6.92, but the biases that remain (selection of people who stay with e-cigarettes after smoking; prior tobacco history not adjusted) run away from the null, so no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational (cross-sectional survey) evidence starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. The National Academies rate the lower-dependence comparison moderate and the dependence finding substantial, and the UK review repeats those ratings; these are the authors' judgments over mixed study types, not a GRADE rating, and overlapping reports and the two PATH analyses are counted once. Status replicated rests on independent datasets (US telephone survey, PATH, a web survey, English youth surveys) that agree on direction, three of them known here only through the reviews.
