statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether the vapour breathed out by people who vape harms the health of people nearby: no study read measured disease, or early markers of disease, in people exposed to it, so what is known is exposure. Compared with the same air before or without vaping, chamber, home and convention studies found higher airborne nicotine and fine particles than background in every study that measured them, by the National Academies' account (one home study's median fine-particle level matched a non-vaping home although it rose in real time during vaping; in a chamber with five people vaping, one-hour air nicotine 3.32 µg/m3 against undetectable and fine particles (PM2.5) 152 against 32.4 µg/m3; at a vaping convention an estimated 24-hour average PM10 of 1,800 µg/m3, 12 times the US 24-hour standard), rising with the number of people vaping; in homes, cotinine (a breakdown product of nicotine) in saliva and urine was higher in 5 non-smoking people living with someone who vaped than in people in control homes; and in six biomarker studies summarised by the UK review, short exposures produced no detectable change in nicotine, volatile organic compounds or tobacco-specific nitrosamines, while longer exposure during heavy sustained vaping raised nicotine or breakdown products of toxicants. Against second-hand cigarette smoke, levels were lower in the four studies that compared them (airborne nicotine 3.32 against 31.60 µg/m3 and PM2.5 152 against 819 µg/m3 in one chamber; 0.13 against 0.74 µg/m3 airborne nicotine in homes), which the National Academies rated moderate evidence while adding that the health effects of the lower exposures are unknown and that children, pregnant women, older people and people with heart or lung disease may be at special risk; a modelling study found a high-emitting device in a bar scenario exceeding acute reference levels for formaldehyde and acrolein, with estimated health loss in some scenarios comparable to second-hand smoke. A Dutch risk assessment (Visser et al., 2019) measured the first breath of 17 volunteers after one puff (nicotine in all but one, propylene glycol in 4, tobacco-specific nitrosamines in the 9 tested, glycerol in none) and modelled worst-case scenarios: the margins between modelled exposure and the level at which effects are expected were small for nicotine's effect on heart rate and blood pressure in a car (2.1), for propylene glycol irritation (17), and below the authors' threshold for nitrosamines and tumour risk in both a car and an office (521 and 2,297 against 10,000); nothing was measured in a room, a car or a person nearby, and the authors call the effects relatively mild even in the extreme scenario. The Australian review rated the rise in indoor particulate matter conclusive and airborne nicotine limited, and the evidence that these are at hazardous levels insufficient (Banks et al., 2023). The studies were single sessions of minutes to hours or one-off home measurements, in small groups, and mostly published between 2014 and 2017; no study followed people nearby for weeks or years. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (the exposure findings).
plain: When someone vapes in a room, studies find more nicotine and tiny particles in the air than before, but less than cigarette smoke gives off. In the few homes tested, people living with someone who vaped had more of a nicotine breakdown product in saliva and urine than people in homes without vaping. Nobody has measured whether this harms the health of people nearby: no study read followed them for disease. A Dutch computer model of worst-case rooms found small safety margins for some chemicals, but nothing was measured in a real room, car or person. The studies were short, small and mostly from 2014 to 2017.
population: People who do not vape who are near someone vaping (volunteers in chambers and rooms, people living with someone who vapes, people at vaping conventions); 17 adults who vaped daily whose breath was measured (Netherlands)
exposure: Breathing air in which someone has vaped (second-hand vapour)
comparator: The same air without vaping (background), and, in four studies, air with cigarette smoke
outcome: Health effects in people nearby (not measured in any study read); exposure measures: airborne nicotine, fine particles and other chemicals, and nicotine biomarkers
magnitude: Health effects in people nearby: not measured in any study read. Exposure, as the National Academies describe the studies (vaping against baseline or control): chamber with 5 people vaping, one-hour air nicotine 3.32 (SD 2.49) vs undetectable µg/m3 and PM2.5 152 (86.8) vs 32.4 µg/m3; 9 volunteers for 2 hours in a café-like room, PM2.5 197 vs 6 µg/m3 and nicotine 2.2 vs below 0.04 µg/m3; 37 volunteers over 4 hours, nicotine 0.38 to 2.83 µg/m3 (several-fold below workplace limits); homes of people living with someone vaping more than 2 hours a day vs control homes, median air nicotine 0.11 vs 0.01 µg/m3, salivary cotinine 0.24 vs 0.05 ng/mL, urinary cotinine 2.64 vs 0.72 ng/mL; convention, estimated 24-hour PM10 1,800 µg/m3. Against second-hand cigarette smoke: one chamber, airborne nicotine 3.32 vs 31.60 µg/m3 and PM2.5 151.7 vs 819.3 µg/m3 (stated as 10 and 7 times; editors' calculation from the raw means 9.5 and 5.4 times); homes, airborne nicotine 0.13 vs 0.74 µg/m3 (5.7 times) and salivary cotinine 0.19 vs 0.38 ng/mL; surface nicotine 7.7 vs 1,303 µg/m2 (found in half of 8 vaping homes vs all 6 smoking homes). UK review: 6 biomarker studies, none from the UK; short exposures no detectable change. Dutch measurement and model (Visser et al., 2019): first breath after one puff, nicotine median 108 ng (below the limit to 2,140 ng), propylene glycol seen in 4 of 17, glycerol in none, nitrosamines up to 77 pg (NDMA equivalent); modelled car / office: nicotine 0.16 / 0.036 mg/m3, propylene glycol 9.5 / 2.16 mg/m3; margins 2.1 / 6 (nicotine, heart rate and blood pressure), 17 / 74–81 (propylene glycol, irritation), 521 / 2,297 (nitrosamines, against 10,000).

evidence.locator: Results › 3.3 Analysis of Exhaled Vapor, 3rd to 6th paragraphs; Table 3
evidence.extracted: In 17 adults who vaped daily (9 also smoked), using three tobacco-flavoured products chosen by the researchers and with their own breath before the first puff as the control, the first breath after one puff held nicotine in all but one person (median 108 ng, up to 2,140 ng), propylene glycol in 4 of 17 (up to 127 µg; median below the limit), glycerol in none (below the limit of quantification), tobacco-specific nitrosamines, measured in 9 people (total up to 77 pg as NDMA equivalent, median 28 pg, lowest value below the limit of quantification; no difference between people who also smoked and people who only vaped, p = 0.79), formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein in none of the 4 tested, and of 13 metals in 3 people only copper (up to 2.92 ng). Only the first exhalation after each puff was sampled.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC6539638

evidence.locator: Results › 3.4 Bystander Exposure, 1st paragraph; Tables 4 and 5; Methods › 2.7, last paragraph
evidence.extracted: Modelled scenarios, not measurements in any person nearby: a car (2 people vaping at 0.5 puffs a minute for 1 hour in 2 m3 with no ventilation, the bystander a child; the authors say it approximates the highest exposure expected in everyday situations) and an office (1 person at 2 puffs a minute for 4 hours in 30 m3 with ventilation of 0.5 per hour; the authors consider it more indicative of typical exposure), both built from the single highest exhaled amount for each chemical and an assumed share of the inhaled amount (40% for local effects, 33% for systemic effects) appearing in the first exhalation. Modelled air concentrations (car / office): propylene glycol 9.5 / 2.16 mg/m3; nicotine 0.16 / 0.036 mg/m3; nitrosamines as NDMA equivalent 5.8 / 1.31 ng/m3; copper 219 / 50 ng/m3. Editors' calculation: the Table 5 values are reproduced from the Table 3 maxima and these settings.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC6539638

evidence.locator: Results › 3.7 Propylene Glycol; 3.9 and 3.10 Nicotine; 3.11 Nitrosamines; 3.12 Copper; Table 6; Conclusions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Margins between the modelled exposure and the level at which an effect is expected (car / office): nicotine's effect on heart rate and systolic blood pressure 2.1 / 6 (the authors say such effects should be expected in the car and cannot be excluded in the office, of a size they compare with the caffeine in 2 or 3 cups of coffee); propylene glycol airway and eye irritation 17 / 74 or 81 (cannot be excluded in the car, mild if it occurs); tobacco-specific nitrosamines and tumour risk 521 / 2,297 against the authors' threshold of 10,000 for low concern (risk cannot be excluded in the car and cannot be assessed with sufficient certainty in the office; all four nitrosamines were treated as equally potent as N-nitrosodimethylamine, which the authors say probably overestimates the risk). Local airway effects of nicotine were not expected in either scenario. Copper stayed below a tolerable air concentration.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC6539638

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusions › Regulatory Implications; Abstract; Funding; Conflicts of Interest
evidence.extracted: The authors call the effects on bystanders relatively mild even in extreme scenarios, say the nitrosamine risk could be avoided if liquids had no detectable nitrosamines and that only a limited number of liquids on the market contain significant amounts (no citation in the passage), and describe this, to the best of their knowledge, as the first toxicological risk assessment of e-cigarette vapour to bystanders. The abstract states that vaping can clearly affect bystanders' health and names glycerol as an irritant, although glycerol was below the limit of quantification in all 17 volunteers. Funding as printed: Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport; the authors declare no conflict of interest.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC6539638

evidence.locator: Methods › 2.7; Results › 3.5; Discussion, 3rd to 7th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Limits the authors state: only the first exhalation after each puff was sampled and the rest estimated with an assumed retention from a model developed for cigarette smoking; the highest concentration was used; the highest emissions seen probably do not represent the worst case with so few volunteers, and low-powered products probably lead to underestimation; changes of the vapour in air, nitrosamine formation from nicotine in air, and deposits on surfaces were not modelled; toxicity data are missing for most flavour compounds. Nothing was measured in a room, a car or a person nearby, and no cigarette was measured.

evidence.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Characteristics and Chemical Composition of Secondhand E-Cigarette Aerosol, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, two modelling studies (Logue 2017, Rostami 2016); the passage gives results for Logue 2017 only. In a home scenario the contribution of second-hand vapour did not exceed California 8-hour reference exposure levels except with a high-emitting device (4.8 V; up to 12 µg/m3 formaldehyde and 2.6 µg/m3 acrolein); in a bar scenario, formaldehyde (mean 135 µg/m3) and acrolein (28 µg/m3) exceeded the acute 1-hour level for the highest-emitting device and voltage and exceeded 8-hour levels in several bars under less intense vaping. Health-loss estimates (disability-adjusted life years; also Logue 2017) for device and voltage combinations were lower than, but in some instances comparable to, those estimated for second-hand tobacco smoke. The committee identified no study of health effects or early biomarkers of disease from second-hand e-cigarette aerosol.

risk_of_bias.note: Small, mostly single-session studies (4 to 37 volunteers in chambers; 5 people living with someone who vaped), read here through the National Academies' and the UK review's descriptions, which cannot be appraised from the summaries; the one primary source read in full (card sc_visser_2019, 17 volunteers and a model with worst-case assumptions) is rated high risk of bias on the editors' checklist.

inconsistency.note: The exposure findings point the same way; levels differ with setting and number of people vaping (one home study found a median similar to a control home despite real-time rises), which the sources explain by exposure conditions.

indirectness.note: The outcome of interest, health of people nearby, was not measured; air and cotinine measures and a model stand in for it. Chambers and conventions differ from everyday rooms, and the studies are mostly from 2014–2017, with the devices of that period.

imprecision.note: Small samples are counted under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Observational and laboratory exposure evidence starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on health effects, which is what the sources support: the National Academies, the UK review and the Australian review all say that health effects of second-hand vapour have not been measured or cannot be concluded. The National Academies' conclusive rating concerns the rise in airborne particles and nicotine, not harm. Status replicated applies to that exposure finding, shown by independent studies in different settings.

statement: How much less harmful vaping is than smoking is contested, and no source read measures it: none compares how often disease or death occurs over many years in people who only vape with people who smoke (the one national cohort read, followed for up to about four years, compared people who vape with people who use neither product; see the claim on vaping and disease), so every estimate rests on levels of chemicals in the body, short-term measurements and expert judgement. Lower exposure is not disputed in the sources read: compared with people who smoke, people who vape had lower levels of many smoke-related toxicants in the body (UK review, pooled analyses: breakdown products of tobacco-specific nitrosamines 58% to 94% lower), and in the National Academies' account of 15 human studies, lasting from single sessions to about two years, people who switched completely from smoking showed better short-term respiratory, cardiovascular and oral measures in all but one. What is disputed is what that shows about overall harm. On one side, the UK government-commissioned review judges its own 2015 estimate, that vaping is at least 95% less harmful than smoking (smoking at least 20 times more harmful), still broadly accurate over the short and medium term and prefers to say that vaping carries only a small fraction of the risks of smoking (McNeill et al., 2022); the National Academies rated the evidence of lower exposure to toxicants conclusive and of reduced short-term adverse outcomes in several organ systems substantial (the committee's judgments; National Academies, 2018); and a 2022 commentary on the Australian review (Mendelsohn et al., 2022), which does not mention the figure, argues that the comparison that matters is with continuing to smoke and cites far lower toxicant exposure, short-term improvements in people who switched and a modelled lifetime cancer risk below 0.5% of smoking's (studies not read). On the other, a BMJ analysis published in September 2015, shortly after the report (McKee & Capewell, 2015), and an editorial (Eissenberg et al., 2020) give the same account of where the figure came from, one meeting of 12 people who rated products by putting their opinions into a decision model (in July 2013, per the editorial), and both quote that exercise's authors listing the lack of hard evidence for most harms as a limitation (the 2014 paper reporting it was not read); the 2015 analysis adds that the chief executive of the meeting's sponsor and the chief scientific adviser of a supporting organisation are reported elsewhere to have received tobacco-company funding (the 2014 paper states its sponsor had no role) and that the panel's selection was not explained, argues that where risks are uncertain the burden of proof lies with those who act and that people who do not smoke should also be a comparison, and offers no estimate of its own, and the editorial argues that the figure should not be relied on now that devices and liquids have changed; the Australian government-commissioned review holds that comparisons with smoking cannot establish the direct health effect of vaping, takes people who have never smoked and people who use no nicotine as the main reference, found no evidence on clinical cardiovascular disease or invasive cancer, and rated certainty low or very low for most outcomes (Banks et al., 2023). Each side concedes part of the other's case: the editorial that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines; the Australian review that people who switch completely and promptly may benefit; the UK review that vaping is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked, and that exposure to harmful substances is similar or higher than with using no nicotine product; the 2015 analysis that e-cigarettes lack some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes, such as tar; the 2022 commentary that human evidence on cardiovascular outcomes is limited, that nicotine may carry some risk for people with existing heart disease and that the effects of inhaled flavourings are largely unknown. The longest follow-up the UK review could summarise was 12 months, and many of its pooled biomarker results come from tobacco-industry-funded trials in confinement of up to 7 days; the funders and interests of each source are given in the anchors and the flag note. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: People who smoke and switch completely to vaping have much lower levels of many smoke chemicals in their bodies than people who keep smoking, and in short studies their lung and heart checks did better. But how much less harmful vaping is over a whole life is argued over, and nobody has measured it yet: no study has followed people who only vape for decades to count illness or death. A UK review says the old estimate that smoking is at least 20 times more harmful still fits the short and medium term. Two critiques, from 2015 and 2020, say the estimate began as the opinions of 12 people at one meeting in 2013 and should not be relied on, and an Australian review says that comparing with smoking cannot show what vaping does to health by itself; a 2022 critique of that review says the comparison that matters is with carrying on smoking. None of the sources read says vaping is risk-free, most of all for people who have never smoked, and compared with using no nicotine at all, exposure to harmful substances is similar or higher.
population: Adults who smoke or have smoked and who vape or switch completely to vaping (mostly short studies); people who have never smoked and who vape; as covered by two government-commissioned reviews, a National Academies report, an editorial, a 2015 analysis article and a 2022 commentary
exposure: Vaping nicotine e-cigarettes (alone, or replacing smoking completely)
comparator: Continuing to smoke cigarettes; and, as a second comparison, using no nicotine product
outcome: Overall harm to health, disease and death (not measured in any source read); what was measured instead: levels of chemicals in the body, short-term lung, heart and blood-pressure measures, laboratory emissions, and expert ratings
magnitude: Not estimable from the sources read: none gives the rate of any disease or death in people who only vape, against people who smoke or people who use no nicotine. The figure in dispute: vaping at least 95% less harmful than smoking, that is smoking at least 20 times more harmful, stated in the UK 2015 report and described in 2022 as broadly accurate over the short and medium term (McNeill et al., 2022); described as arising from a July 2013 rating by 12 experts of 12 products on 14 criteria (Eissenberg et al., 2020; the rating itself not read), and as coming from a single meeting of 12 people who built a multicriteria decision analysis model of their opinions (McKee & Capewell, 2015). Estimate cited on the other side: lifetime cancer risk from vaping less than 0.5% of that from smoking, modelled from what aerosol contains (two studies cited by Mendelsohn et al., 2022; not read). Measured, people who vape against people who smoke (UK review, pooled analyses): nitrosamine breakdown products NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94%, NNN 90% lower; acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 71%, acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA 94%, butadiene metabolite MHBMA 83% lower; blood carboxyhaemoglobin lower; nicotine not different in 5 analyses of people who vaped and smoked at least weekly; formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive; metals mixed. Against people who use no nicotine: nicotine biomarkers higher; volatile organic compounds not significantly different except CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study); nitrosamine breakdown products higher in 3 cross-sectional analyses (past smoking not separable); metals mostly higher. As described by the National Academies: smoke constituents 9- to 450-fold higher than aerosol (15 puffs assumed equal to one cigarette; Goniewicz et al., 2014); toxicants 82% to more than 99% lower per puff (Margham et al., 2016); about 1,500 times more harmful and potentially harmful constituents in smoke (Tayyarah and Long, 2014); 4 of 11 metals higher in one aerosol than in smoke (Williams et al., 2013); in people who switched, urinary biomarkers 29% to 95% lower after 5 days (105 people), NNAL down 57% after 1 week and 64% after 2 weeks (20 people); all but one of the human studies showed short-term improvement, none showed more harm among people who switched. Follow-up: the UK review could summarise at most 12 months; the Australian review found no available evidence on clinical cardiovascular disease (21 studies) or invasive cancer (1 study).

evidence.locator: Chapter 16 › Overall findings in the context of our series of evidence reviews, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The UK review's authors recall that their 2015 report estimated vaping to be at least 95% less harmful than smoking (smoking at least 20 times more harmful to the person), a statement offered to help the public and professionals grasp the size of the gap. They write that summarising relative risks across many products, behaviours and biomarkers can be simplistic and misread; that, on the evidence reviewed, they judge the at-least-95% estimate still broadly accurate for the short and medium term; that it may now be more fitting to summarise their findings with their other firm statement, that vaping carries only a small share of smoking's risks; and that this does not mean vaping is free of risk, particularly for people who have never smoked. They add that the size of this gap is not reflected in current public perceptions. The pages read give no source or calculation for the 2015 figure. This is the authors' judgment on an estimate from their own earlier report.

evidence.quote: vaping poses only a small fraction of the risks of smoking

evidence.locator: Main findings page › 2.1 Overall conclusions; 2.2 Biomarkers of toxicant exposure; 2.3 Biomarkers of potential harm
evidence.extracted: The review's overall conclusions, on the evidence it reviewed: in the short and medium term vaping carries a small share of smoking's risks; it is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked; evidence is mostly limited to short and medium term effects, so studies of vaping for more than 12 months are needed; more standardised methods in future studies would improve interpretation. Biomarkers of toxicant exposure: significantly lower exposure to harmful substances from vaping than from smoking, as shown by biomarkers associated with the risk of cancer, respiratory and cardiovascular conditions; similar or higher exposure than with not using nicotine products; no significant increase of toxicant biomarkers after short-term second-hand exposure among people who do not smoke or vape. Biomarkers of potential harm: the team could draw only limited conclusions, but better-run studies of short and medium term risks found no major causes of concern associated with vaping.

evidence.locator: Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Main findings › Nicotine; Volatile organic compounds; Tobacco specific nitrosamines; Other potential toxicants; Carbon monoxide; Metals
evidence.extracted: The systematic review's biomarker chapter (60 studies of nicotine, 24 of volatile organic compounds, 28 of tobacco-specific nitrosamines, 9 of other toxicants, 33 of carbon monoxide and 10 of metals; designs, definitions and exposure periods varied and few studies were from the UK). People who vape compared with people who smoke, pooled analyses: nicotine and its breakdown products not significantly different in 5 analyses of people who vaped and smoked at least weekly; volatile organic compound breakdown products mostly significantly lower in 15 analyses (acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 71%, acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA 94%, 1,3-butadiene metabolite MHBMA 83% lower), with formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive; nitrosamine breakdown products significantly lower in all 5 analyses (NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94%, NNN 90% lower); blood carboxyhaemoglobin significantly lower in both analyses; metals mixed. People who vape compared with people who use no nicotine: nicotine biomarkers higher, as expected (4 analyses); volatile organic compounds not significantly different in the pooled analyses except the acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study); nitrosamine breakdown products higher in 3 cross-sectional analyses, which make it difficult to distinguish exposure from vaping from earlier tobacco use, while a randomised trial and a cross-over study suggest levels might fall to those of people who use no nicotine; metals mostly higher; carbon monoxide: no pooled analysis, but some interventional studies of people who switched completely suggested exposure might fall to levels similar to non-use.

evidence.locator: Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Evidence reviewed, 5th to 7th paragraphs; Implications › Vaping reduces toxicant exposure compared with cigarette smoking; Methodological improvements needed; Improvements in definitions needed, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review states that studies used a range of definitions, with some classing people who vape and smoke, vape occasionally or vape daily as one group; that studies with more than one time point mostly explored acute exposure (single use to 7 days) or followed people for 8 days to 12 months, so findings on vaping for more than 12 months could not be summarised; and that few studies could be pooled. Its implications: compared with smoking, vaping leads to a substantial reduction in biomarkers of toxicant exposure associated with cigarette smoking, but the degree of any residual risk remains unclear, mainly because comparisons are lacking between people who smoked for many years and have quit and now vape and those who have quit and do not vape, and with people who have never smoked or vaped; past tobacco use can greatly affect many of the biomarkers and most people who vape smoked for many years before; and no difference between people who vape and people who use no nicotine could reflect insensitive measures, background exposure, or relatively similar exposure between people who only vape and people who use no nicotine.

evidence.extracted: The review states that in its meta-analyses many findings were from tobacco industry-funded randomised trials conducted in confinement (closed settings such as research centres or hospitals) for periods of up to 7 days, and that future research needs to include more independent research on biomarkers of exposure in people who vape, people who smoke and people who use no tobacco or nicotine, outside confinement and with longer follow-up. evidence.locator: Chapter 8: Biomarkers of potential harm › Main findings › Issues caused by differences between studies, 1st paragraph; Inflammation; Endothelial function, last paragraph; Implications › Need for methodological improvements and longer term studies, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Need to distinguish between biomarkers of potential harm from smoking or vaping from other sources, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review covered 41 studies (43 publications) of oxidative stress, inflammation, endothelial function and platelet activation; most assessed acute vaping effects and most had methodological concerns. Inflammation: pooled cross-sectional studies showed lower blood C-reactive protein and sICAM-1 in people who vape than in people who smoke, but controlled and longitudinal studies did not confirm this. Endothelial function: acute sessions of vaping (with and without nicotine) and of smoking produced similar short-term reductions in flow-mediated dilation, while a single randomised trial found that switching from smoking to vaping for 4 weeks significantly improved it; the review writes that acute vaping might cause endothelial dysfunction as much as acute smoking, and that switching might improve endothelial function in the longer term. It concludes that most studies in the chapter cannot inform medium or long term risks through these biomarkers, and that studies are needed with people who use no nicotine as a comparison group and longer follow-up.

evidence.locator: Chapter 9: Cancers › Main findings › Toxicants and carcinogens; Cancer risks; Inflammation and oxidative stress; Existing or previous cancer conditions; Cell and animal studies; Implications › Longer follow up periods are needed
evidence.extracted: The review's cancer chapter calls the exposure-biomarker studies conclusive evidence that vaping generally leads to lower exposure to many of the carcinogens responsible for the health risks of smoking (exposure, not cancer). It adds that the National Academies found no available evidence on whether the chemicals in vaping aerosols or vaping behaviour were associated with cancer risk relative to smoking or non-use; that evidence on inflammation and oxidative stress is insufficient for conclusions; that no study assessed people with an existing or previous cancer; and that cell and animal studies suggest vaping aerosols are not benign for people who have never smoked while also suggesting alterations in gene expression to a lower extent than tobacco smoke, though translating such studies to human risk is challenging. Its implications: studies of exposure biomarkers need longer follow-up to tell whether vaping reduces cancer risk compared with smoking.

evidence.locator: Chapter 11: Cardiovascular diseases › Main findings › Heart rate; Blood pressure; Peripheral resistance and arterial stiffness; Comparisons with other reports, 1st paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph; Implications, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review concludes that the extent to which vaping presents a risk for cardiovascular health remains uncertain, but that based on the toxicant profile in vaping products and aerosols the risk is expected to be much less than that of cigarette smoking (an expectation, not a measured rate). It states that, as in 2018, there is still no available evidence on whether vaping is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis; that 27 of the 41 included studies were cross-over or acute exposure studies, which cannot answer questions about the cardiovascular health outcomes most relevant to public health; and that studies comparing rates of cardiovascular diseases between non-users, users of tobacco and users of nicotine vaping products are needed. Measured: immediately after use vaping increased heart rate less than smoking; in pooled cross-sectional studies of longer vaping (at least 3 months or one year) people who vaped had lower blood pressure than people who smoked and no difference from people who neither vaped nor smoked; the longest follow-up of arterial stiffness after switching was 4 months.

evidence.locator: Summary page › Chapter 16 › introductory paragraphs, 2nd paragraph; Evidence statements, 1st paragraph; Chapter 1 › Objective of the report, 1st paragraph; Issues addressed, 3rd paragraph and its list; Authors and citation. Main findings page › 1. The review, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review's closing chapter states that, despite the increase in research on vaping since 2015, weaknesses in the choice of assessments and biomarkers, populations, groups studied and exposure, and study designs all limit the conclusions that can be drawn. Its 61 evidence statements broadly follow the National Academies' definitions of level of evidence, and the authors write that, as the National Academies noted, the framework is a guide and a great deal of expert judgement, here by the report's co-authors, is involved. The scope left out two questions: vaping and later smoking (a Cochrane review of people under 30 was examining it) and the effectiveness of vaping for stopping smoking (covered in the series' previous report and by a Cochrane living review). The report is the eighth in a series described as independent and commissioned by Public Health England and then the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities; it was led by academics at King's College London with international collaborators (eight authors are named); the pages read carry no competing-interest statement.

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Methods, 1st paragraph; Evidence Review: Results › Comparison of Toxic Levels in E-Cigarettes and Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes, 3rd to 6th paragraphs and Synthesis
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, four studies compared emissions from e-cigarettes and combustible cigarettes (three laboratory studies and one comparison based on published literature). Using published data and assuming 15 puffs equal one cigarette, selected toxic compounds in smoke were 9- to 450-fold higher than in aerosol (Goniewicz et al., 2014). Of 150 chemicals examined, about 100 were detected in smoke and 16 were generated by one e-cigarette, and toxicants were 82% to more than 99% lower per puff in the aerosol depending on the list and puffing method (Margham et al., 2016). Smoke held about 1,500 times more harmful and potentially harmful constituents than aerosol or room air (Tayyarah and Long, 2014). Of 11 metals with smoke data, the aerosol of one cartomizer was higher for four (aluminium, iron, nickel, sodium), within the smoke range for five and lower for two (Williams et al., 2013). The committee's synthesis: aerosol is substantially less complex than smoke and, except for nicotine, exposure to potentially toxic substances under typical conditions of use is significantly lower (substantial evidence, Conclusion 5-3). The studies are laboratory measurements, not measurements in people.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 18 (Harm Reduction)

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched from Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes to E-Cigarettes › Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure, 2nd to 11th paragraphs (Cravo; 5-day study; Goniewicz; McRobbie; Shahab); Synthesis; Conclusion 18-1
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, studies that followed people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes lasted from 5 days to 8 months; examples: a 12-week trial of 420 people (urinary biomarkers of benzene, acrolein and a nitrosamine fell); a 5-day trial of 105 people (urinary biomarkers 29% to 95% lower in those who switched partly or completely; exhaled carbon monoxide down 88% to 89% in the groups that switched completely or stopped all nicotine); 20 people over 2 weeks (a nitrosamine breakdown product, NNAL, down 57% after 1 week and 64% after 2 weeks); and 40 people over 4 weeks (carbon monoxide down 80% in those who only vaped and 52% in those who also smoked). One cross-sectional study compared 181 people who had used these products for a long time, in five groups: nitrosamine and volatile organic compound breakdown products were lower in people who only vaped, or only used nicotine replacement, than in people who smoked, and similar in people who smoked only, vaped and smoked, or used nicotine replacement and smoked (Shahab et al., 2017). Synthesis: all studies showed significantly reduced biomarkers of exposure to potentially toxic chemicals in people who switched, and nicotine intake in people who had stopped smoking and were experienced at vaping was comparable to that from cigarettes. Conclusion 18-1: conclusive evidence that completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens (the committee's judgment).
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 18 (Harm Reduction)

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Methods, 2nd paragraph; Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched… › Health Risk Profile (Carnevale; Cibella; Flouris; Wadia), Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure (Martin), Toxicity in In Vitro and Animal Studies, 1st paragraph; Synthesis (after the animal studies); Conclusion 18-2
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, the committee found 15 longitudinal observational and cross-over studies of health outcomes in people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes (follow-up from single sessions to about two years; several retrospective record reviews). Examples: a one-year randomised trial of 300 people found no significant differences in lung-function indexes between groups defined by what people did after the trial began, except one flow measure (forced expiratory flow 25-75%) that rose in those who quit smoking, with cough, phlegm and breathlessness falling over follow-up (Cibella et al., 2016); in 15 people white blood cell counts rose after cigarettes but not after e-cigarettes in 30-minute sessions (Flouris et al., 2012); in a cross-over study of 20 adults who smoked and 20 who did not, acute use of either product changed markers of oxidative stress and blood-vessel function, with flow-mediated dilation and vitamin E effects not statistically different between the products and the e-cigarette showing a lesser effect on three other markers (Carnevale et al., 2016); and gingival inflammation increased in 20 people after 2 weeks of vaping instead of smoking (Wadia et al., 2016). A cross-sectional study, a design the Methods say was left out of the 15, compared nasal biopsies from 12 people who vaped, 14 who smoked and 13 who did neither: immune genes suppressed in people who smoked were also suppressed in people who vaped, with more gene changes and stronger suppression (Martin et al., 2016). In cell studies 21 of 27, and in animal studies 3 of 5, favoured e-cigarettes as less harmful than cigarettes and none found them more harmful than cigarettes. Synthesis: health effects of e-cigarettes are still not well understood but current evidence points to them being less harmful than cigarettes; all but one of the human studies showed significant short-term improvements in people who switched, though most studies were small; some studies found similar harm and none found e-cigarettes more harmful among people who switched to exclusive e-cigarette use; whether e-cigarettes reduce health risk still needs support from epidemiological studies and randomised trials. Conclusion 18-2: substantial evidence that completely switching from regular cigarette use to e-cigarettes results in reduced short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems (the committee's judgment).
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 18 (Harm Reduction)

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › opening section, 4th paragraph; Evidence Review: Levels of Evidence Available, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: As described in the chapter's opening, the committee writes that e-cigarettes have not been theoretically or experimentally proven to be safe, and that the evidence reviewed in the report suggests they may be less harmful than combustible cigarettes in at least some scenarios. It adds that, because the efficacy of e-cigarettes to actually reduce harm remains unclear, some researchers have raised concerns, citing McKee and Capewell (2015): continued use of a substance with its own potential health risks (including uncertainty about long-term risks), a possible increase in use of conventional tobacco products through starting and relapse, and questionable terms of engagement with the tobacco industry. The chapter states that epidemiological studies and randomised trials of the long-term health effects of exclusive e-cigarette use would give the strongest evidence of harm reduction and that, in their absence, the committee looks at biomarkers of disease and exposure levels. The chapter gives no overall figure for how much less harmful e-cigarettes are. The McKee and Capewell article itself (a BMJ Analysis) is anchored separately in this claim.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 18 (Harm Reduction)

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Use E-Cigarettes Concurrently with Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes (Dual Users) › Synthesis; Conclusions 18-3 and 18-4
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, for people who keep smoking while also using e-cigarettes (dual use) the committee found limited evidence on patterns of use and a lack of evidence on exposure and health outcomes among those who do not reduce their smoking. People with dual use did not on average smoke fewer cigarettes than people who smoked only, although e-cigarettes may help some of them maintain a reduction in smoking; the committee writes that it is very unlikely that people who do not reduce smoking after starting e-cigarettes will reduce the health risks of smoking, and that they may be exposed to additional adverse effects of e-cigarettes. Conclusion 18-3: no available evidence whether or not long-term dual use changes illness or death compared with smoking only. Conclusion 18-4: insufficient evidence that e-cigarette use changes short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems in people who continue to smoke. These are the committee's judgments.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 18 (Harm Reduction)

evidence.locator: Opening section (before the first heading), 1st and 2nd paragraphs; References 1 to 3
evidence.extracted: The editorial states that in July 2013 a group of 12 experts rated the relative harm of 12 nicotine-containing products on 14 criteria for harm to self and others (reference 1, Nutt et al., 2014, not read), concluding that combustible cigarettes were the most harmful and e-cigarettes substantially less harmful, and that the result was repeated in the popular media as e-cigarettes being 95% less risky or 95% less harmful than combustible cigarettes. It adds that the authors of the 2013 work noted as a limitation the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most of the criteria (quoted from page 224 of that paper); that Public Health England and the Royal College of Physicians endorsed and publicised the assertion; that senior Public Health England staff emphasised the evidence underlying the figure despite its being lacking; and that much was written questioning the figure's validity in 2014 to 2016 (no source cited for the last two). All of this is the authors' account: none of the originals was read.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC6951374

evidence.locator: Today's Electronic Cigarettes Are Different, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors argue that products today differ from those of July 2013 to the extent that the 2013 estimate, even if valid then, can no longer apply: many devices reach a power output 10 to 20 times that of most over-the-counter 2013 models and so make more aerosol, exposing the person vaping to more nicotine and other toxicants and people nearby to more of any harmful aerosol constituents, and raising the chance of malfunction; there are thousands of flavours whose lung toxicity is unknown; and liquids with protonated nicotine (nicotine salt) are widely marketed and, relative to free-base nicotine, are less aversive to inhale, which the authors say allows higher nicotine concentrations and likely more dependence. No source is cited in the text for the statements on power, flavours or dependence; reference 4 (Jackler and Ramamurthi, 2019, not read) is cited for the marketing of protonated nicotine liquids and the 'nicotine arms race'; the online Appendix A, a nonexhaustive list of evidence of harm, was not read.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC6951374

evidence.locator: Second headed section (harm to cells), 1st paragraph; third headed section (harm in people), 1st paragraph; references 5 and 6
evidence.extracted: The authors state that e-cigarette aerosols contain toxicants and are harmful to living cells in vitro and in vivo (volatile aldehydes, carcinogenic furans, chloropropanols and acetal compounds are named) and that animals exposed to aerosol show adverse effects, including in cardiovascular models (no source cited). For people they cite one report of airway epithelial injury in healthy young adults who smoked cigarettes occasionally and used an e-cigarette with or without nicotine (two randomised trials, Chaumont et al., 2019); state without a citation that wheezing has been associated with use and that heart rate, blood pressure and platelet activation rise while flow-mediated dilation and heart rate variability fall; and cite a one-page item in a journal supplement (reference 6, a conference abstract by its citation), which they call a preliminary report, for a possibly higher risk of heart attack and coronary artery disease in people who vape. The section headings state harm categorically; the conclusion speaks of potential harm.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC6951374

evidence.locator: Electronic Cigarettes Increase Smoking Risk, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors quote the National Academies' conclusion of substantial evidence that e-cigarette use raises the risk of ever using cigarettes among young people and young adults, and argue that, to the extent that first use of e-cigarettes causes later smoking in someone who would otherwise never have smoked, vaping could be considered as harmful as smoking for that person. The statement is conditional on causation and concerns a person who would not otherwise have smoked, not the comparison of vaping with smoking in people who already smoke.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC6951374

evidence.locator: Electronic Cigarette Aerosol Is Not Harmless, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors argue that differences in toxicant content between aerosol and smoke, by themselves, cannot show lesser lethality, because toxicity depends on the extent and mode of use; that propylene glycol is toxic when injected over days and that aerosols containing it and glycerol cause inflammation in human lungs (no source cited); and that, because the toxicants sometimes differ, so might the diseases. They also state that there is little doubt that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, largely absent from the aerosol, and that what diseases they may die of, and whether use hastens death, will be part of the evidence needed for valid risk estimates. The editorial offers no estimate of the size of the difference.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC6951374

evidence.locator: Conclusions; Call to Action
evidence.extracted: Conclusion: the 2013 estimate, which lacked evidence, cannot be valid today and should not be relied upon further; future estimates should rest on the evidence now available and be revised as evidence accrues. The call to action calls the 95% safer estimate a factoid, unreliable information repeated until accepted as fact, and asks readers to highlight its unreliable provenance, the changes in devices and liquids, the accumulation of evidence of potential harm, the increased prevalence of use and the growing evidence that e-cigarette use is associated with later smoking. The editorial gives no alternative figure and does not weigh the evidence on lower toxicant exposure in people who switch: it is an argument, with no data, search or appraisal of the studies it cites.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC6951374

evidence.locator: Acknowledgments; Conflicts of Interests
evidence.extracted: Funding as printed: US National Institutes of Health grants and the Center for Tobacco Products of the US Food and Drug Administration; the sponsor had no role in the preparation of the work. Interests as printed: two authors are paid consultants in litigation against the tobacco industry and are named on a patent for a device that measures the puffing behaviour of people who use electronic cigarettes; one of them has also, since September 2019, been a consultant in litigation against the electronic cigarette industry; another author reports personal fees from Hydra Biosciences LLC and Sanofi SA and non-financial support from GlaxoSmithKline Pharmaceuticals, outside the submitted work. No tobacco or vape industry funding of the editorial is stated.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC6951374

evidence.locator: Abstract › Data sources, Data synthesis, Registration; Methods › 1st paragraph; Top-up review; Inclusion and exclusion criteria, 1st paragraph; Risk of bias assessment; Integrated data analysis › GRADE assessment, Data synthesis; Discussion › 3rd paragraph, last sentence
evidence.extracted: The Australian review combines an umbrella review of 8 major independent reviews published 2017 to 2021 with a top-up systematic review (searched July 2020, for studies published July 2017 to July 2020), 400 publications in all; the systematic review is registered in PROSPERO and labelled prospective, but its protocol was posted on 31 August 2020, after the search; the top-up studies were appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools and the evidence graded with GRADE and the National Academies framework. It is based on work commissioned by the Australian Department of Health. It looked at the health effects of e-cigarettes in people and excluded animal, in vitro and biomarker studies as outside its scope, so, on the editors' reading, the biomarker evidence on which the UK review's conclusion on relative harm mainly rests was not counted (the Australian authors note that the UK review focused on comparing e-cigarettes with smoking and on biomarkers).
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC10952413

evidence.locator: Results › Health outcomes, Box 3, rows 'Cardiovascular disease (21)', 'Cancer (1)' and 'Respiratory disease (58)'; the three paragraphs after Box 3
evidence.extracted: Australian review, Box 3 (health outcome, number of studies): cardiovascular disease (21 studies): clinical outcomes such as heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death, and subclinical atherosclerosis: no available evidence; other cardiovascular outcomes in people who smoke: moderate evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes acutely increase heart rate, blood pressure and arterial stiffness, limited evidence of endothelial dysfunction and limited evidence that long-term nicotine e-cigarette use after switching from smoking reduces blood pressure; in people who do not smoke, insufficient evidence. Cancer (1 study): invasive cancer and pre-cancer outcomes: no available evidence. Respiratory disease (58 studies): asthma, bronchitis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: insufficient evidence in people who smoke and none for people who do not; reduced exacerbations or progression in people who smoke and switch: insufficient evidence. The review states that evidence is insufficient or unavailable on cardiovascular disease, cancer, respiratory conditions other than lung injury and most other conditions, and rated the certainty of evidence for clinical and subclinical outcomes low or very low.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC10952413

evidence.locator: Limitations, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review states that e-cigarettes are relatively new, diverse and changing rapidly, that long-term evidence is unavailable and that the products studied do not necessarily reflect current options (limited information on newer nicotine salt products). It describes confounding between the effects of e-cigarette use and of smoking as a major problem that statistical adjustment is unlikely to fully overcome, particularly for the health conditions most affected by smoking, because older people who vape generally smoke regularly, are trying to quit or have quit, while younger people who vape often do not smoke regularly; it concludes that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to quantify the effects of e-cigarettes and that people neither smoking nor using e-cigarettes should be the main comparison group. Statements that e-cigarettes are safer than smoking, and terms such as tobacco harm reduction, may be useful when discussing the minority of people who smoke who use e-cigarettes to quit completely but are not applicable to people who do not smoke; comparisons with the effects of smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC10952413

evidence.locator: Limitations, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review rated the certainty of evidence very low for most clinical and subclinical outcomes. It notes that the tobacco and related industries can influence research, so its risk-of-bias assessment took account of competing interests such as financial support from tobacco or pharmaceutical industries; it writes that risks of bias were noted across health outcomes, but significant concerns in other domains meant they were unlikely to have large effects on its interpretation or the overall certainty of evidence. It states that it applies the precautionary principle (exposure to an agent with uncertain effects to be avoided), which it considers appropriate when serious adverse impacts are scientifically plausible, particularly those affecting future generations. Products not reported as nicotine or non-nicotine were assumed to be largely nicotine e-cigarettes (Box 3 note).
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC10952413

evidence.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review states that a key finding of its synthesis was the general paucity of evidence on the effects of nicotine and non-nicotine e-cigarettes on many major clinical outcomes, including cancer, cardiovascular, metabolic, mental health, developmental, reproductive and neurological outcomes (other than seizures). It describes an English review it found after its search (reference 40, the UK review of 2022) as noting the lack of direct evidence on major clinical outcomes and that most serious adverse events were infrequent, as focusing on comparing the effects of e-cigarette use with those of smoking and on biomarkers, and as generally finding more favourable results for e-cigarettes than for cigarettes. It concludes that its findings concur broadly with those of other major reviews, including that the direct impact of e-cigarettes on clinical disease outcomes is largely unknown.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC10952413

evidence.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review notes that in many countries dual smoking and e-cigarette use is the most frequent pattern of e-cigarette use and that the direct health impact of dual use is unknown. It writes that e-cigarettes may be beneficial for people who smoke who use them to quit completely and promptly, but that the limited evidence, their risks, uncertainty about effects on major clinical outcomes and continued smoking by most people who use them leave their overall safety and efficacy unclear. Its conclusions: strong or conclusive evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes can be harmful to health, particularly for people who do not smoke and for children and adolescents (a statement not framed against smoking); evidence for effects on most important health outcomes uncertain; people who smoke and switch completely and promptly may benefit.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC10952413

evidence.locator: Results › Smoking behaviour, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Box 4, row 'Smoking uptake (28)'; Discussion, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Meta-analyses of 25 longitudinal studies found strong evidence that young people who have never smoked and who use e-cigarettes are about three times as likely as those who do not to start smoking tobacco and to go on to smoke regularly (residual confounding cannot be excluded; the review deemed the link likely causal on Bradford-Hill criteria); limited evidence that people who had stopped smoking and use e-cigarettes are about twice as likely to resume smoking. The review names this, with poisoning, dependence (addiction) and toxicity from inhalation, among the risks that disproportionately affect people who do not smoke and young people. This concerns the harm of starting to smoke, a different comparison from vaping against smoking, and the UK review left it out of its scope.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC10952413

evidence.locator: Acknowledgements, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Competing interests; Methods, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Funding and interests as printed: the review was conducted as part of an independent programme examining the health impacts of e-cigarettes, funded by the Australian Department of Health and the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC); the report on which the article is based was reviewed by members of the NHMRC Electronic Cigarettes Working Committee and staff of the Australian Department of Health and went through an independent methodological review as part of standard NHMRC processes; competing interests: no relevant disclosures. The work also provided evidence for the 2021 update of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners smoking cessation guidelines and a 2022 statement of the NHMRC Chief Executive Officer.
evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC10952413

evidence.locator: Quality of the evidence, 3rd paragraph, 1st and 2nd sentences; 4th paragraph, last two sentences; reference 12
evidence.extracted: The authors write that the prominently featured 95% less harmful figure in the 2015 English report was not, as might be expected, based on a detailed review of evidence supplemented by modelling, but came from a single meeting of 12 people convened to develop a multicriteria decision analysis model synthesising their opinions on the harms of different nicotine-containing products, summarised in a research paper (Nutt et al., 2014, reference 12, not read). They report that the paper itself conceded, as a limitation, the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most criteria, and that none of the links or limitations they describe is discussed in the 2015 report. This is the authors' account; the 2014 paper and the 2015 report were not read. It matches the account in the 2020 editorial anchored above, which quotes the same limitation, so the two are critics' accounts that agree, not independent checks.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/McKee_2015_ECigaretteEvidenceRockOrSand.pdf (BMJ 2015;351:h4863), read in full

evidence.locator: Quality of the evidence, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; references 13 to 17
evidence.extracted: On the meeting's funding and membership, as the authors report it: one sponsor, a company called EuroSwiss Health, is one of several companies registered at one address near Geneva with the same chief executive, who is reported to have received funding from British American Tobacco for a book on nicotine as harm reduction (the book states that its conclusions were developed independently of the company) and who endorsed that company's public health credentials in its 2013 sustainability report; a supporting organisation, Lega Italiana Anti Fumo, had as chief scientific adviser one of the 12 attendees, who declared funding from an e-cigarette manufacturer but not funding he is reported elsewhere to have received from Philip Morris International. The rationale for choosing the panel is not given; it included several known e-cigarette advocates, some declaring industry funding in the paper, and some people not known for expertise in tobacco control; Public Health England's tobacco lead attended. The authors quote the paper's statement that the sponsor had no role in any stage of the process or in the writing and was not present at the workshop. The ties are sourced to a company register entry, two Tobacco Tactics web pages, the book and a company report (none read) and are worded as reported; the article does not claim that they changed the ratings. Recorded as a reason to read the 2014 paper closely, not as evidence about harm.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/McKee_2015_ECigaretteEvidenceRockOrSand.pdf (BMJ 2015;351:h4863), read in full

evidence.locator: Quality of the evidence, 2nd paragraph (begins on p. 1); reference 11
evidence.extracted: The authors argue that where risks are uncertain the precautionary principle should apply, so that, without scientific consensus that a substance is not harmful to the public, the burden of proof lies with those taking an action; that the report's headline message, widely quoted in the media, that best estimates show e-cigarettes to be 95% less harmful to health than cigarettes seemingly left little room for uncertainty about long-term risks; and that the report did not cite a 2014 systematic review (Pisinger and Døssing, reference 11, not read) that found serious methodological problems in many of its 76 studies, a third (34%) published by authors with conflicts of interest, and concluded that no firm conclusions on safety could be drawn, while adding that e-cigarettes could hardly be considered free of harm.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/McKee_2015_ECigaretteEvidenceRockOrSand.pdf (BMJ 2015;351:h4863), read in full

evidence.locator: Defining the role of e-cigarettes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; references 8 and 9
evidence.extracted: The authors describe two sides that compare with different references: supporters focus on people who already smoke and compare e-cigarettes with smoking, while those concerned about uptake by people who would not otherwise smoke and about long-term effects argue that, although e-cigarettes lack some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes, such as tar, they contain others, such as formaldehyde (a carcinogen) and diverse flavourings, so non-smoking should also be a comparison. They add that reduced smoking, as opposed to quitting, may not lower the overall risk of death (a 16-year Copenhagen cohort of 19,732 people, reference 8, not read); that two thirds of people who use e-cigarettes also smoke (no source given), a pattern the 2015 report rarely mentions; and that in one cohort dual use among people who vaped daily apparently stayed above 80% after 12 months of follow-up (reference 9, not read).
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/McKee_2015_ECigaretteEvidenceRockOrSand.pdf (BMJ 2015;351:h4863), read in full

evidence.locator: Uncertainty around harms, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Where next for policy on e-cigarettes?, 2nd paragraph (ends on p. 3); Key messages box (page headed Page 4 of 3)
evidence.extracted: The authors state that none of the research so far (in context, on youth uptake and a gateway to smoking) can be considered conclusive and longer-term studies are needed; that the report seemed to equate a lack of evidence of risk to bystanders with evidence of no effect; that it omitted the lack of evidence on the risks of long-term dual use; that perhaps its most striking feature was a consistent adoption of the most optimistic position on limited evidence; and they agree with England's chief medical officer that evidence on the long-term use of e-cigarettes is still lacking. Key messages: Public Health England's endorsement of the safety and efficacy of e-cigarettes rests on uncertain evidence, and public health strategies should follow the precautionary principle until better evidence is available. The article offers no estimate of its own of how much less harmful e-cigarettes are than cigarettes, presents no new data, does not discuss measurements of toxicant exposure or short-term health measures in people who switched from smoking, and reports no reply from the authors of the 2015 report or of the 2014 paper. The National Academies' summary of its concerns (the National Academies anchor above) matches its themes, except relapse, which the article does not mention.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/McKee_2015_ECigaretteEvidenceRockOrSand.pdf (BMJ 2015;351:h4863), read in full

evidence.locator: Author affiliations (p. 1); Competing interests; Provenance and peer review (p. 3)
evidence.extracted: Interests as printed: the authors have read and understood BMJ policy on declaration of interests and have no relevant interests to declare. Provenance: not commissioned; externally peer reviewed. No funding statement is printed. The article is a BMJ Analysis article, not an editorial; its authors are professors of European public health (London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine) and of clinical epidemiology (University of Liverpool).

evidence.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 1st to 4th paragraphs; references 28 to 31
evidence.extracted: In a 2022 commentary on the Australian review, the authors argue that the review did not address relative risk and that a meaningful assessment of the risk of vaping nicotine compares it with the far greater risk of continuing to smoke, because most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods (no source given). They write that harm reduction from vaping rests on substantially lower exposure to toxins and carcinogens in vapour than in smoke (references 28 and 29) and is confirmed by considerably lower biomarkers in the blood, urine and saliva of people who switch (references 30 and 31, which by their titles compare exposure between groups, one of them cross-sectional), and that smoke contains over 7,000 toxic chemicals and solid particles while vaping aerosols generally have fewer than 100 detectable chemicals, most at far lower concentrations (reference 29). None of the cited studies was read. The commentary does not mention the 95% figure, the 2015 report or the 2015 critique.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full

evidence.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 11th and 12th paragraphs; references 49 and 50
evidence.extracted: The authors write that, given the reduced number and dose of carcinogens in vapour, lifetime cancer risk from vaping has been estimated at less than 0.5% of that from smoking (references 49 and 50, which by their titles estimate cancer potency or lung cancer risk from emissions and particle measurements; not read), and that the Cochrane review detected no evidence of harm in studies of up to 2 years, although the studies were few and longer ones are needed. The cancer figure is a modelled estimate from what aerosol contains, not a measured rate of cancer in people who vape.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full

evidence.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 5th to 9th paragraphs; references 32 to 45
evidence.extracted: The commentary grants several limits: the effect of inhaled flavourings is largely unknown and could carry risk, with no harm shown so far and ongoing monitoring needed; most cardiovascular effects of vaping are consistent with those of nicotine (transiently raised pulse and blood pressure, cardiac contractility, arrhythmogenesis), and nicotine may pose some risk in people with existing cardiovascular disease; and human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited. For benefit it cites two studies with sustained falls in blood pressure and one with better vascular function after 4 weeks in people who switched, and improved respiratory symptoms, lung function, asthma, COPD, mucociliary clearance and fewer respiratory infections after switching. Seven of the nine human studies or reviews cited (references 35, 36 and 38 to 42) share authors, by the author lists printed, and the sentence on in vitro and animal studies cites two human studies (references 39 and 40, by their titles) and no animal study.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full

evidence.locator: 5 Net public health effects of vaping, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; references 51 to 54
evidence.extracted: The authors argue that the key public health question is the net population effect, which depends on the harm difference between vaping and smoking, on effectiveness for stopping smoking and on uptake by people who do and do not smoke; they report that numerous modelling studies, with one exception, conclude that benefits considerably exceed harms (one US model, under current patterns of vaping and substitution: 1.8 million premature smoking- and vaping-attributable deaths avoided and 38.9 million life-years gained from 2013 to 2060). As they describe them, these models evaluate net effects under a wide range of assumptions about the reduction in harm compared with smoking, so they take the size of the difference as an input rather than measuring it (editors' reading). None of the models was read.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full

evidence.extracted: No funding statement is printed.
