risk_of_bias.note: The 95% figure began as an expert rating (known here only through the editorial's account); the UK review's pooled biomarker results include many tobacco-industry-funded confinement trials of up to 7 days and most of its studies had methodological concerns; the National Academies' human studies were mostly small and several tested a manufacturer's own product (the chapter does not say who funded them); the editorial, the 2015 analysis and the 2022 commentary appraise nothing (cards sc_eissenberg_2020, sc_mckee_2015 and sc_mendelsohn_2022: overall high) and the Australian review applies a precautionary principle and excluded biomarker studies. The reviews are read as summaries, not at the study level.

inconsistency.note: Counted once, under risk of bias: the sides read a largely shared body of evidence differently and answer different questions (exposure and short-term measures against clinical outcomes and starting to smoke); the exposure findings themselves point the same way.

indirectness.note: The question is lifetime harm (disease and death). What is measured is exposure biomarkers, short-term measurements (single sessions to 12 months in the UK review; to about two years in the National Academies' studies) and expert ratings; products have changed since most of the studies and newer ones are little studied.

imprecision.note: No estimate of harm is pooled, so precision is not rated.

grade.reasoning: Observational, indirect evidence (exposure biomarkers, short-term measurements and expert judgement) starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on the size of the difference, which is what the sources support, with the direction (lower exposure to smoke toxicants) reported beside it. The National Academies' conclusive and substantial ratings concern exposure and short-term outcomes in people who switched completely, not lifetime harm; the UK review's statement is an expert judgment on a body of evidence that reaches only 12 months, as its authors say, and the Australian review's reading rests on a different set of evidence. Overlapping reports are counted once. The 2015 analysis and the 2022 commentary, read in full (McKee & Capewell, 2015; Mendelsohn et al., 2022), add arguments about where the figure came from and which comparison matters, not measurements, and change no rating.

debate.question: How much less harmful than smoking is vaping: does the evidence support the often-quoted figure of at least 95% less harmful (smoking at least 20 times more harmful), and can anyone show the size of the difference yet?
debate.evidence_yes: The UK government-commissioned review (McNeill et al., 2022, King's College London, commissioned by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities) states that, on the evidence it reviewed, its own 2015 estimate that vaping is at least 95% less harmful than smoking remains broadly accurate over the short and medium term, and that it may now be better to say that vaping carries only a small fraction of the risks of smoking. Under that sits its systematic review of exposure biomarkers: against people who smoke, people who vape had lower levels in pooled analyses of nitrosamine breakdown products (58% to 94% lower), of acrolein, acrylonitrile and butadiene breakdown products (71%, 94% and 83% lower) and of blood carboxyhaemoglobin, with nicotine levels not different in people who vaped and smoked at least weekly; the better-run studies of short and medium term effects found no major causes of concern; immediately after use vaping raised heart rate less than smoking; in longer cross-sectional studies blood pressure was lower in people who vaped than in people who smoked; and the review expects cardiovascular risk to be much less than that of smoking from the toxicant profile (an expectation, not a measurement). The National Academies (2018, chapter 18, as the committee describes it) rated as conclusive the evidence that completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens, and as substantial the evidence that completely switching reduces short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems: all but one of the human studies it reviewed, lasting from single sessions to about two years, showed short-term improvement and none found e-cigarettes more harmful among people who switched; laboratory emissions of smoke constituents were 9- to 450-fold higher than of aerosol, toxicants were 82% to more than 99% lower per puff, and 21 of 27 cell studies and 3 of 5 animal studies favoured e-cigarettes. A 2022 commentary on the Australian review (Mendelsohn et al., 2022; no funding statement; interests as printed, in full in the anchor: two of the four authors were or are board members of the Australian Tobacco Harm Reduction Association, a registered health promotion charity that accepted unconditional seed funding from the vape retail industry until March 2019, and both state they have never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies; one is the author of a book titled Stop Smoking Start Vaping; the other two declare no interests) does not mention the 95% figure but argues that a meaningful assessment compares vaping with the far greater risk of continuing to smoke, since most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods. It cites substantially lower exposure to toxins and carcinogens from vapour than from smoke (over 7,000 toxic chemicals in smoke against fewer than 100 detectable chemicals in aerosols, as cited), lower biomarkers in people who switched (cited to two group comparisons of exposure), sustained falls in blood pressure, better vascular function and better respiratory measures in people who switched (seven of the nine human studies or reviews it cites share authors), modelled estimates that lifetime cancer risk from vaping is less than 0.5% of that from smoking, and no evidence of harm in the Cochrane review's few studies of up to 2 years; none of these studies was read. Even the critics grant part of this: the editorial says there is little doubt that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, the Australian review says people who smoke and switch completely and promptly may benefit, and the 2015 analysis grants that e-cigarettes lack some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes, such as tar.
debate.evidence_no: The earliest critique read is a BMJ analysis article published in September 2015, shortly after the English report (McKee & Capewell, 2015; not commissioned; externally peer reviewed; no relevant interests declared; no funding statement). It argues that the prominently featured figure came not from a detailed review of evidence with modelling but from a single meeting of 12 people who built a multicriteria decision analysis model of their opinions on the harms of nicotine-containing products, and that the resulting paper conceded the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most criteria (Nutt et al., 2014, not read); that the chief executive of the meeting's sponsor and the chief scientific adviser of a supporting organisation, who attended, are reported elsewhere to have received tobacco-company funding (sources: a company register, web pages, a book and a company report; the 2014 paper states that its sponsor had no role and was not present); that the panel's selection was not explained and included known e-cigarette advocates; and that the English report discussed none of this. It argues that where risks are uncertain the precautionary principle should apply, with the burden of proof on those who act; that the report did not cite a 2014 systematic review of 76 studies that found serious methodological problems and concluded that no firm conclusions on safety could be drawn; that people who do not smoke should also be a comparison, because e-cigarettes, while lacking some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes such as tar, contain others such as formaldehyde and flavourings; and that dual use matters (two thirds of people who use e-cigarettes also smoke, no source given; above 80% after 12 months among people who vaped daily in one cohort), because cutting down, unlike quitting, may not lower the risk of death. It offers no estimate of its own and presents no data. Five years later a six-author editorial in the American Journal of Public Health (Eissenberg et al., 2020; funding and interests as printed: US National Institutes of Health grants and the FDA Center for Tobacco Products; two authors are paid consultants in litigation against the tobacco industry and named on a patent for a puffing-behaviour device, one of them also a consultant in litigation against the e-cigarette industry since September 2019; one author reports fees from two pharmaceutical companies) argues that the figure came from a July 2013 rating by 12 experts of 12 products on 14 criteria whose own authors listed the lack of hard evidence for most harms of most products on most criteria as a limitation (as the editorial quotes; the 2013 paper was not read), that Public Health England and the Royal College of Physicians nonetheless endorsed it, that devices and liquids have changed (power output 10 to 20 times higher in many devices, thousands of flavours, nicotine salts), that evidence of potential harm from cell, animal and short-term human studies has accumulated, that lower toxicant content in aerosol does not by itself show lower lethality, and that the estimate cannot be valid today; it offers no alternative figure and cites a conference abstract for its heart-attack claim. The Australian review (Banks et al., 2023; funded by the Australian Department of Health and the National Health and Medical Research Council; no relevant disclosures) holds that comparisons with smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes, that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to quantify effects and people who neither smoke nor vape the main comparison group, that evidence on clinical cardiovascular disease and invasive cancer is not available, and that certainty is very low for most clinical and subclinical outcomes; it rates acute rises in heart rate and blood pressure after nicotine e-cigarette use in people who smoke as moderate evidence. The National Academies state that e-cigarettes have not been proven safe, give no overall figure for how much less harmful they are, say that long-term epidemiological studies and randomised trials would be the strongest evidence and are lacking, and describe concerns raised by McKee and Capewell (2015) about continued use of a product with its own risks, more use of conventional tobacco products and engagement with the tobacco industry (their summary matches the themes of that article, described above, except relapse, which it does not mention). The UK review itself says that, against people who use no nicotine, exposure to harmful substances is similar or higher; that the degree of any residual risk remains unclear; that acute vaping might impair blood-vessel function as much as acute smoking; that its findings reach at most 12 months of follow-up; and that vaping is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked. The 2022 commentary on the other side grants that human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited, that nicotine may pose some risk in people with existing cardiovascular disease and that the effects of inhaled flavourings are largely unknown.
debate.neither_can_show: No source read reports how often any disease, or death, occurs in people who only vape compared with people who smoke or who use no nicotine: the UK review could summarise follow-up of no more than 12 months and says the size of any residual risk is unclear; it and the Australian review each report no available evidence on clinical cardiovascular outcomes such as heart attack and stroke, and no evidence on cancer risk relative to smoking or non-use (UK, quoting the National Academies) or on invasive cancer (Australian). The 95% figure was an expert rating across several criteria, not a ratio of disease rates (as the 2020 editorial and the 2015 analysis describe it, two critics' accounts that quote the same limitation; the 2014 paper and the 2015 report were not read, the UK pages read give no basis for the 2015 figure, and no source read reports a reply from the figure's authors to this account), and the UK review's reaffirmation is its own judgment from biomarker evidence, not a measured ratio. A level of a chemical in the body is not a risk: a 90% lower level of a carcinogen breakdown product does not by itself give a 90% lower risk of cancer. Most people who vape smoked for many years before, and past smoking changes many biomarkers; no study read compares people who smoked for many years and quit, whether or not they now vape, or follows people who vape and have never smoked for years, so neither the comparison with smoking nor the comparison with using no nicotine can be made cleanly. The two reviews do not weigh the same evidence: the UK review rests mainly on exposure and potential-harm biomarkers, which the Australian review excluded, while the Australian review asks about clinical outcomes (and about starting to smoke, which the UK review left to a Cochrane review) and takes people who use no nicotine as its main comparison. The 2022 commentary on the Australian review states the same divide from the other side: the comparison that matters is with continuing to smoke, argued from exposure, short-term and modelled evidence, while the 2015 analysis asks for both comparisons; none of these sources brings a measured rate of disease. Both are government-commissioned and both rest on judgment: the UK authors assess an estimate stated in their own earlier series of reports (three of the eight 2022 authors are among the six named for the 2015 report in the editorial's reference list) and say a great deal of expert judgement is involved in their evidence statements; many of their pooled results come from tobacco-industry-funded trials in confinement of up to 7 days, with independent work still called for; the Australian review applies a precautionary principle and assumed products not reported as nicotine or non-nicotine were nicotine e-cigarettes; the editorial argues one side with no data, and its authors' interests are as printed above. In many countries the most frequent pattern is to vape while still smoking (the Australian review), and the National Academies found no evidence on the long-term health of people who do so; products have changed since most of these studies and newer ones are little studied.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). From the sources read so far (the Australian review, the editorial, the 2015 analysis and the 2022 commentary read in full; a National Academies chapter and the UK review's summary pages as they describe the studies), two things are reported consistently: against people who smoke, people who vape have much lower levels of many smoke-related toxicants in the body and, in people who switched completely, better short-term measures of breathing and circulation, although some short-term effects, such as blood-vessel function after a single session, were similar to smoking; and nobody has measured how much the rates of disease and death differ. Against people who use no nicotine, exposure to harmful substances is similar or higher. Neither the lower exposure nor the lack of long-term data is disputed in the sources read; the editorial disputes only that lower toxicant content by itself shows lower lethality. What is disputed is whether the old at least 20-fold figure, which began as an expert rating, can still stand as a size: the UK review says it broadly does for the short and medium term, as its own judgment; the 2015 analysis, the editorial and the Australian review say it cannot be relied on. The strongest argument for the figure is the consistency and size of the exposure reductions across independent pooled analyses and the finding that no study showed more harm in people who switched completely; the strongest against is that none of this is a rate of disease, the longest follow-up summarised was a year, and the pooled evidence rests on measurements of chemicals in the body, some from industry-funded trials. The 2015 analysis and the 2022 commentary, now read in full, do not change this: the first questions where the figure came from and how the meeting behind it was chosen and funded, the second argues for the comparison with smoking from exposure and modelled evidence, and neither brings a measured rate. The editors offer no number: any figure would claim more than the sources show, and both halves belong together: much lower exposure to smoke toxicants than smoking, and not risk-free.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Cohorts that follow people for decades with biologically verified use and count disease and death separately for people who only vape, people who smoke, people who smoked and have quit with and without vaping, people who both smoke and vape, and people who have never used nicotine, reported as absolute risks so that the difference can be read directly; independent biomarker studies outside confinement, with follow-up beyond 12 months and agreed biomarkers and definitions (the UK review's own list); a transparent, repeatable estimate that sets out the outcomes, their weights and the evidence for each, updated for current devices and liquids and pre-registered (as the editorial calls for), produced by a panel chosen by stated rules with declared interests (the 2015 analysis's objection); and trials or natural experiments comparing people who switch completely with people who keep smoking on clinical outcomes. None of the sources read reports any of these: the longest follow-up the UK review could summarise was 12 months and the longest in the National Academies chapter was about two years.

statement: In adults who smoke and had not smoked for at least 2 hours, who were not using nicotine replacement or in a stop-smoking programme and were mostly not trying to quit, in 19 randomized trials pooled from their raw data (a systematic review searched to May 2011; 15 trials with 797 observations for strength of desire to smoke and 17 with 837 for desire to smoke; Haasova et al., 2013), a short bout of exercise, mostly moderate walking or cycling, compared with sitting quietly or a similar passive activity is associated with less desire to smoke rated right afterwards: about 2 points less on a 1-to-7 scale (strength of desire −1.91, 95% CI −2.59 to −1.22; desire to smoke −2.03, −2.60 to −1.46). The abstract calls these standardized mean differences, but the methods compute differences in scale points. Every trial pointed the same way, but the size ranged from a fraction of a point to more than 4 points (I² 92% to 94%), and the three trials that included isometric (muscle-tensing) exercise showed among the smallest effects. Craving was rated only once, immediately or 5 minutes after exercising, so how long the reduction lasts, and whether it helps people stop or stay stopped, were not studied. Participants knew whether they had exercised, the review did not assess the trials' risk of bias, and 17 of the 19 trials list at least one of the review's authors. The review was paid for from internal institutional funds, and its authors report no connection with the tobacco or pharmaceutical industries. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In 19 small studies, people who had not smoked for a few hours rated their urge to smoke lower straight after a short walk or bike ride than after sitting still, by about 2 points on a 7-point scale. Every study found the same direction, but the size varied a lot, and tensing muscles while sitting helped least. The urge was measured only minutes later, people knew whether they had exercised, and no study here checked whether exercise helps people stop smoking.
population: Adults who smoke, abstaining for at least 2 hours in laboratory studies, not using nicotine replacement or in a cessation programme, mostly not trying to quit
exposure: A single short bout of physical activity, mostly moderate walking or cycling (study conditions in the study card)
comparator: Sitting quietly or another passive condition (listening, a video, a cognitive task, body scanning)
outcome: Self-rated strength of desire to smoke and desire to smoke (single 7-point items) immediately or 5 minutes after the bout, adjusted for the rating before
magnitude: Two-stage random-effects IPD meta-analysis: strength of desire −1.91 points (95% CI −2.59 to −1.22), 15 trials, 797 observations, I² 94.2%; desire to smoke −2.03 (−2.60 to −1.46), 17 trials, 837 observations, I² 92.0%. One-stage model: −1.89 and −2.03, with 95% of trials' true effects expected between −3.56 and −0.22 and between −3.45 and −0.62. Single trials −0.22 to −4.54.

risk_of_bias.note: Participants could not be blinded to exercising and the outcome is a self-rating taken minutes later; the trials' risk of bias was not assessed; most trials are by the review's authors.

inconsistency.note: All trials favour exercise, but the size ranges from about 0.2 to 4.5 points (I² 92% to 94%), only partly explained by the kind of exercise.

indirectness.note: Worded for the population and timing studied (temporary abstinence, craving minutes after exercise); quitting is not claimed.

publication_bias.note: Unpublished theses were included and gave similar results; no small-study test; not downgraded.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high. Risk of bias −1 (unblinded self-rated outcome, no appraisal of the trials, trials mostly by the review's authors) and inconsistency −1 (a tenfold range in size) give low. Worded as an association because the size, and how much of it is exercise rather than expectation, are uncertain, although the design is randomized. Status replicated: 19 trials from several research groups point the same way; agreement with an earlier aggregate meta-analysis (Roberts et al., 2012) is not counted as independent because the trials overlap.

statement: In adults who smoked, mostly moderately to heavily, and stopped (12 placebo-controlled trials published from 1984 to 2000, with 15 to 240 people each; a systematic review without pooling, funded by SmithKline Beecham; West & Shiffman, 2001), using nicotine gum (8 trials), a nicotine inhaler (3) or a sublingual nicotine tablet (1) compared with a placebo product is associated with fewer withdrawal symptoms in the first week after stopping: irritability was lower in all 9 trials that reported it, total withdrawal discomfort in 6 of 7, anxiety in 3 of 4 and low mood in the only trial that reported it, while results were mixed for restlessness (2 of 5), poor concentration (5 of 9), sleep disturbance (1 of 2) and hunger (2 of 5). Craving was lower in 7 of 11 trials: in all 4 trials of the inhaler or tablet but in only 3 of the 7 gum trials. The review counted significant results and gives no sizes; where a trial did not report a symptom the table is blank, so non-significant results may be missing. Five trials kept people who had smoked again in their analyses, more people dropped out of the placebo groups in three, and one trial used low-nicotine gum as its comparator. No trial of the lozenge was found, nothing is known beyond the first week, and patches and nasal spray were not included. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In 12 older studies, people who had just stopped smoking were less irritable in the first week if they used nicotine gum, an inhaler or a tablet than if they used a dummy product without nicotine. Most studies also found less overall discomfort and anxiety. Cravings were lower in all the inhaler and tablet studies but in fewer than half of the gum studies. The review only counted which studies found a difference, not how big it was, and a medicine company (SmithKline Beecham) paid for it.
population: Adults who smoked (mostly moderate to heavy smoking), without psychiatric or acute physical illness, who stopped in placebo-controlled trials published 1984 to 2000
exposure: Oral nicotine products: nicotine gum, inhaler or sublingual tablet (study conditions in the study card)
comparator: A placebo product of the same kind (low-nicotine gum in one trial)
outcome: Withdrawal symptoms and craving in the first week of abstinence, counted as significant or not in each trial

risk_of_bias.note: Five trials kept people who smoked again in the analyses, attrition was high and sometimes unequal, one comparator contained nicotine, and blinding was not assessed.

inconsistency.note: Irritability and total discomfort are consistent; the mixed symptoms are reported as mixed.

indirectness.note: Worded for the products, people and first week studied.

imprecision.note: No estimate is claimed; the statement says sizes are unknown.

publication_bias.note: Counts of significant results in published trials, with blanks that may hide unreported null results, in a manufacturer-funded review.

grade.reasoning: Randomized placebo-controlled trials start high. Risk of bias −1 and publication or reporting bias −1 give low. The claim gives directions only; the size of any reduction is unknown. Status replicated: all nine trials that reported irritability, from several groups, agree, as do six of seven for total withdrawal; craving with gum is not replicated (3 of 7).
